items.title: Huntingdon train attacker found guilty of all 14 counts of attempted murder
items.summary: Anthony Williams, 33, is convicted of 10 attacks on a train and four in Peterborough and London.

scraped.title: Huntingdon train knifeman guilty of trying to murder 14 people
scraped.description: Anthony Williams, 33, is convicted of 10 attacks on a train and four in Peterborough and London.
scraped.author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
scraped.h1: Huntingdon train knifeman guilty of trying to murder 14
scraped.body_text:
Anthony Williams, 33, will be sentenced across two days in February

A knifeman has been found guilty of attempting to murder 14 people, including 10 on board a train to London.

Passengers on the Doncaster to King's Cross service fought off Anthony Williams, 33, with a frying pan and a toaster as the attack unfolded on 1 November 2025.

Some hid in toilets and bike racks before the driver was forced to make an unscheduled stop in Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, where Williams was arrested by armed police.

As well as the train attacks, Williams, of Langford Road, Peterborough, was found guilty of attempting to murder four other people in separate incidents and will be sentenced at Cambridge Crown Court on 4 and 5 February.

Jurors deliberated for 15 hours and 53 minutes before delivering seven guilty verdicts, and then returned an hour later to give the final seven.

The judge, Mr Justice Calver KC, said the victims handled themselves with "great dignity throughout" the trial.

Aside from the attack on the LNER train, Williams also attempted to murder a boy and two men in Peterborough on 31 October 2025, and then a teenager on a DLR train in east London hours later.

The defendant, who appeared at court via a video link from a secure hospital, showed little emotion as each verdict was delivered.

Reacting to the verdicts, Ben Samples, of the Crown Prosecution Service, said: "The fact that nobody was killed in his rampage is down to the courage, quick thinking and good fortune of the people he attacked."

This video can not be played

Watch: How knife attack on train unfolded

It has now emerged that in the month before the attacks, Williams twice contacted his GP to say the anti-psychosis drugs he was taking for schizophrenia were not working.

A spokesperson for NHS East of England said it would be investigating the care provided to Williams.

Cambridgeshire Police has also apologised for missed opportunities "that may have prevented" the stabbings.

Assistant Chief Constable Leighton Hammett said an alleged assault in Peterborough on 27 September 2025, several weeks before the train attacks, had been linked to Williams.

Darryl Preston, police and crime commissioner for Cambridgeshire and Peterborough, said two officers faced misconduct proceedings over their handling of the incident and the investigation remained ongoing.

How the Huntingdon train attack unfolded - carriage by carriage

Williams's knife attack on the LNER service began when he stabbed Jonathan Gjoshe – then a Scunthorpe United footballer – at 19:37 GMT.

The defender later informed police his whole arm was "drenched with blood".

Other victims included Scott Bletcher, stabbed six times in his seat as he returned from a Christmas shopping trip.

Bletcher told jurors he thought, "This is what it feels like to die" after being knifed.

The court also heard from Nottingham Forest football fan Stephen Crean, who decided "he had to try to stop" the attack and "launched himself towards and at" Williams.

Crean said Williams asked, "Do you want to die?" as he stabbed him several times.

Stephen Crean told the BBC he felt the knife "twist and turn" in his hand

CCTV footage played to the jury showed LNER staff member Samir Zitouni use a frying pan to fend off Williams.

He said to the knifeman "we love you, we can help you" as he thought it was "better than swearing at him".

After the train stopped, Zitouni fell between the train and the platform. His lungs were punctured and he needed four blood transfusions, chest drains and the assistance of a ventilator.

Having been arrested in Huntingdon railway station's car park, Williams was said to be "acting strangely" and "completely unfazed by what had occurred... he was rocking and laughing".

If you've been a victim of crime, details of help and support are available at BBC Action Line .

One police officer noted he "appeared to be talking to himself" and spoke about the devil.

Consultant forensic psychiatrist Dr Bernard Chin told the trial Williams, who did not give evidence in his defence, was "suffering from an acute relapse of schizophrenia" at the time of the attacks.

Jurors heard Williams had "the delusional premise that his life was at risk by a wide-ranging conspiracy by the devil".

Williams was confronted by staff and passengers using saucepans and kitchen equipment to defend themselves

As well as Gjoshe, Bletcher, Crean, and Zitouni, Williams was also convicted of attempting to murder Raza Aslam, Sachin Balakrishnan, Kevin Deely, Scott Green, Michael Paffett and David Presland on the train.

Williams also attempted to murder Dawid Taborski, William Ogelby and a 14-year-old boy, who cannot be identified, in Peterborough the night before.

The boy, who was about to go trick or treating with a friend, told police: "This random guy… he just pulled out a knife and stabbed me."

He said it "didn't feel like [Williams] was mentally sane. His eyes were wide open, like he was on something."

After those attacks, Williams boarded a London-bound train where he was heard saying: "I am the baddest, no-one is as bad as me".

Williams brandished a knife inside a barber's shop in Peterborough in the build-up to his attacks

A passenger texted British Transport Police (BTP) reporting a male behaving erratically, but the man dropped down on to the tracks at Stevenage and police officers deemed it unsafe to pursue him.

Then, in the early hours of 1 November, Williams sliced the face of teenager Isaiah Idris on a DLR train in east London with a knife.

Idris described how his attacker had repeatedly asked: "Are you beefing the devil?"

Det Supt Sam Blackburn, from BTP, said Williams' offending had sparked "one of the most significant and complex" investigations in the force's history.

"The events that unfolded onboard the train on 1 November were unlike anything previously encountered before, and Anthony Williams created what I can only describe as a terrifying scene of fear and violence."

In Court: Huntingdon Train Attack

Follow all the developments from the trial as they unfold on our BBC podcast In Court

scraped.title: Huntingdon knifeman told doctor psychosis drugs weren't working
scraped.description: Now his trial has concluded over the LNER train attack, we can report Anthony Williams' long history of criminality.
scraped.author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
scraped.h1: Violent knifeman told doctor his psychosis drugs weren't working days before train attack
scraped.body_text:
This video can not be played

Could the Huntingdon train attack have been prevented?

Hurtling along at more than 120mph, passengers on an East Coast Mainline train bound for London King's Cross found themselves caught up in one of the worst acts of violence on Britain's rail network in recent times.

Anthony Williams stabbed 10 people in five minutes on board the train last November, near Huntingdon, in Cambridgeshire, leaving some seriously injured. On Thursday, a jury found him guilty of 14 counts of attempted murder.

It has now emerged that, in the month before that attack, the knifeman had twice contacted his GP to say the anti-psychosis drugs he was taking for schizophrenia were not working.

But he never saw a doctor and did not receive additional mental health treatment.

Now his trial at Cambridge Crown Court is over , BBC News can also report his long history of violent criminality, revealed through old court transcripts we have obtained.

It stretched back two decades. In his teens Williams robbed people at knife point, including on a train. Even after he had started his 25-hour rampage, culminating in the Huntingdon attack, there were potential opportunities to arrest him.

Williams, who was born Anthony Abiola Oluwatuyi in London in 1993, first arrived on the police radar aged 12, when he was excluded from school for arson after setting fire to the toilets.

One acquaintance from the time - who would only speak on condition of anonymity - told BBC News Williams would "turn people's pockets inside out just because he wanted to". They said: "He was a thug who brought a knife to class."

Over the next seven years, he was convicted of 14 further offences, including five thefts, three robberies, and two offences of possession of a knife.

In October 2012, aged 19, he robbed two fellow teenagers of their smartphones at knife point on a train, warning them: "If you tell, I will come back and find you."

Train attacker found guilty of all 14 counts of attempted murder

How the Huntingdon train attack unfolded - carriage by carriage

Williams with a knife in Ritzy barbers in Peterborough the night before the train attack

When he was sentenced for that at Wood Green Crown Court to three and a half years detention in March 2013, the judge referred to his "sorry record of previous convictions".

Williams' barrister, Victoria Kerly, told the court he had mental health problems, adding: "They are things that I have myself experienced with him and they do raise some concerns for me."

By the time Williams appeared at St Albans Crown Court in February 2020 he was a crack cocaine and heroin addict, as well as a drug dealer.

He had been arrested the previous year in possession of heroin, crack cocaine and cannabis, as well as a pair of scales and 12 "burner" phones. Asked about his drug dealing, he told police: "If I don't do it, not good things will happen to me."

He was sentenced to four years in prison, where he was sectioned and held in a psychiatric hospital until his release.

Upon release, he moved to Peterborough to live with his mother and stepfather. At this stage it is unclear exactly what mental health treatment he received there, but the BBC understands that, following last year's train attack, Cambridgeshire and Peterborough NHS Foundation Trust launched an internal review.

On 30 September 2025 - a month before the Huntingdon attack - Williams contacted his GP online about what he described as his "deteriorating mental state", saying his drugs were not working.

This video can not be played

Footage of Williams' arrest and passengers fleeing was shown to the jury

The doctor told him he should be taking 200mg of the Quetiapine he had been prescribed to treat his paranoid schizophrenia, but he was only taking 100mg.

The GP invited him to a meeting on 14 October which he did not attend. Williams contacted the doctor again on 23 October, again saying the medication was ineffective - but he did not respond when the GP tried to get back to him.

In a phone call with a taxi firm on 31 October, the night before the train attack, Williams can be heard apparently speaking to voices in his head, saying things like "devil wanna play", and making strange noises, before then resuming the conversation normally.

Following the attack, Williams told psychiatrists "things were bad" in the days before it.

"I was paranoid people were going to attack me. They were coming for me. I was hearing a lot of voices, feeling a lot of fear," he said. "I just needed to protect myself. It was me or them."

Psychiatrists who assessed Williams after the attack concluded he had been "acutely psychotic".

Dr Bernard Chin said Williams was suffering from "paranoid persecutory delusions" that he was the focus of "an organised conspiracy that came about because of the machinations of the devil".

Following the guilty verdicts, NHS England's East of England division said it would commission an independent investigation into the healthcare provided to Williams "to help identify any opportunities for learning and improvement".

Anthony Williams taking a drink on the train in the middle of his attack

A month before the Huntingdon attack, a man was attacked close to Williams' home.

Two officers from Cambridgeshire Police now face a gross misconduct hearing over their handling of the alleged assault. The Independent Office for Police Conduct said one of the officers allegedly failed to conduct appropriate inquiries and both officers were alleged to have concealed this by falsely claiming no CCTV was available.

Having been in and out of court for two decades, Williams, now 33, continued his violence before boarding the train.

The day before the train attack, on 31 October, Williams carried out three knife attacks in Peterborough, injuring one person. None were recorded on CCTV.

He then went into Ritzy's Barbers in the city, threatening those inside with a knife. That incident was caught on camera. It was reported to police two hours later, but officers did not collect the CCTV until three days later - two days after the Huntingdon train stabbings.

Forensic teams combed the train at Huntingdon station as part of a major investigation

On the morning of the Huntingdon attack, on 1 November, Williams stabbed a teenager on a Docklands Light Railway (DLR) train near Pontoon Dock station, in east London. British Transport Police (BTP) said initial CCTV of the attack was of poor quality.

However, the force tracked the knifeman to nearby Poplar DLR station where officers obtained clearer CCTV images.

Using reactive facial recognition software they generated a match with Williams, who had two addresses recorded on police systems - one in Waltham Cross, in Hertfordshire, the other in Peterborough.

Officers prioritised the Waltham Cross address because there was a "recent financial trace" to it, and it was closer to the DLR attack.

At 6:48pm that day, BTP officers turned up at the address to arrest Williams. But half an hour earlier, at 6:16pm, Williams had left his actual home - in Peterborough - to travel to the station and launch his stabbing spree on a London North Eastern Railway (LNER) train.

BTP Deputy Chief Constable Stuart Cundy said "it was certainly not for want of trying by the officers who responded and commenced our investigation immediately after the attack on the train at Pontoon Dock".

But when it comes to other incidents during Williams' chequered past, whether criminal or health-related, various authorities will now have to assess whether anything could have been done before he boarded that LNER train.

Additional reporting by Robbie Kalus

scraped.h1: Zelensky questions 'strange' Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview
scraped.body_text:
This video can not be played

Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced his frustration with the United States and questioned Donald Trump's relationship with Vladimir Putin in an interview with the BBC.

In a picture posted to Truth Social on Saturday, where Trump and Putin embrace, the US president described his Russian counterpart as "my friend".

"Of course it's up to the President of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky told the BBC's Sarah Rainsford at his office in central Kyiv.

"He [Putin] is an aggressor, and a killer…He can't be a friend. Just cannot be."

scraped.title: ‘I’m no longer a UAE official’: UN hopeful Lana Nusseibeh tries to shake off Sudan record
scraped.description: The US and Russia’s candidate for secretary general is on a charm offensive. Can she overcome London’s resistance to her bid?
scraped.author: https://www.theguardian.com/profile/patrickwintour
scraped.h1: ‘I’m no longer a UAE official’: UN hopeful Lana Nusseibeh tries to shake off Sudan record
scraped.body_text:
The US and Russia’s candidate for secretary general is on a charm offensive. Can she overcome London’s resistance to her bid?

L ana Nusseibeh is in Britain this week, attempting to present herself as a potential future UN secretary general, and shift the focus from her past as a United Arab Emirates diplomat who denied the country’s role in arming a militia accused of war crimes and genocide in Sudan’s four-year civil war.

It is a high-risk strategy that involves meeting ministers, MPs, academics and holding a public event with the UN Association.

Labelled by many British NGOs and others as an apologist for war crimes, Nusseibeh is presenting herself as a skilled diplomat with the network to put the UN back at the centre of mediation, development and human rights.

“These are very geopolitical times,” she said in an interview. “You need a geopolitical secretary general, because the fact is these geopolitical ruptures are not going away. These fissures in the international system are not going to dissolve any time soon.”

Nusseibeh had a setback last Friday, when three permanent members of the UN security council, China, France and the UK , all voted to “discourage” her candidature. The UN’s electoral system requires that she secure nine positive votes from the 15-strong security council, and no discouragement from the permanent five (P5) before being recommended to the UN general assembly.

She has the backing of the US and Russia, and thinks her cause is not lost. “Sometimes, the use of the veto is tactical. Sometimes, it’s a holding position, sometimes it’s a leveraging position. There are a number of different theories”.

The centre of the resistance to Nusseibeh’s candidacy is probably London, and specifically the Foreign Office, the penholder on Sudan at the UN, and this may explain the UK political blitz.

When questioned about her role in Sudan, she asked that her candidacy be seen in the round, highlighting her role in forcing humanitarian aid into Gaza, her support for Afghan women and promoting interfaith tolerance.

“Like every candidate, I come from somewhere, but the independence of the incoming secretary general is the key to their credibility.

“I’ve taken a leave of absence from my role in [the] UAE government in order to independently campaign for this role. But I think that if I was secretary general, Sudan would be the litmus test of success for any incoming secretary because it’s such a horrific humanitarian crisis.”

The war in Sudan, which erupted in April 2023 after a power struggle between the ​military and the Rapid Support Forces, has displaced more than 14 million people and created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. Multiple regional powers, including the UAE , have backed different local proxies since the beginning of the conflict in an attempt to win influence and strategic resources.

The UAE has long been accused of supporting the RSF in Sudan, a charge repeatedly denied by Nusseibeh, who has publicly disputed the findings of UN investigators.

A UN panel of experts suggested last month that the UAE had supplied crucial support to the RSF.

Asked if she regretted dissembling during her time as a diplomat, by denying the UAE had armed the RSF, or her personal role in challenging the UN reports critical of the UAE, Nusseibeh said she regretted that “the Sudanese civil war had continued for so long”.

Nusseibeh added: “But I don’t think saying that is enough for the Sudanese people and the people in the surrounding countries where they’ve also felt the impact of this war, or for the victims of sexual violence and in this conflict, the atrocities committed in El Fasher without accountability, and the use of chemical weapons against the civilian population; all of these are a litany of suffering that has been inflicted on the Sudanese people.”

Asked if the UAE had been supplying weapons to the RSF in a breach of a UN embargo, she replied: “I’m aware of the allegations. I haven’t read the last UN panel of experts report, but I’m not going to comment as I’m no longer a UAE official. In this campaign, I am a secretary general candidate.

“As secretary general, I would fully back the findings of all UN panel of experts reports and I’m aware that I think several countries have been mentioned in various reports.”She later added: “I would call out countries that are supplying arms to any of the parties, including those in the RSF … this needs a process that requires accountability for atrocities that have been committed. That it needs to be a process primarily led by the Sudanese people.”

Nusseibeh said she was willing to take risks to mediate and to put UN values, expertise and its development toolkit at the centre of disputes. Her analysis of contemporary diplomacy was that the world had descended into a default setting of non-cooperation, and the UN needed to restate the case for collaboration between nations as being in the self-interest of everyone.

The UN had been missing from too many conflicts, she argued, and she would set up a mediation board to try to use the full UN toolkit, ranging from confidence-building measures to development to secure peace. “What’s missing is this idea of a secretary general that is a strategist and a mediator-in-chief that is looking at the sort of the blips on the dashboard of conflict and saying, ‘How do we deploy to have maximum impact for most effective use of resource and cost?’ Because resources are not going up, they’re going down. I mean, we’re looking at, since 2010, 40% increase in military spending. So we’re using a lot of hard power as countries and systems to deter, but it’s not actually working.”

That would require some prioritisation at the UN – it has 4,000 different open mandates.

Her intelligence and skills as a diplomat are not in question. However, her track record over Sudan is.

One critic said: “It is a very smart strategic play by the UAE that seeks autocratic capture, and then the asset-stripping of the UN and its standards. The UAE would end the UN’s role on climate. It would be a catastrophe.”

The next security council vote is on Monday. By then some of the backmarkers may have dropped out of the race. The diplomats of the P5 may also be clearer on the flexibility of their mandates, in which case the papal conclave may finally produce white smoke.

scraped.title: Congo Ebola outbreak reaches 12,000 cases as some responders evacuate
scraped.description: As the fast-moving outbreak continues to spread in eastern Congo, fighting between rebels and the army is disrupting efforts to contain the spread of the disease.
scraped.h1: Congo Ebola outbreak reaches 12,000 cases as some responders evacuate
scraped.body_text:
By

The Associated Press

Relatives and healthcare workers prepare to bury a victim of Ebola, in Beni, North Kivu province, Congo, Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026. Sebastien Kitsa Musayi/AP hide caption

BUNIA, Congo — The fast-moving Ebola outbreak in eastern Congo has topped 12,000 confirmed cases, government data showed Thursday, as fighting between rebels and the army disrupts efforts to contain the spread of the disease.

It is the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history and nearly half the 12,021 people confirmed to have the virus have died, according to data from Congo's Ministry of Health. It is also the deadliest of Congo's 17 outbreaks and is on track to surpass the death toll from the West African outbreak that killed 11,000 people between 2014 and 2016.

The outbreak declared in May is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus , for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment. Response teams are battling armed conflict, poor roads and violence from residents fueled by mistrust and misinformation .

Ebola spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of people who are sick or have died from the disease. Containing the disease requires quickly identifying and treating patients in isolation, monitoring people who may have been exposed and safely burying the dead.

Fighting between the army and the Convention pour la révolution populaire rebels resumed Thursday morning in Iga-Barrière, a mining town about 25 kilometers (15 miles) north of Bunia in eastern Congo, sending new waves of displaced people toward the city. Bunia is the capital of northeastern Ituri province and a major hub for the Ebola response.

CRP is one of more than 100 armed groups in eastern Congo, where conflict has created one of the world's most severe humanitarian crises . The group was founded last year by former warlord Thomas Lubanga, who was convicted by the International Criminal Court in 2012 of recruiting children under 15 and using them in fighting.

Fighting between the army and the rebels earlier this week had already prevented teams from reaching some communities, disrupted monitoring of people exposed to the virus and left some treatment centers with fewer staff, Dr. Catherine Smallwood, the World Health Organization's Ebola incident manager, said Wednesday.

Smallwood said that about a dozen people, including two WHO personnel and Congolese health officials, were evacuated to Bunia on Tuesday after three full days trapped in a hospital in Akwe, northeast of the provincial capital, amid intense crossfire.

items.summary: Leader Kim Jong Un reportedly visited facilities that produce nuclear ingredients and called for building more nuclear weapons to cope with threats from the U.S. and South Korea. scraped.title: North Korea's Kim vows to build more nuclear weapons after ignoring Trump's overture
scraped.description: Leader Kim Jong Un reportedly visited facilities that produce nuclear ingredients and called for building more nuclear weapons to cope with threats from the U.S. and South Korea.
scraped.h1: North Korea's Kim vows to build more nuclear weapons after ignoring Trump's overture
scraped.body_text:
By

The Associated Press

In this photo provided by the North Korean government, leader Kim Jong Un inspects a facility the government says is for producing weapons-grade nuclear material at an undisclosed location in North Korea, Monday, Nov. 25, 2026. Korean Central News Agency/Korea News Service via AP hide caption

SEOUL, South Korea — North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited facilities that produce nuclear ingredients and called for building more nuclear weapons, days after ignoring U.S. President Donald Trump's offer to meet during his recent visit to Asia.

Experts say Kim likely wants to show off his evolving nuclear arsenal, the backbone of his authoritarian rule, and reaffirm his rejection of any future talks on dismantling his nuclear program.

The North's official Korean Central News Agency said Thursday that Kim inspected two nuclear materials production factories, one newly inaugurated and the other being expanded. KCNA photos showed Kim and senior military officials walking between dense rows of what appeared to be centrifuges used to produce weapons-grade uranium and touring halls displaying what were believed to be warheads. Some of the images were blurred.

KCNA said Kim visited a nuclear-powered equipment production base and a nuclear research institute as well on Wednesday.

North Korea has disclosed a uranium enrichment site a few times since it showed one at its main Yongbyon nuclear complex to visiting American scholars in 2010. North Korea didn't say where the nuclear materials production factories that Kim visited this week are located. In June, when North Korea disclosed parts of a uranium enrichment site while reporting on Kim's visit there, outside experts assessed it was likely an additional uranium enrichment facility at Yongbyon.

Kim justifies nuke program by citing threats from US, South Korea Kim said his latest inspection visit was part of efforts to strengthen North Korea's defense capabilities in response to "variable nuclear threats approaching the Korean Peninsula moment by moment." He accused the U.S. of inciting its regional allies to possess nuclear-powered submarines and committing to sharing its nuclear weapons with them, KCNA said.

"The validity and substantiality of our possession of nuclear weapons and the trend of bolstering up its nuclear capability in quality and quantity are an irreversible reality," Kim said, according to KCNA.

Kim also said the deployment of low-yield battlefield nuclear weapons across multiple domains for various missions is crucial and urgent given North Korea's "inevitable reality facing the border with the most dangerous enemy state," a reference to South Korea. North Korea has in recent years focused on developing such tactical nuclear weapons amid heightened animosity with South Korea.

"Trump has talked about a willingness to meet Kim Jong Un, but the basic U.S. position that North Korea must denuclearize remains unchanged. So Kim Jong Un wants to say 'Look at how powerful we are. Don't talk about denuclearization if you want to meet us,'" said Moon Seong Mook, an analyst for the Seoul-based Korea Research Institute for National Strategy.

Moon said Kim's visit to the nuclear facilities was also likely meant to check on how state objectives on the nuclear program have progressed this year and what future goals must be set ahead of a year-end Workers' Party conference.

South Korea's Defense Ministry said it takes Kim's comments on battlefield nuclear weapons seriously and added that Seoul maintains a firm military readiness against Pyongyang's nuclear threats under an alliance with the U.S. South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff declined to share an analysis of the North Korean nuclear facilities reported by KCNA, calling it confidential information for South Korea and the U.S.

Trump still hopes to meet Kim Trump reiterated his eagerness to restore diplomacy with Kim as he visited China last week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. But a Trump-Kim meeting didn't happen, with Pyongyang not publicly responding to Trump's overture.

In an interview with the New York Post this week, Trump dismissed the suggestion that Kim had rebuffed his outreach, saying, "No, he didn't ignore it. You know, we had many leaders there … There'll be a time when we meet … It was just not really the right time. It was a very busy two-day period."

Trump also claimed he could revive diplomacy with Kim at any time by restarting the exchange of letters they maintained during his first term, although he acknowledged that the two leaders had not corresponded "recently."

Kim has previously said he could return to talks if the U.S. drops its "hostile policy" against his country and respects what he calls the North's status as a nuclear state. Experts say Kim aims to win international recognition as a nuclear state so that he could demand the lifting of international sanctions.

Last week, International Atomic Energy Agency Director General Rafael Grossi assessed North Korea has been expanding its original uranium enrichment facility at Yongbyon, calling the move "a cause for serious concern."

Nuclear weapons can be built using either highly enriched uranium or weapons-grade plutonium, and North Korea has facilities to produce both at Yongbyon. Last year, South Korea's Unification Minister Chung Dong-young said that North Korea was operating four uranium enrichment facilities and that they were running every day.

scraped.h1: Storms disrupt Thanksgiving travel. And, FCC violated ABC's free speech, judge says
scraped.body_text:
By

Brittney Melton

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Severe storms sweeping across the nation threaten to cause widespread travel delays today , as millions of people gather with their loved ones. New York City officials announced that the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been rescheduled to Saturday due to the threat of powerful wind gusts that could reach up to 60 mph. This year marked the 100th procession, and the first time the iconic event is being postponed.

Workers inflate the Spider-Man balloon during Macy's Balloon Inflation 2026 on November 25, 2026 in New York City. Macy's plans to celebrate its 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade with a record 100 inflatables, but forecasted high winds are threatening to ground the giant balloons. Adam Gray/Getty Images hide caption

The Trump administration has proposed new tariffs targeting goods from 14 major U.S. trading partners , including China, Japan and the European Union. Administration officials argue the measures counter unfair foreign trade practices, though critics question their ultimate effectiveness. Proposed rates may reach 40% on Chinese imports, 35% on Vietnamese goods, and 20-25% on products from other targeted nations. Additional tariffs on Brazilian sugar and aircraft are also being suggested.

Federal scientists are testing the air, soil and water in Eastern Iowa for lead contamination after the U.S. Army detonated thousands of pounds of unstable lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown yesterday. Officials said the controlled explosion was the only safe way to dispose of the bomb-making compound.

A federal judge has blocked Trump from challenging the ABC television network's broadcast licenses. U.S. District Court Judge Loren AliKhan ruled that the president retaliating against satire and commentary he dislikes is unconstitutional. AliKhan issued the preliminary injunction yesterday and dismissed the administration's request to throw out ABC and Disney's lawsuit challenging the review of the local license . Licenses typically last eight years and are rarely revoked. AliKhan's decision drew heavily on Trump's public statements and social media posts against ABC and Disney, as well as comments from Brendan Carr, the president's pick for chair of the Federal Communications Commission.

Our brains are wired to seek out newness, and the retail industry is set up to keep us coming back for more as quickly as possible. J Studios/Getty Images hide caption

Holiday shopping season is in full swing. Before you spend, consider if you actually need what's in your cart. Sales are exciting because our brains are wired to seek newness. Retailers capitalize on that urge. To escape the cycle of constantly wanting more, shop intentionally and appreciate what you already own, says Eric Athas, author of Saying No to New . He shares his insights on breaking this cycle and finding joy in your current possessions with Life Kit .

For more guidance on how to reclaim joy without seeking newness, listen to this episode of NPR's Life Kit . Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.

Apple farmers across the Pacific Northwest are ripping out thousands of acres of orchards and grinding trees into mulch because growing the fruit no longer pays. Many say they're being crushed by soaring labor and equipment costs and international tariffs. Even multigenerational growers are leaving land unused rather than hemorrhaging money. Thousands of acres of fruit have been left to rot unpicked on branches, pushing some well-established farms into bankruptcy. Federal farm relief has also largely failed to reach specialty-crop growers. Take a look at photos and videos of affected farms , and read more about how the region that supplies the majority of the U.S.' fresh apples is handling the challenge.

Aaron Rodgers #8 of the Pittsburgh Steelers walks off the field after their 19-16 loss to the Philadelphia Eagles at Lincoln Financial Field on Nov. 22, 2026, in Philadelphia. Emilee Chinn/Getty Images hide caption

items.title: MAC admits that officials incorrectly cost Kent State touchdown with blown call against Eastern Michigan
items.summary: The Mid-American Conference admitted officials erred overturning Kent State's touchdown against Eastern Michigan, citing insufficient video evidence. While the MAC initially accepted the results, they then issued a statement criticizi...

scraped.title: MAC admits that officials incorrectly cost Kent State touchdown with blown call against Eastern Michigan
scraped.description: Kent State football should have beaten Eastern Michigan on a walk-off touchdown catch, the Mid-American Conference admitted, citing insufficient video evidence to overturn.
scraped.author: Ian Miller
scraped.h1: MAC admits that officials incorrectly cost Kent State touchdown with blown call against Eastern Michigan
scraped.body_text:
"A referee gets tough because he's got a whistle. Screw these guys. Like at least the guys in the, at least the guys in Major League Baseball, just big fat guys that wallow around. Now, I think every ref should be suspended for the conduct of others. I hate them, I hate refs, I hate umpires, I hate officials, I hate all of them."

Officiating in college football has become a major, major problem.

Earlier this season, the Michigan Wolverines miraculously escaped against Western Michigan thanks to a controversial second being added to the game clock due to incorrect replay review procedures. While the MAC initially accepted the results, they then issued a statement criticizing how the situation was handled.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

The Big 12 Conference admitted to several officiating mistakes, most of which benefited the BYU Cougars . During their game against Notre Dame, the referees failed to notice that the Irish should have had one second left to try and pull off a comeback win.

CLOCK CONTROVERSY: NCAA SAYS OFFICIALS BOTCHED REPLAY PROTOCOL IN MICHIGAN'S WIN OVER WESTERN MICHIGAN

BYU Cougars quarterback Bear Bachmeier (47) runs the ball defended by Notre Dame Fighting Irish safety Luke Talich (28) during a college football game between the Notre Dame Fighting Irish and the BYU Cougars on October 17, 2026 at LaVell Edwards Stadium in Provo, UT. (Photo by Aaron Baker/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) (Aaron Baker/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

"Following the Big 12's review of the final play of Saturday's Notre Dame-BYU game , it was determined that time remained on the clock when the ball hit the ground and the play was incorrectly cleared by the replay officiating crew," they explained in a statement. "The Conference will conduct a complete review of its end-of-game officiating process in advance of next week's games."

Then there was the inexplicable handling of the end of the BYU-UCF game , where a facemask penalty flag was picked up, and the Knights were incorrectly assessed a 10-second runoff at the end of regulation. Amazingly, the next week, the Cougars were given a touchdown on a fumble recovery that should not have been allowed thanks to a blown whistle.

In the SEC, the Texas-Missouri game featured several contentious calls that went the Longhorns' way, including the most absurd, awarding Arch Manning and Texas a first down on a fumble, though his arm was clearly moving forward. Analysts were so critical of the officiating in that game that they drew a rebuke from Greg Sankey afterward.

Notre Dame-Miami came down to what looked to be a massive touchdown catch for the Irish, waved off as incomplete. Those are just a few examples. And now we have another one. This time, ironically, involving MAC officials.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

During some recent late-night MACtion , a Kent State appeared to come down with a walk-off touchdown catch to beat Eastern Michigan. After an insane five-minute review process, the officials overturned it, based on, well, not much, and handed the win to the Eagles.

THE ABSOLUTE WORST CALL OF THE COLLEGE FOOTBALL SEASON HAPPENED LAST NIGHT WHILE YOU WERE SLEEPING

Kent State Golden Flashes wide receiver Wayne Harris attempts a catch against Ball State Cardinals safety Ashton Whitner in the first half at Scheumann Stadium in Muncie, Ind., on Nov. 5, 2025. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

On Wednesday, the conference admitted that the officials erred in making the call and that Kent State should have won the game.

In a statement, they acknowledged that there was "insufficient video evidence to overturn the ruling on the field."

"The video evidence did not meet the clear and obvious standard required to overturn the ruling on the field," they added. "The decision to overturn the touchdown was incorrect, and the original ruling should have been upheld. The Mid-American Conference recognizes the significance of this error and regrets its impact on the outcome of the game. Our student-athletes, coaches, institutions and fans deserve the highest standards of officiating. The Conference remains committed to those standards and to maintaining the competitive integrity of our contests."

SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER

Kent State head coach Mark Carney told ESPN that he was "heartbroken" by the outcome.

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

"In 25-plus years of playing and coaching college football, I have never felt the disappointment I felt last night postgame," Carney said. "Heartbroken for our players and staff who pour so much of themselves into what we do - especially those playing their last game of college football. We are extremely proud of the way our young men represent Kent State, our football program, and themselves."

Kent State Golden Flashes quarterback Dru DeShields looks for an open receiver during the fourth quarter of an NCAA football game against Miami (OH) at Dix Stadium in Kent, Ohio, on Nov. 17, 2026. (Brian Fisher/Cal Sport Media/Sipa USA via Reuters Connect)

Man, it doesn't get worse than that. Having the outcome of a game be directly affected by the officials making the wrong ruling. You have to feel terrible for Kent State players, fans, and coaches. And frustrating that officiating continues to be such a disaster when there's no excuse for it to be. Gotta be better and let the MACtion dictate the outcome, not the refs.

Ian Miller is a writer at OutKick.

items.summary: Todd Barbee, the voice of Charlie Brown in "A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving," says he got no residuals for decades until SAG-AFTRA renegotiated old contracts. scraped.title: ‘Charlie Brown’ voice actor received zero residuals for nearly 50 years due to banned ’70s contract
scraped.description: Former child actor Todd Barbee, the voice of Charlie Brown in "A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving," says he got no residuals for decades under a 1970s buyout contract.
scraped.author: Stephanie Nolasco
scraped.h1: ‘Charlie Brown’ voice actor received zero residuals for nearly 50 years due to banned ’70s contract
scraped.body_text:
This material may not be published, broadcast, rewritten, or redistributed. ©2026 FOX News Network, LLC. All rights reserved. Quotes displayed in real-time or delayed by at least 15 minutes. Market data provided by Factset . Powered and implemented by FactSet Digital Solutions . Legal Statement . Mutual Fund and ETF data provided by LSEG .

Former Charlie Brown voice actor Todd Barbee spoke out on "Nostalgia Tonight with Joe Sibilia" about going decades without "Peanuts" residuals under a 1970s buyout contract.

Good grief — it turns out the voice of Charlie Brown didn't even make peanuts in residuals.

Todd Barbee was just 10 when his father's connection to producer Lee Mendelson landed him the iconic role of Charlie Brown in 1973's "A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving." Generations grew up watching his performance on network TV, yet Barbee, now 63, revealed to host Joseph Sibilia on his podcast, "Nostalgia Tonight with Joe Sibilia," that he didn’t receive residual checks until about six years ago.

"Aside from the bountiful residuals I'm sure you've collected for the last 50-plus years, what has been the most rewarding part of being a part of the 'Peanuts' legacy?" Sibilia asked Barbee.

‘BRADY BUNCH’ CAST MADE NEARLY NOTHING FROM DECADES OF RERUNS, EVE PLUMB CLAIMS

"A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving" premiered on Nov. 20, 1973. Todd Barbee was about 10 years old when he voiced Charlie Brown in the special. (Allstar Picture Library Ltd / Alamy Stock Photo)

"Well, let me correct you on one front," Barbee replied. "... We were actually under an old contractual relationship from the '70s that is no longer allowed by Screen Actors Guild and AFTRA, which is American Federation of Television and Radio Artists. The contract was a buyout, and that is not allowed by the unions anymore. I think it was overturned in the '80s."

"So, we did not receive any residuals at all," Barbee noted. "In fact, I didn't receive a single residual until about six years ago."

The initial gig paid "pretty handsomely" at the time "in 1970 dollars." He used his paycheck to help his mother buy the house that she still lives in to this day after his parents divorced . However, he didn't see any residual checks, no matter how massive the special became as a holiday tradition.

WATCH: CHARLIE BROWN VOICE ACTOR TODD BARBEE WENT DECADES WITHOUT ‘PEANUTS’ RESIDUALS

"Peanuts" made its debut on Oct. 2, 1950. The travails of the "little round-headed kid" Charlie Brown and his pals eventually ran in more than 2,600 newspapers, reaching millions of readers in 75 countries.

According to Barbee, everything changed after union renegotiations around streaming rights following Apple TV's acquisition of the "Peanuts" catalog. The streaming service obtained the exclusive rights to the "Peanuts" catalog in 2020, including the widely beloved "A Charlie Brown Christmas."

Charles M. Schulz holds a drawing of Charlie Brown, one of his "Peanuts" characters, on Jan. 1, 1962. (CBS via Getty Images)

"... During the big strike, writers' strike and everything that happened about five or six years ago ... Screen Actors Guild renegotiated some of these things," said Barbee. "And they determined Apple TV right now actually has the entire 'Peanuts' catalog . And what Screen Actors did [was say], 'Look, that doesn't have anything to do with these old contracts. That was for broadcast television. You're a streaming service. And as such, you need to pay these people current residuals.'"

The SAG-AFTRA logo is displayed outside the National Headquarters on Wilshire Boulevard during the actors strike in Los Angeles on Oct. 24, 2023. (AFP via Getty Images)

"So now, I do make some money every year off all the specials," said Barbee. "It's not giant amounts of money, but you know, it's significant. And I look forward to getting that check every year."

Fox News Digital reached out to SAG-AFTRA, Apple and Peanuts Worldwide for comment.

The Charlie Brown balloon is seen during the 90th annual Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade on Nov. 24, 2016, in New York City. (WireImage)

From 1972 to 1974, Barbee voiced several "Peanuts" characters across five different TV specials. Because producers insisted on authentic kids' voices rather than adults imitating children, every young actor received what Barbee called a "Dear John" letter.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"One of the things that's very interesting about all the characters in 'Peanuts' is you got a 'Dear John' letter the moment your voice changed," he told Sibilia.

Snoopy, Lucy, Charlie Brown and Linus stand in a line in a 1968 drawing from Charles Schulz's comic strip "Peanuts." (Getty Images)

"... They were looking for kids whose voices hadn't changed. They really ... had an idea about the intonation and the character of the voice, and it needed to be a kid's voice. And so, there was an audition. They wanted to do a number of specials at the same time, one after the other. They were talking about Thanksgiving and Easter and others."

"I was about 10 then, maybe a little bit more than 10 years old," Barbee reflected. "And the next thing you know, they had me voice for Charlie Brown and they selected me."

After leaving acting behind, Barbee pivoted to graphic, commercial, and site design in the San Francisco Bay Area . In a fitting nod to "Peanuts" creator Charles Schulz, an avid hockey fan who built a famous ice arena in Santa Rosa, Barbee's design work includes the site plan for Fisherman's Wharf's observation wheel and its inaugural seasonal outdoor ice-skating rink.

In the 1973 special, Charlie Brown wants to do something special for the gang, but the dinner he arranges becomes a disaster when caterers Snoopy and Woodstock prepare toast and popcorn as the main dish. Humiliated, it will take all of Marcie's persuasive powers to salvage the holiday for Charlie Brown. (Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)

For decades, Barbee kept his "Peanuts" past under wraps.

"People that were in the know knew about it," said Barbee. "But many of the people that I've known throughout the years, I never talked about it. It was just not a big thing for me. It was just kind of a funny insider thing. And if you really got to know me, you either found out, maybe I dropped it or a friend mentioned it."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Peanuts characters appear in a scene from "A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving," 1973. (Alamy)

Today, Barbee says the greatest reward is knowing his voice still brings holiday cheer into homes across America half a century later.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"... I get this fan mail with frequency still to this day," said Barbee. "And that just always puts a smile on my face because I realize how this character has influenced so many people's lives over the course of, you know, half a century. And there's something very, you know, very special about that. So, it's cool to be involved in that."

Snoopy and Woodstock appear with Charlie Brown in "A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving," 1973. (Alamy)

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

items.title: Aaron Rodgers vs Mike McCarthy: Timeline of beloved Super Bowl duo's descent into baffling NFL soap opera

scraped.title: Aaron Rodgers vs Mike McCarthy: Timeline of beloved Super Bowl duo's descent into baffling NFL soap opera
scraped.description: Aaron Rodgers accused Steelers coach Mike McCarthy of falling asleep in meetings and holding a grudge over his Packers firing. The Steelers have released Rodgers.
scraped.author: Jackson Thompson
scraped.h1: Aaron Rodgers vs Mike McCarthy: Timeline of beloved Super Bowl duo's descent into baffling NFL soap opera
scraped.body_text:
Famed NFL agent Leigh Steinberg says Aaron Rodgers’ public rupture with the Pittsburgh Steelers and his allegations against coach Mike McCarthy could prompt questions from agents advising potential players about joining the Steelers.

Aaron Rodgers and Mike McCarthy made divorce the theme of this Thanksgiving.

Rodgers accused McCarthy of falling asleep in meetings, skipping team activities and harboring resentment over his 2018 firing in Green Bay, even claiming he had covered for his coach for years. McCarthy denied holding a grudge against Rodgers.

But long before their reunion in Pittsburgh imploded, the two men shared a complicated 21-year history that included an NFL Draft rejection, a Super Bowl triumph, public confrontations and seemingly heartfelt reconciliations.

Alex Smith, Antrel Rolle, Aaron Rodgers, Braylon Edwards, Ronnie Brown and Cedric Benson pose during the 70th NFL Draft on April 23, 2005, at the Jacob K. Javits Convention Center in New York City. (Getty Images)

Before Rodgers ever played a snap in the NFL, McCarthy helped deny him a childhood dream.

McCarthy was the San Francisco 49ers' offensive coordinator in 2005 and helped evaluate Rodgers, a Northern California native and lifelong 49ers fan who starred at nearby Cal. But San Francisco selected Utah quarterback Alex Smith with the No. 1 overall pick, leaving Rodgers to endure an infamous, hours-long wait in the NFL Draft green room on national television before Green Bay selected him 24th overall.

Former 49ers head coach Mike Nolan acknowledged McCarthy's influence on the decision in Ian O'Connor's 2024 biography of Rodgers, saying McCarthy was the most knowledgeable member of the group when it came to quarterbacks.

"It was my first head coaching job, and Mike was the guy who was most knowledgeable on quarterbacks of the group, and as a group that's what we decided. … He had a lot to do with picking the other one (Smith), and in the end he got the one (Rodgers) that he didn't pick, and it elevated his career," Nolan said in the book.

McCarthy was quoted in the book giving his side of that story, saying "I was the offensive coordinator, and I did express my opinion. But those selections are made by a group of people, and ultimately a lot of information goes into that. I thought both quarterbacks were very young, talented guys who you could win with."

Aaron Rodgers and head coach Mike McCarthy of the Green Bay Packers look on after the NFL Hall of Fame Game against the Indianapolis Colts was cancelled due to poor field conditions at Tom Benson Hall of Fame Stadium in Canton, Ohio, on Aug. 7, 2016. (Getty Images)

Three years after passing on Rodgers in the draft, McCarthy publicly admitted he had misjudged the quarterback.

"Aaron is extremely athletic," McCarthy said . "I've said it before, I did not evaluate him properly in the movement phase at quarterback coming out of college. I did not see the athletic ability that I have been able to witness since we've worked together."

McCarthy had spent the previous two seasons developing Rodgers and was preparing him to take over as the Packers' starting quarterback following Brett Favre's retirement.

But when Favre came out of retirement that summer, Rodgers suddenly found himself facing the possibility of having to compete for the job he had waited three years to inherit.

Rodgers was met with boos from some Packers fans during the team's annual Family Night scrimmage on Aug. 3, the night Favre returned to Green Bay.

"They're booing all of us, probably me mostly. So, yeah, I take it personally," Rodgers told reporters that night.

McCarthy met privately with Favre for several hours the following evening. The meeting ran so long that the Packers canceled a scheduled press conference, and a team spokesman said McCarthy had not spoken to Rodgers that day, according to The Washington Post.

But McCarthy ultimately stood by Rodgers, publicly defending the young quarterback amid the controversy.

"He's done everything right to this point, so why would I put him through any more than he needs to go through?" McCarthy told reporters Aug. 5.

Favre was traded to the New York Jets the following day.

Green Bay Packers quarterback Aaron Rodgers and linebacker Clay Matthews celebrate after the Packers defeated the Pittsburgh Steelers 31-25 in Super Bowl XLV in Arlington, Texas on Feb. 6, 2011. (TIMOTHY A. CLARY/AFP via Getty Images)

Around 2010, Rodgers and McCarthy began meeting privately on Thursday afternoons after practice.

"Some about football, but a lot about life. Lessons, thoughts and dreams," Rodgers recalled in December 2018, shortly after McCarthy was fired.

McCarthy reminisced about those meetings during a 2019 interview with NFL.com, acknowledging how much he missed those conversations. In November 2022, McCarthy revealed how those encounters would typically end.

"And it always ended with a hug and, 'I love ya,'" McCarthy told reporters.

Their partnership reached its pinnacle on Feb. 6, 2011, when the Packers defeated, ironically, the Pittsburgh Steelers 31-25 in Super Bowl XLV.

Rodgers was named Super Bowl MVP the following night. Neither man has won another Super Bowl since.

McCarthy briefly handed his play-calling duties over to Rodgers during the Packers' 2011 regular-season finale against the Detroit Lions.

With Rodgers resting ahead of the playoffs, McCarthy tasked him with calling the offensive plays for backup quarterback Matt Flynn throughout the first half. Flynn went on to set franchise records with 480 passing yards and six touchdown passes in a 45-41 victory.

"He's got a bright future in coaching," McCarthy joked to reporters the following day.

McCarthy expanded Rodgers' play-calling responsibilities in 2012 before scaling them back in 2013, determining he had put too much responsibility on his quarterback.

The tension between Rodgers and McCarthy spilled onto the sideline on national television during a Week 3 game against the Cincinnati Bengals.

Rodgers had been stopped at the 1-yard line on a third-down scramble in the second quarter, prompting the Packers to settle for a field goal. An animated Rodgers confronted McCarthy on the sideline over his play-calling, and Fox's television cameras captured defensive tackle B.J. Raji extending an arm between the two men as they argued.

The Packers went on to squander a 16-point second-half lead, losing 34-30. Rodgers threw multiple interceptions in a regular-season game for the first time in nearly three years.

McCarthy downplayed the confrontation after the game, even suggesting Rodgers' willingness to express his frustration was something he admired about his quarterback.

"He's competitive, man. That's what I love about him. I don't think it's that big of a deal," McCarthy told reporters.

Rodgers confirmed the argument was over play-calling but refused to disclose the specifics of what was said between them.

Two days later, Rodgers addressed the incident again on his ESPN Milwaukee radio show, insisting the two had resolved their disagreement and emphasizing their history of success and mutual respect.

"There's a lot of competitiveness and passion on both sides, and every now and then that passion collides," Rodgers said.

As Rodgers and McCarthy prepared for another playoff run after a 12-4 regular season, some of Rodgers' teammates revealed how intense the relationship between the two men could get behind the scenes.

Former Packers backup quarterback Seneca Wallace told NFL.com that McCarthy would become frustrated when Rodgers independently called plays without his knowledge, sometimes prompting the coach to blurt out, "What the f---? What is he calling?"

Wallace estimated Rodgers could call 40 of the team's 70 offensive plays in a given game.

"Coach McCarthy always talks about alpha dogs — well, they're like two alphas going at it," Packers linebacker and close friend of Rodgers, A.J. Hawk, told NFL.com.

Rodgers suggested their occasional confrontations had only strengthened their relationship.

"But I think we both know each other well enough that the last thing that either of us want to do is disrespect each other," Rodgers said.

Speculation about tension between Rodgers and McCarthy became so widespread among Packers fans that the two agreed to give separate interviews to Green Bay Press-Gazette reporter Pete Dougherty to address their relationship.

The Packers had just finished their worst regular season in total offense since Rodgers became the starting quarterback.

"This is the most frustrated I've ever seen him," McCarthy said of Rodgers.

McCarthy suggested he was uniquely positioned to challenge Rodgers, while the quarterback maintained their disagreements had always been constructive and rooted in mutual respect.

Just two days after the interviews were published, television cameras captured Rodgers and McCarthy sharing playful moments on the sideline during a 35-18 playoff victory over Washington.

McCarthy acknowledged the significance of those images amid the speculation about their relationship.

"I enjoy our relationship. I guess it's good everybody got to see good clips," McCarthy told reporters the following day.

Four years after their heated sideline confrontation in Cincinnati, another game against the Bengals produced an awkward moment between Rodgers and McCarthy.

CBS cameras captured Rodgers looking toward the Packers' sideline and appearing to mouth, "Stupid f---ing call!" twice after taking a sack late in the third quarter.

When Rodgers arrived for his individual meeting with McCarthy the following week, the head coach already had footage of the incident pulled up on a screen, according to a November 2018 Sports Illustrated report.

McCarthy had worked with Rodgers early in his career on controlling his body language when frustrated. More than a decade into their partnership, the two reportedly revisited those lessons.

The Packers ultimately won the game 27-24 in overtime.

Alex Van Pelt, who played quarterback at the University of Pittsburgh while McCarthy was a graduate assistant there, had served as Rodgers' quarterbacks coach since 2014.

But McCarthy brought in a new quarterbacks coach after Van Pelt's contract expired following the 2017 season.

Rodgers publicly expressed his displeasure during an appearance on ESPN Radio's "Golic and Wingo" during Super Bowl week.

"Well, my quarterback coach didn't get retained," Rodgers said. "I thought that was an interesting change, really without consulting me."

McCarthy had previously characterized Van Pelt's departure as a mutual decision, as the assistant had aspirations of becoming an offensive coordinator.

However, several sources close to the Packers later told Sports Illustrated they believed McCarthy had come to view Van Pelt as a threat because of his close relationship with Rodgers.

Van Pelt ultimately took another quarterbacks coaching job with the Cincinnati Bengals.

Rodgers was celebrating his 35th birthday on Dec. 2, 2018, when he learned McCarthy had been fired.

"I was at home with my folks in town for my birthday. When I found out, I was as shocked as many of you were, I'm sure," Rodgers said .

The Packers had fallen to 4-7-1 after an embarrassing 20-17 home loss to the Arizona Cardinals earlier that day, prompting the franchise to abruptly end McCarthy's tenure after nearly 13 seasons.

Fox Sports' Terry Bradshaw suggested Rodgers was responsible for McCarthy's firing, an assertion Packers president Mark Murphy publicly disputed the following day.

Rodgers also pushed back against speculation about their deteriorating relationship, revealing that he and McCarthy had actually spent more time talking to each other during the 2018 season than in previous years.

But it was a chance encounter outside Lambeau Field in the days after the firing that made the separation particularly surreal for Rodgers.

While driving to work one morning, Rodgers looked across an intersection and spotted McCarthy sitting in his truck. Rodgers recounted the encounter to reporters four years later.

"It was a really weird feeling," Rodgers said, recalling the moment it finally sank in that McCarthy was no longer his head coach.

Four months after their separation, an extensive Bleacher Report investigation exposed alleged dysfunction between Rodgers and McCarthy dating back to the early years of their partnership.

The report alleged McCarthy would miss team meetings to receive massages in his office, while Rodgers had privately questioned his coach's football intelligence and harbored resentment dating back to the 2005 NFL Draft.

McCarthy denied the massage allegations, calling them "utterly absurd."

But perhaps McCarthy's most prominent defender was Rodgers himself.

During an April 8 appearance on ESPN Wisconsin's "Wilde and Tausch," Rodgers characterized the report as a "smear attack," defended McCarthy's character and revealed he regretted publicly criticizing his coach's game plan after the Buffalo game the previous September.

"I love Mike McCarthy. He's a great man, he has a huge heart," Rodgers said.

Rodgers also pointed to his decision to sign a four-year, $134 million contract extension in August 2018 as evidence against the notion that he disliked playing for McCarthy, arguing he had anticipated spending the remainder of his career with him.

Rodgers even made a personal plea to Packers fans in Green Bay, where McCarthy and his family still lived.

"If you see Mike, shake his hand. Tell him thanks for the memories. Tell him thanks for the coaching job that he did," Rodgers said.

Four years after their separation, McCarthy returned to Lambeau Field to face Rodgers as opponents for the first time, with McCarthy coaching the Dallas Cowboys .

The two men had been communicating more frequently over the previous year, according to Rodgers, and exchanged compliments publicly in the days leading up to the game.

Television cameras captured Rodgers and McCarthy sharing an embrace during pregame warmups. But Rodgers later revealed the two had arranged a private meeting well before kickoff, away from the cameras.

"We had a really beautiful conversation before the game. Just really thankful for that time," Rodgers told reporters.

Rodgers then led the Packers to a 31-28 overtime victory, overcoming a 14-point fourth-quarter deficit and spoiling McCarthy's return to Green Bay.

After the game, an emotional and visibly frustrated McCarthy was less inclined to discuss the sentimental significance of his homecoming.

"I'm not trying to be rude, (but) I'm humble pied out," McCarthy told reporters.

Rodgers played a role in bringing McCarthy back to the NFL.

Following Mike Tomlin's resignation in January, Rodgers encouraged Steelers general manager Omar Khan to interview McCarthy, later admitting he had not expected the franchise to seriously consider his former coach.

During a March 4 appearance on ESPN's "The Pat McAfee Show," Rodgers learned that McAfee had also vouched for McCarthy after working with him as a regular guest on the show throughout the 2025 season. McAfee specifically praised McCarthy's preparation and work ethic.

Rodgers agreed with McAfee's assessment and expressed enthusiasm about McCarthy returning to his hometown to coach the Steelers.

Meanwhile, McCarthy returned to Lambeau Field on March 23 for a tribute to former Packers president Bob Harlan. When asked about potentially coaching Rodgers again, McCarthy said, "Yes, it would be a great story."

Rodgers officially re-signed with Pittsburgh on May 18, committing to playing his final NFL season under McCarthy.

Rodgers revealed two days later that sitting in McCarthy's first morning meeting had transported him back to being a 22-year-old quarterback in Green Bay.

"It's like a pinch-me moment," Rodgers said.

However, Rodgers acknowledged that McCarthy had changed aspects of his offense during their eight years apart and indicated there were certain elements of his coach's play-calling terminology he would push back on.

Just six months after describing his reunion with McCarthy as a "pinch-me moment," Rodgers publicly aired grievances against his longtime coach that dated back more than a decade.

The Steelers announced late Tuesday night that Rodgers would be inactive for Friday's game against the Denver Broncos in favor of Mason Rudolph. Rodgers claimed he learned of the decision during a phone conversation with teammate Pat Freiermuth, not from McCarthy himself.

During an explosive appearance on ESPN's "The Pat McAfee Show" the following afternoon, Rodgers accused McCarthy of repeatedly falling asleep in meetings, missing walkthroughs and failing to adequately prepare for games.

Rodgers said one of the breaking points came during halftime of Pittsburgh's 19-16 loss to the Philadelphia Eagles on Sunday, when McCarthy mistakenly broke down the team's huddle by saying, "One, two, three, Packers."

But Rodgers' allegations extended well beyond their brief reunion in Pittsburgh. The quarterback claimed similar issues had persisted throughout much of their time together in Green Bay.

"I covered for him for a lot of years and we worked around it," Rodgers said.

Rodgers also alleged McCarthy had privately expressed resentment over his firing in Green Bay eight years earlier, believing Rodgers was responsible for it.

Ultimately, the relationship came to a head over the same issue that had repeatedly generated friction between the two men over the previous 15 years: play-calling.

Rodgers said he told McCarthy the Steelers would be better off with someone else calling offensive plays and asked to be released if the team was unwilling to make that change.

The Steelers officially released Rodgers on Wednesday afternoon.

McCarthy subsequently told reporters the quarterback had issued an ultimatum that was "clearly out of his job description." He acknowledged the embarrassing halftime incident in Philadelphia but denied harboring a grudge against Rodgers over his departure from Green Bay.

After 21 years, two franchises and a Super Bowl championship together, McCarthy was once again the coach who decided to move forward without Aaron Rodgers.

items.title: Trump to visit Arizona manufacturer of semiconductor chips
items.summary: President Trump will visit the Phoenix TSMC facility, one of the largest manufacturers of advanced chips, including Nvidia's.

scraped.title: Trump to visit Arizona manufacturer of semiconductor chips, including Nvidia's
scraped.description: President Trump will visit the Phoenix TSMC facility, one of the largest manufacturers of advanced chips, including Nvidia's.
scraped.h1: Trump to visit Arizona manufacturer of semiconductor chips, including Nvidia's
scraped.body_text:
Watch CBS News

November 26, 2026 / 4:46 PM EST / CBS News

A White House official said Thursday that President Trump is planning to visit the groundbreaking of a Phoenix facility for a manufacturer of semiconductor chips, including for Nvidia, a trip that comes as the company is under increasing scrutiny for the president's involvement in reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO after he had an affair with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy.

On Dec. 4, Mr. Trump will tour and deliver remarks at the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) facility in Phoenix, Arizona, a White House official confirmed Thursday. The Taiwan-based company has been expanding in Arizona since 2020, according to the company's website , and next week's visit will be to the latest expansion of its facilities.

The official said the new expansion is expected to fund more than 10,000 direct jobs and another 11,000 indirect jobs in the surrounding community.

It's unclear whether Arizona Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs or the state's Democratic Sens. Mark Kelly and Ruben Gallego would attend the event next week.

The planned visit comes amid scrutiny of Nvidia, one of the world's most valuable companies, with its high-powered chips emerging as integral to the race for AI dominance between the U.S. and China. Co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang earlier this month resigned after the news broke of his alleged affair with Alice Huang, a former top executive at Singapore-based tech firm Megaspeed and who U.S. intelligence agencies suspected of spying for China . China has denied it.

Mr. Trump advocated for Jensen Huang to be reinstated at Nvidia, with an official saying earlier this week that reinstating him would "preserve America's technological edge over China, strengthen our national security" and ensure the future of AI will be built in the U.S. Sources also told CBS News that Mr. Trump was privately concerned about the broader implications for the U.S. economy should Nvidia's value collapse.

Nvidia's board reinstated Huang on Monday , and Mr. Trump touted his return in a social media post shortly afterward.

scraped.title: Trump spends Thanksgiving at golf club, accuses Commerce Department of releasing "fake economic numbers"
scraped.description: President Trump demanded an investigation into the Commerce Department's recent revising of the GDP, which happens routinely.
scraped.h1: Trump spends Thanksgiving at golf club, accuses Commerce Department of releasing "fake economic numbers"
scraped.body_text:
Watch CBS News

November 26, 2026 / 2:49 PM EST / CBS News

President Trump is spending Thanksgiving in Florida, where he had a policy meeting early Thursday morning and then headed to his golf club nearby.

He and first lady Melania Trump, who are staying at Mar-a-Lago, are planning to call U.S. service members on Thursday evening.

On Thursday morning, Mr. Trump posted a holiday message on social media, wishing a happy Thanksgiving to the "American patriots who have worked so hard to make our country great!" He continued in the lengthy post to wish a happy Thanksgiving to several others with whom he has grievances, including the Commerce Department, immigrants, "the radical far left" and more.

Mr. Trump claimed that before the midterm elections where Republicans suffered heavy losses , there were "fake Economic Numbers" released. Mr. Trump cited the Commerce Department on Wednesday revising the gross domestic product in the third quarter to 4.3% on an annual basis, up from a prior estimate of 3.4%. The Commerce Department regularly updates its monthly economic data to improve its accuracy, including not just the GDP but also the monthly employment data.

Although he did not present any evidence, the president demanded an investigation.

Mr. Trump also wished a happy holiday to "all of those people that have worked so hard to bring our Country to the Radical Far Left, those that are looking to change our Court System to that of Sharia, those who want to redistribute Property, so that all of the hardworking people that have built up, over a lifetime, a certain Wealth, will now be forced to distribute it throughout the Country, even to those who refuse to work."

The president continued his post with messages about the Somali community, deported immigrants and those who he believes do not appreciate the White House ballroom he is constructing.

Overnight, Mr. Trump praised the Army's controlled detonation of about five tons of degraded lead azide in Iowa, blaming former President Barack Obama for the situation and writing that no "carcinogens were released into beautiful Iowa air." Although Mr. Trump and other administration officials have praised the detonation, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News on Wednesday that prior to it, there was a chaotic lead-up inside the Trump administration about what went wrong and who was to blame for not elevating the matter to senior officials sooner.

On Wednesday night, Mr. Trump met with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, and the pair issued a joint statement describing the meeting as "very impactful" and focused on Russia, Ukraine and Iran. The statement said they discussed "the importance of Russia avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war."

Mr. Trump earlier in the week continued the annual tradition of pardoning turkeys, sending turkeys named Freedom and Feathers to live on a farm in Texas. Melania Trump, meanwhile, welcomed the official White House Christmas tree on Monday.

Kristin Brown contributed to this report.
