items.title: Thanksgiving storm damages buildings, floods streets, causes power outages
items.summary: Gov. Kathy Hochul's office declared a State of Emergency on Thanksgiving.

scraped.title: New York declares emergency as Thanksgiving storm threatens East Coast
scraped.description: Gov. Kathy Hochul's office declared a State of Emergency on Thanksgiving.
scraped.author: ABC News
scraped.h1: New York declares emergency as Thanksgiving storm threatens East Coast
scraped.body_text:
Gov. Kathy Hochul's office declared a State of Emergency on Thanksgiving.

Strong winds ripped the roof off a building in Maryland, as an extreme storm began to move up the East Coast on Thanksgiving morning.

Swaths of southern New York, including New York City and Long Island, were placed under a State of Emergency ahead of the storm that prompted the postponement of the annual Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade and moved Philadelphia's parade indoors.

"The weather system is expected to bring severe impacts statewide -- including damaging winds and heavy rainfall -- which could lead to travel disruptions and power outages," Gov. Kathy Hochul's office said in a press release announcing the emergency on Wednesday.

Hochul's office said coastal flooding was possible in New York City and parts of Long Island, "with locally major flooding possible on Long Island’s South Shore Back Bays."

New York City officials, the NYPD and Macy's decided on Wednesday to postpone the annual Thanksgiving Day parade due to unfavorable weather , the department store said.

More than 724,000 utility customers in nine states from West Virginia to New Jersey were without electrical power on Thursday afternoon, according to PowerOutage.us , which tracks power outages across the nation. The outages include more than 200,000 utility customers in Virginia, more than 151,000 in Maryland, 70,000 in Pennsylvania and 60,000 in New Jersey, according to the website.

More than 50 million people across the East are under wind alerts Thursday afternoon as a powerful storm takes shape on the East Coast, bringing the threat of damaging winds, significant coastal flooding and heavy rain to the area.

High wind warnings are in effect from Philadelphia to New York City, across much of eastern Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Long Island and up through Cape Cod.

A wind gust of 74 mph was recorded on Snowshoe, West Virginia. A 65 mph gust was reported in Barnegat Light, New Jersey, while a 64 mph gust was recorded in Wildwood Crest, New Jersey. Atlantic City recorded a wind gust of 58 mph on Thursday.

The storm has dumped more than 9 inches of rain on Emerald Isle, North Carolina, and 8.64 inches in Cape Carteret, North Carolina.

There is a level 2 of 4 threat for flash flooding from Virginia to New York City on Thursday, with widespread 2 to 3 inches of rain expected. Heavy rain from Philadelphia to New York will continue through Thursday evening and then move northward into Hartford, Connecticut, and Boston Thursday night.

The strong winds were already wreaking havoc in Maryland, where powerful easterly winds ripped the roof off a building in Ocean City around 8:24 a.m. on Thursday, according to police.

No injuries were immediately reported.

ABC affiliate station WJLA recorded footage of the roof blowing off what appeared to be a multi-story apartment building.

In Rockville, Maryland, firefighters rescued two people after the facade of a commercial building they were in collapsed amid high winds on Thursday morning, according to the Montgomery County Fire and Rescue Service.

A Level 2 of 4 flood threat is in place from Norfolk and Richmond, Virginia, to Washington, D.C., Baltimore, Philadelphia and New York City, as well as the southern Hudson Valley. The heavy rain could lead to isolated instances of flash flooding throughout the day.

The heaviest rain so far has hit coastal North Carolina. Wilmington had already recorded 4 inches of rain by sunrise, while areas farther north around Emerald Isle and Morehead City had seen 5 to 7 inches over the past 24 hours.

Raleigh was under a flash flood warning Thursday morning as heavy rain pounded the city overnight.

Heavy rain is forecast to arrive in New York City between 3 p.m. and 9 p.m.

There is also a slight chance of an isolated tornado in coastal North Carolina, Virginia and Maryland, along with the possibility of severe thunderstorm wind gusts.

But damaging winds are expected even outside of thunderstorms. As the storm moves north along the East Coast, wind gusts of 50 to 70 mph could affect millions of people in the nation's most populated corridor.

The combination of heavy rain and powerful winds could bring down trees and power lines across parts of the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast, potentially causing power outages. The conditions could also disrupt travel on roads and in the air, as well as Thanksgiving preparations for millions of people.

Coastal flooding is another major threat Thursday, with moderate to major high tide flooding expected from coastal Virginia to New York.

According to NOAA, tides above 8 feet can cause severe flooding, including structural damage and widespread roadway flooding. Cape May Harbor, New Jersey, could reach its record of 9.4 feet as could the Delaware Bay at Lewes, Delaware. Ocean City, Maryland, could also see a new record high tide on Thursday, around 6 feet.

As water levels rise further above that threshold, vulnerable homes and businesses could be severely damaged or destroyed. Numerous roads could become impassable, some neighborhoods could be isolated, and floodwaters could pose a danger to anyone attempting to cross them on foot or in a vehicle.

Rain is expected to reach Boston around 5 p.m. Thursday and continue until approximately 2 a.m. Friday.

Windy conditions will continue Friday, though they are expected to be much less extreme. Much of the Interstate 95 corridor is forecast to be dry.

By Saturday, conditions are expected to improve in time for the rescheduled Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade. Skies are forecast to be dry, with wind gusts between 20 and 25 mph — below the threshold for grounding the large balloons.

items.summary: Bands from across the country are drumming up support to stay in New York City through the weekend for the now-postponed 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade.

scraped.title: Bands drum up support so the show goes on for postponed Macy's Thanksgiving parade
scraped.description: Bands from across the country are drumming up support to stay in New York City through the weekend for the now-postponed 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade.
scraped.author: ABC News
scraped.h1: Bands drum up support so the show goes on for postponed Macy's Thanksgiving parade
scraped.body_text:
Some, like University of Alabama, will have to bow out.

Many bands set to perform at the iconic Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York City were forced to quickly adjust schedules, hotel stays and travel after a massive storm prompted organizers to postpone the iconic holiday celebration.

Citing safety concerns for participants and spectators, New York City officials, the NYPD and Macy's announced on Wednesday that the 100th annual parade would instead take place on Saturday.

Despite the weather-induced setback , this once-in-a-lifetime experience for so many of the performing groups meant strategizing and fundraising on social media so that the show could go on.

The Pride of Pearland High School Band and Color Guard from Texas raised enough funds in under 24 hours to help cover the unexpected costs of extra days in the Big Apple. The group's director confirmed to ABC News that band members are ready to go for Saturday, marking their first Macy's parade experience.

Ryan Demkovich, director of bands at Pearland High School, told ABC News he had to act fast to keep his talented squad in town.

"My brain quickly started shifting into trying to figure out what needed to be done to help us be able to stay and not forfeit this once-in-a-lifetime opportunity for these kids," he said. "Thankfully we have an incredible team of people and the best trip company that were instrumental in making this happen."

Demkovich said this trip had been in the works since September of 2025.

"Through the unbelievable generosity of thousands of donors and businesses we were able to raise over $350,000 to make this a reality," he said of the community's support.

The biggest challenge facing many groups that traveled in for the festivities was "finding the hotel and transportation accommodations for a group that largely exceeds 500," according to Demkovich.

"The most helpful thing was the incredible generosity of our incredible Pearland and Houston communities, in addition to the people all over the country who gave to make this dream a reality," he said. "Even people on the street in New York were giving kids cash once they heard the news."

He added, "Life throws curveballs at us all the time and some things are just out of our control. Choosing the right attitude and opting to turn a negative into a positive situation is making all the difference in the ability to make this positively memorable for everyone involved."

Other groups like the Concord Community High School's Marching Minutemen of Elkhart, Indiana, were already planning to be in New York through the weekend.

"The band was already scheduled to be in the New York area through Saturday, so the students are able to take part in the rescheduled parade," Bryan Golden, Concord High School director of music, said in an announcement on Facebook.

"Our students have spent months preparing for this performance, and I’m proud of the work they’ve put in together," Golden continued. "We're excited they still get to march in New York City, and we know there will be a lot of people back home cheering them on."

For others, scheduling conflicts meant they would unfortunately have to miss this year's parade entirely.

The University of Alabama's Million Dollar Band announced that after conversations with the Macy’s parade team, "we made the decision to return to Tuscaloosa to perform in the Iron Bowl and cheer on the Crimson Tide."

"While we are disappointed to miss the parade, we support the decision to postpone this great holiday tradition so it can be conducted safely," the university said in a statement.

The Macy's Thanksgiving parade is now scheduled to begin at 8:30 a.m. ET on Saturday.

items.title: Report: CIA tortured more people with waterboarding than US agency admitted
items.summary: A New York Times report lends credence to long-held belief that torture method was more widely used than acknowledged.

scraped.title: Report: CIA tortured more people with waterboarding than US agency admitted
scraped.description: A New York Times report lends credence to long-held belief that torture method was more widely used than acknowledged.
scraped.author: Brian Osgood
scraped.h1: Report: CIA tortured more people with waterboarding than US agency admitted
scraped.body_text:
A New York Times report lends credence to the long-held belief that the torture method was more widely used than acknowledged.

Save

Share

The New York Times has reported that the United States Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) may have waterboarded more people than it previously admitted.

Wednesday’s report comes after the newspaper filed a lawsuit to obtain material gathered by special prosecutor John Durham, who was appointed in 2008 to investigate the CIA’s activities.

Durham’s probe ended without any criminal charges. But The New York Times obtained partially redacted documents from his investigation, including a summary of a 2012 interview with an interpreter who described a previously unconfirmed act of waterboarding.

The account sheds new light on one of the most infamous methods of torture utilised by the intelligence agency after the attacks on September 11, 2001.

Waterboarding involves restraining a person and pouring water on their face through a cloth, to mimic the experience of drowning.

The CIA called the practice an “enhanced interrogation technique”. As part of the US’s so-called “war on terror”, the agency sent suspects to overseas prisons, known as black sites, where they would be tortured in secret, including through waterboarding.

While the practice was shielded from scrutiny for years, a 2009 executive order eventually barred continued waterboarding. Congress has likewise passed restrictions.

But rights groups have long suspected that such abuses were much more widespread than the CIA admitted. The agency had previously acknowledged waterboarding three detainees.

According to the documents The New York Times received, a contract translator who worked with the CIA observed an additional case of waterboarding.

While the documents do not specify where the translator worked, the newspaper said it determined that the location was likely a black site outside of Bagram Air Force Base on the outskirts of Kabul, Afghanistan.

The translator, The New York Times explained, referenced a detainee death that matched a facility known as Detention Site Cobalt or the “Salt Pit”, which became infamous for abusive conditions.

In an interview with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the translator stated that he had seen a man referred to as “Bashir” facing the torture practice.

He described Bahir as “lying on the board with the head of the board tilted downward into the water”.

“There were approximately three to four people ‘doing this,’” the document said, summarising the translator’s statements.

The FBI summary explains that the translator “saw the incident in passing but did not participate himself”. The incident allegedly took place in a hallway.

The CIA did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment by the time of this article’s publication.

The agency has also not acknowledged waterboarding detainees at any site in Afghanistan. The three detainees it has acknowledged torturing were held at black sites in Thailand and Poland.

One was Abu Zubaydah, the first detainee the CIA held in a black-site prison, located in Thailand. The US government for years falsely depicted him as one of the highest-ranking members of al-Qaeda, a group of which he was not a member, according to US intelligence reports.

A 2014 report on the CIA torture programme by the Senate Intelligence Committee found that Zubaydah was waterboarded 83 times, sometimes as a means of helping instruct torture methods.

Another was Khalid Shaikh Mohammed, accused of being the architect of the September 11 attacks.

The third was Abd al-Rahim al-Nashiri, who is accused of helping plan al-Qaeda’s 2000 bombing of a Navy destroyer, the USS Cole.

All three are currently being held in the Guantanamo Bay military prison in Cuba.

items.title: Egypt detains driver over Cairo fuel tanker fire that killed 31
items.summary: Prosecutors order drug tests for the 21-year-old suspect, who says he was overtaking when the crash happened.

scraped.title: Egypt detains driver over Cairo fuel tanker fire that killed 31
scraped.description: Prosecutors order drug tests for the 21-year-old suspect, who says he was overtaking when the crash happened.
scraped.author: Al Jazeera Staff
scraped.h1: Egypt detains driver over Cairo fuel tanker fire that killed 31
scraped.body_text:
Prosecutors order drug tests for the 21-year-old suspect, who says he was overtaking when the crash happened.

Save

Share

Prosecutors in Egypt have ordered the detention of a 21-year-old driver suspected of causing a collision on Wednesday that overturned a fuel tanker on Cairo’s ring road, starting a fire that killed 31 people .

The Public Prosecution announced on Thursday that it had ordered the man to be held pending an investigation, and sent him to the Forensic Medicine Authority for tests to determine whether he had taken drugs.

The tanker burst into flames at about 6:30pm (16:30 GMT) on Wednesday, at the height of the evening rush hour, on an elevated stretch of the ring road in al-Waraq, a densely populated district of Giza on the western edge of the capital. The fire spread to passing traffic and destroyed 27 vehicles, including cars and motorcycles.

In an earlier statement, prosecutors said the driver told investigators he had been travelling from al-Marg towards al-Haram at 110km/h (68mph), with his father in the car, and was switching lanes to overtake other vehicles when the front left of his car struck the rear right of the tanker.

The man told prosecutors he then lost control and his car veered to the far right of the road. One of the tanker’s tyres burst, the statement said, before the vehicle hit a concrete barrier and overturned. Petrol leaking from the truck caught fire.

Prosecutors said they identified the driver after inspecting the scene and interviewing witnesses, and had since spoken to all the injured whose condition allowed them to be questioned. Forensic teams are taking DNA samples from victims’ relatives to identify some of the bodies. Relatives posted appeals on Facebook for men who had been on the road and had not been heard from since, the Reuters news agency reported.

The investigation will determine whether the driver bears criminal responsibility.

The Ministry of Health and Population on Thursday put the final toll at 31 dead and 26 injured, up from the 21 injured it had reported on Wednesday. Five of the injured have left hospital. The other 21 are still being treated, including eight transferred to other hospitals for further care. The bodies of the dead are in the custody of prosecutors, the ministry said.

By Thursday morning, traffic was moving again after crews cleared most of the burned wreckage. Salah Ahmed, a microbus driver, told the AP news agency that he had been on the ring road when the tanker caught fire but was held back by traffic, which saved his life.

“It was God’s hellfire on the ring road,” he said. “Why is a truck like this on the ring road at a rush hour? Who gets penalised for this happening?”

A 2018 cabinet decision barred trucks carrying more than four tonnes from the ring road between 6am and midnight, the AFP news agency reported. Prosecutors have not said why the tanker was on the road at the time.

“The tanks were exploding, the tyres were exploding, and there was fire,” Zaghlol al-Me, a local resident who reached the scene shortly after the crash, told Reuters. “We just didn’t know what to do or how to save anyone.”

The Public Prosecution’s statements are the first official account of how the crash happened. Early reports in local media suggested that a high-voltage cable had fallen in front of the tanker. On Wednesday night, the Ministry of Transport denied issuing any statement to that effect and said the cause was a matter for prosecutors.

The Ministry of Electricity and Renewable Energy said the overhead lines were taut when the fire began and that two circuits tripped only after it started. The ministry’s spokesman, Mansour Abdel Ghani, told the Egyptian Youm7 daily newspaper that the lines had no connection to the crash and melted in the heat. A high-voltage line lay twisted on the ground on Thursday, AP reported.

President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi ordered full medical care for the injured and support for the families of those killed. Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly visited the injured on Thursday with Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar and Social Solidarity Minister Maya Morsy. Madbouly said the government, civil society and businesspeople would provide bank investment certificates to give bereaved families a stable income, and replacement vehicles for people whose cars burned.

“We realise that no compensation or money can make up for those we have lost,” Madbouly said.

Egypt’s Ministry of Social Solidarity said on Thursday that people could donate through the InstaPay app to help the injured and the families of those killed. It also opened an account at Nasser Social Bank for donations from businesses and civil society groups. The cabinet said the ministry had received 24 million Egyptian pounds (about $445,000) from seven charities.

The crash has renewed questions about road safety in Egypt. The Ministry of Transport says it spent about $37bn on transport between 2014 and 2024, yet 5,829 people were killed on the country’s roads in 2025, up 10.8 percent from the year before, and about 84,000 were injured, according to the state statistics agency, CAPMAS.

Egyptian legislators demanded accountability on Thursday. Mahmoud Samy, an MP, said the government needed to move from “building roads and expanding them to managing their safety professionally”. Abdel Moneim Imam, a politician who chairs the liberal Justice Party, said the cabinet bore full responsibility and should resign.

Amr Moussa, Egypt’s former foreign minister and former secretary-general of the Arab League, also criticised what he described as a deterioration in government oversight.

“Trading accusations and evading responsibility leads to the next disaster,” Moussa said, according to Reuters.

Transport Minister Kamel al-Wazir was appointed in 2019 after a train crash at Cairo’s Ramses station triggered a fire that killed 25 people, according to Reuters. He has rejected calls to resign since then, including after a lorry crash in the Nile Delta that killed 19 people, almost all of them young women, last year. The ministry declined to comment further when contacted by Reuters.

Earlier this month, a train crash, also in Giza, killed at least seven people and injured more than 125, prompting calls from legislators for accountability over recurring transport accidents.

items.title: At odds over the EU budget, European leaders cut summit short - DW has more
items.summary: Even before they met, it was clear the gap between European leaders' demands for the EU budget would make negotiations difficult. They ended a summit meeting early and aim to agree on EU funding in December. DW has more.

scraped.title: At odds over the EU budget, European leaders decided to cut summit short
scraped.description: Even before they met, it was clear the gap between European leaders' demands for the EU budget would make negotiations difficult. They ended a summit meeting early and aim to agree on EU funding in December. DW has more.
scraped.h1: At odds over budget, EU leaders break off summit early
scraped.body_text:
Even before they met, it was clear the gap between European leaders' demands for the EU budget would make negotiations difficult. They ended a summit meeting early and aim to agree on EU funding in December. DW has more.

You can follow developments from the EU summit taking place on Thursday 26th and Friday 27th November below:

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said EU leaders will try to reach an agreement on the next multi-annual budget for the EU by the end of this year.

Merz said a day of talks among EU leaders in Brussels had brought "new movement" toward a reduction of the proposed size of the next budget, as demanded by Germany and other countries that are net contributors to the bloc's finances.

The leaders will try to hammer out a deal during a two-day summit starting December 17, Merz said.

Germany has been leading calls to attach a durable funding scheme for Ukraine to the EU's next budget.

Merz has made clear that his country would approve the next budget if all countries backed a loan for Ukraine.

Last year, the EU reached an agreement on a €90 billion loan to Ukraine through a compromise loan after a much-discussed frozen-asset plan failed .

The Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia opted out of backing the loan.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Contrary to earlier expectations, European Union leaders weren't quite done for the day, even if it was well past 2200 local time.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said that rather than meet again as scheduled on Friday, leaders would hold a final round of discussions around midnight and end the summit.

Thank you for reading along with our coverage of the Euro Summit on Thursday.

We will be back tomorrow to bring you the latest from the second day.

Until then, you can watch DW's analysis of the event:

Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar has said the chances of reaching an agreement on Thursday are "virtually zero."

Leaders of the European Union are gathered today in Brussels to agree on the bloc's budget proposal for 2028 to 2034.

In an X post, Magyar said he outlined "Hungary’s priorities and the red lines" to the other member states.

"Having heard the completely opposing positions around the table, I would put the chances of reaching an agreement today at virtually zero," he wrote.

He also said "an agreement around Christmas looks unlikely" as well.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez celebrated "a Spain that leads in Europe like never before," after the nomination of Pablo Hernandez de Cos as the next European Central Bank (ECB) chief.

Hernandez de Cos is set to become the new ECB head as the European Union (EU) leaders are gathered in Brussels for the Euro Summit.

Sanchez welcomed the news in a post on X, pointing out that the top EU positions held by Spanish officials Teresa Ribera, the European Commission's First Executive Vice-President, and Nadia Calvino, head of the European Investment Bank.

"In short, Spain leads in Europe like never before," he wrote.

Spanish candidate Pablo Hernandez de Cos will become the next president of the European Central Bank (ECB) , after being endorsed by the majority ‌of ​eurozone countries, news agencies reported.

As the leaders gather for the Euro Summit, the Financial Times first reported that de Cos will be the next ECB chief, citing ​people ​familiar with ​the matter. This was confirmed by Reuters and AFP, citing EU diplomat sources.

The decision came after the Netherlands said it would support the Spaniard as a consensus candidate.

Christine Lagarde has been president since November 2019 but has announced her intention to step down on February 7, 2027.

De Cos was up against Dutch central bank chief Klaas Knot for the presidency, while France's Laurence Boone and Germany's Markus Brunnermeier have been nominated for the ECB's two other top jobs.

Russia has criticized the European Union's proposed seven-year budget, accusing the bloc of seeking to prolong the war in Ukraine .

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the EU's plans to allocate money for Ukraine in its budget would make Kyiv "less inclined toward a peace process and more determined to continue the war."

Peskov said the result would be more military spending, leaving less for governments to spend on school, hospitals and social facilities.

"This is not money for peace," Peskov said.

Support for Ukraine is among the key areas of discussion in the 2028-2034 budget which includes up to €100 billion for Ukraine, however diplomats say this figure falls well short of Kyiv's needs.

Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has added her voice to those warning that European leaders have their work cut out for them when it comes to agreeing on a multi-year budget proposal.

"We're light-years ‌away from a ‌solution," ​Meloni told reporters ahead of the EU summit in Brussels.

"We are not willing ⁠to ​sign off ​on a budget ​under which ‌we would have to ​give ⁠more to receive less," ⁠she ​added.

Earlier, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the budget was "still too high" and that members states needed to be able to afford the full cost without taking on new debt.

Last week, European Council President Antonio Costa presented a new compromise proposal of €1.78 trillion ($1.95 trillion), around €204 billion lower than the initial proposal by the European Commission.

Every seven years, European leaders gather in Brussels for what is arguably the most consequential negotiation cycle in the European Union. As German Chancellor Friedrich Merz put it upon arrival, it is about "the future of the European Union."

This is not a typical EU summit. The leaders of the 27 member states are confronting a question that will shape all angles of EU politics for years to come: How much money should the EU have, who should pay for it, and what should it be spent on?

It is the essence of EU summit diplomacy: a painstaking exercise in give-and-take, bargaining and compromise.

The European Commission laid down the opening bid over the summer. The proposal was ambitious. Brussels wants an EU budget that reflects a rapidly-changing world: more spending on defence, innovation, research, digital technologies and competitiveness. At the same time, that inevitably means pressure on some of the traditional pillars of EU spending, particularly agricultural subsidies and parts of the bloc's regional development programmes.

Since then, every member has arrived with a shopping list of demands.

Governments have pushed back against cuts, demanded new priorities, sought exemptions and fought for national interests. There have though also been others who are pushing FOR a reduction in spending, including Merz.

The original proposal from Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has already undergone numerous adjustments as negotiators attempted to accommodate competing demands.

The result is an extraordinarily complex puzzle.

At the centre of it all stands European Council President Antonio Costa. He will be shuttling between bilateral meetings with leaders, gather small groups behind closed doors and attempt to construct a package that gives everybody something they can take home and present as a victory.

For Costa, the stakes are high. Delivering an agreement would be a major test of his authority and reputation as the EU's chief broker. Especially as he was not made top negotiator for the EU in the peace talks on Russia's war in Ukraine. Diplomats expressed confidence in his fairness and negotiating skills before the summit, viewing him as someone capable of building trust among leaders who have differing priorities.

Yet nobody in Brussels expects an easy breakthrough. Many officials acknowledge that the pressure on member states may not yet be intense enough to force the final concessions required for a deal. Leaders are still defending red lines rather than crossing them.

So, this summit will highly likely end without a grand agreement. Leaders will probably decide to take stock of the latest negotiating proposals and return home to assess them in detail. There will be a new — and perhaps final — round on the next summit in December, a few days before Christmas.

As leaders grapple with long-term budgets, across Europe, young people are rising up. They're demanding better jobs, more funding for education and lower rents. The problems they are protesting are complex and often specific to their home country.

But there’s also a common message: Young people feel pessimistic about their economic future. A look at the data shows they could be right.

Bulgaria 's Prime Minister Rumen Radev said his country would support a proposed €45 billion ($49 billion) EU loan to Ukraine, but only the funds earmarked for non-military aid.

"Bulgaria is going to take part ​in the loan of €20 billion (for) non-military support for Ukraine," ⁠Radev ​told reporters as he arrived ​at the EU summit in Brussels.

"We ​have a ‌huge historic diaspora of Bulgarians living in Ukraine, our wish ​is ⁠to concentrate our support in that area. ⁠We are ​going to contribute, but no money from Bulgaria for weapons," Radev said.

Last week European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the €45 billion would be split into two parts: ‌up to €25 billion for military aid and up to €20 billion for other ‌help as a means of getting member states to contribute where there were objections to funding weapons for Ukraine.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said that the budget proposal for 2028 to 2034 was "still too too high" and did not provide the basis for an agreement, during comments made as he arrived at the summit.

"After all, the member states must be able ​to afford to pay for ⁠all ​of this," Merz said in Brussels.

​The German leader also said the war in Ukraine needed to be ended as soon as possible and that the country needed help during a "very difficult winter."

Merz said that funding for Kyiv is "a task that we must also accomplish together,” and added: "The European Union consists of 27 member states, not 23 or 24."

Slovakia, the Czech Republic, and Hungary have been exempt from contributing to aid for Ukraine. The countries negotiated, as part of the current €90 billion loan for Ukraine, that they would not have financial obligations in guaranteeing the loan.

Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis did not agree with the German chancellor.

"Funding for Ukraine should be negotiated separately," said Babis, adding that his country needs the money for other expenditures. "I believe we will fight for this money," providing an early indication of how talks might proceed over the next two days.

European Council President Antonio Costa has called on European leaders to seek compromise on the bloc's long-term budget that's up for discussion over the next two days.

"Today as you know we have several points in our agenda, the most important is the approval and the discussion of the next long-term budget for the European Union," Costa said during his doorstop statement.

He said that the budget needed to be "fit to funding our main priorities."

Costa explained that farmers and regions needed support and that there also needed to be more investment in security and defense.

The price of housing and energy also needed to be addressed, Costa said.

Contributions by member states needed to be kept at a "reasonable level" the European Council chief pointed out.

"My objective is to ​bring ‌our leaders closer to a deal," Costa told reporters ahead of the ‌summit in Brussels.

With Ukraine support up for discussion at the two-day summit, Europe remains sidelined in Russia-Ukraine peace talks. But a multinational force is training in Poland to help secure Ukraine and NATO's eastern flank following any future ceasefire.

items.title: Albania's youth are protesting in Flamingo Revolution, not leaving the country anymore
items.summary: Youth protests against a rigid political system and corruption have shaken the government of Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama. They also show that fewer young people are willing to emigrate in search of a better future.

scraped.title: Albania's youth are protesting in Flamingo Revolution, not leaving the country anymore
scraped.description: Youth protests against a rigid political system and corruption have shaken the government of Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama. They also show that fewer young people are willing to emigrate in search of a better future.
scraped.h1: Albania's youth are protesting, not leaving the country anymore
scraped.body_text:
Youth protests against a rigid political system and corruption have shaken the government of Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama. They also show that fewer young people are willing to emigrate in search of a better future.

In mid-October, students in the Albanian capital Tirana set a suitcase on fire and threw it into the courtyard of the Education Ministry. Everyone in the country understood the symbolism: According to the 2023 census, the population of this Western Balkan country shrunk by about 420,000 between 2011 and 2023 — by nearly 15% — primarily because of emigration.

For a generation of young Albanians, this was the response to a system that gave them little voice. But now young people want to stay, and the protesters are saying that the system has to change.

Known as the "Flamingo Revolution," the social movement began in May with demonstrations against a luxury resort in a coastal reserve that US President Donald Trump's daughter Ivanka Trump and her husband Jared Kushner were involved in.

It quickly evolved into broader criticism against corruption, Prime Minister Edi Rama's government and his ruling Socialist Party and the country's entire political class.

Thousands marched almost every evening for four months in protests that were largely peaceful. But on October 13, a student protest escalated and there were clashes with police. Since then, the unrest has continued, with police using tear gas, water cannons and rubber bullets against demonstrators. There have been hundreds of arrests and many injuries, amid damage to public and private property.

The protesters have called for Rama's resignation, a transitional government, electoral reform and fresh elections. The movement, which has no leader, has support from people across the political spectrum. And while the prime minister has blamed "foreign hands" for the movement, there seems to be little evidence that external actors are orchestrating the protests, though they may have attempted to exploit the unrest online.

The protesters, who do not feel represented by Albania's democracy, are driven by domestic issues: corruption, the high cost of living and low wages. This is nothing new, but many factors have converged recently: a series of high-level corruption charges, including against ministers and two of Rama's former deputies, rising prices and the fact that Albania is being measured against EU standards by a new generation.

In certain areas, Rama has transformed Albania since taking office in 2013: the economy has grown significantly, as the government likes to point out, and tourism is booming. But the prosperity remains unevenly distributed. Critics accuse the government of channeling too much taxpayer money into a small number of well-connected companies through prestigious projects and public-private partnerships, and in some cases through corrupt business deals, at the expense of healthcare, education and better economic prospects for the wider population.

Rama has rejected the calls for his resignation and has invited protesters to engage in dialogue, which they have so far refused.

In 2008, Rama and Sali Berisha, the long-time chairman of the opposition Democratic Party, worked on a reform to Albania's constitution and electoral law, which was approved by parliament. Since then, it is party leaders who have determined who enters Parliament, which weakens ties between lawmakers and their constituents.

In addition, it has become significantly more difficult for new parties to win seats. In 2025, a new party received about 64,000 votes, but only one seat. The Socialists, by contrast, won about one seat for every 10,000 votes.

Rama has been the leader of the Socialists since 2005, while Berisha first became the chairman of the Democratic Party in 1991. For 21 years, Albania's prime minister has either been Rama or Berisha. Freedom House, a US nongovernmental organization that promotes democracy worldwide, classifies Albania as "partly free" and describes the country's political parties as being "often organized around leading personalities."

Protesters on the streets have said that they want both men to be jailed. Rama has argued that governments should be replaced at the ballot box, not on the streets.

Though the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) acknowledged that parliamentary elections in 2025 were "competitive and professionally managed" it said that they had taken place "in a highly polarized environment and contestants did not enjoy a level playing field."

It added that there were "reports of intimidation, misuse of public resources and pressure on public employees, which undermined equal opportunities."

The Democratic Party also spoke of election fraud and intimidation. Turnout was below 45%.

Many protesters also allege that when it comes to business, what matters is the proximity to people in power. They criticize the public procurement, public auctions and concessions system, which has led to state-owned land, including coastal and protected areas, being sold to private investors.

Ordinary Albanians are feeling the financial brunt. According to the Albanian Institute of Statistics (INSTAT), half of all employees earn less than 60,000 lek (roughly €620 or $680) per month after taxes. But according to Eurostat, food prices are slightly above the EU average and real estate prices in Tirana have nearly doubled since 2018, with rents rising just as quickly.

For many years, young Albanians who were dissatisfied with the system opted to leave the country. The number of Albanian citizens in Germany more than doubled between 2018 and 2024, reaching almost 120,000.

Though it is still too early to say whether there are fewer Albanians leaving today, for many protesters staying has become a political statement.

Rama has argued that his resignation would jeopardize Albania's bid to join the European Union by 2030, but the vast majority of Albanians are pro-European, including those on the streets and in the opposition. From the protesters' perspective, it is the government headed by Rama that is the real obstacle on the path to the EU.

Though there is currently a wave of protests across Europe, the only obvious comparison is with Serbia, where a student-led movement recently forced a long-time ruler from office. Whether Albania will follow this example depends on whether young people, who have traditionally not been deeply engaged in politics, can turn their protests into votes.

What is certain is that for three decades, Albania's leaders have relied on their citizens' suitcases. Now, the country's students have burned that very luggage.

Andi Balla is a doctoral candidate at the Leibniz Institute for East and Southeast European Studies (IOS) in Regensburg, where he is conducting research on demographic debates in Albania. He has written numerous articles on Albania for an international audience.

This article was translated from German.

items.title: Gerard Depardieu to stand trial in France for rape and sexual assault
items.summary: The Paris Court of Appeal upheld the order for the 77-year-old French actor to stand trial on charges of raping and sexually assaulting an actress in 2018.

scraped.title: French court orders actor Gerard Depardieu to stand trial for rape and sexual assault
scraped.description: The Paris Court of Appeal upheld the order for the 77-year-old French actor to stand trial on charges of raping and sexually assaulting an actress in 2018.
scraped.h1: Gerard Depardieu to stand trial in France for rape and sexual assault
scraped.body_text:
The Paris Court of Appeal upheld the order for the 77-year-old French actor to stand trial on charges of raping and sexually assaulting an actress in 2018.

French actor Gerard Depardieu failed in his attempt to overturn an order for him to stand trial on rape charges.

On Thursday, the Paris Court of Appeal ruled that Depardieu should face trial for the alleged rape and sexual assault that occurred on August 7, 2018. However, the court dismissed the allegations relating to a second incident that occurred six days later.

Depardieu still has the option of appealing to a higher court. His lawyer, Delphine Meillet, told the Associated Press that she disputes Thursday's ruling, though she did not specify whether she will challenge it in France's highest civil and criminal court.

This decision comes just two weeks after the 77-year-old Depardieu dropped his appeal against a sexual assault conviction in a separate case . He accepted an 18-month suspended prison sentence and issued a public apology.

An actress, who was 22 years old at the time, accused Depardieu of raping and sexually assaulting her at his Paris apartment on August 7 and 13, 2018. Depardieu was 69 at the time of the alleged incident.

She reported the allegations to the police a few days later. Depardieu denies the allegations, claiming that the encounter was consensual.

Last year, a trial was ordered regarding the allegations. If the trial goes ahead, Depardieu could face up to 20 years in prison.

Carine Durrieu Diebolt, the victim's lawyer, said that the Thursday decision was a genuine relief and a victory for her client.

Depardieu was born in 1948 into a working-class family in Chateauroux, a city in central France. He overcame a speech impediment to become one of France's most prolific actors.

The film star was a dominant figure in French cinema for half a century, becoming a renowned cultural export. He earned an Oscar nomination for "Cyrano de Bergerac" and a Golden Globe for "Green Card."

Accusations of sexual misconduct and his subsequent conviction, however, have increasingly overshadowed his cinematic legacy.

The international media has also been paying attention to Depardieu's off-screen antics. One of the most notable instances was when he accepted a Russian passport from President Vladimir Putin in 2013 amid a dispute over French taxes.

items.title: Where big U.S. unions stand on Trump's Canada tariffs
items.summary: While U.S. President Donald Trump insists his tariffs will bring a boom in factory jobs, the unions who represent hundreds of thousands of manufacturing workers are largely skeptical of his approach. Nowhere is that skepticism more apparent than big labour's view of Trump's tariffs on imports from Canada.

scraped.title: How big U.S. unions view Trump's tariffs on Canadian goods | CBC News
scraped.description: While U.S. President Donald Trump insists his tariffs will bring a boom in factory jobs, the unions who represent hundreds of thousands of manufacturing workers are largely skeptical of his approach. Nowhere is that skepticism more apparent than big labour's view of Trump's tariffs on imports from Canada.
scraped.h1: Where big U.S. unions stand on Trump's Canada tariffs
scraped.body_text:
While U.S. President Donald Trump insists his tariffs will bring a boom in factory jobs, the unions who represent hundreds of thousands of manufacturing workers are largely skeptical of his approach.

Nowhere is that skepticism more apparent than organized labour's view of Trump's tariffs on imports from Canada.

Despite their long-standing support for targeted tariffs as a tool for protecting U.S. jobs, the leaders of some of the biggest unions in the U.S. are calling on the Trump administration to take a different approach to Canadian products.

Brian Bryant, international president of the IAM Union, formerly known as the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers, says he'll take that message directly to Trump's point man on tariffs, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, at a meeting scheduled for early December.

"We're in favour of strategic tariffs where they're used appropriately to correct bad behaviour," Bryant told CBC News. "Canada's not the problem here."

Bryant says the Trump administration is applying tariffs haphazardly and should focus its attention on countries that pay cheaper wages.

Canada pursues tariff relief through interim U.S. trade deal

The IAM Union is particularly concerned about the Trump administration's tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum, Bryant says.

"We have many manufacturers in aerospace, general manufacturing, shipbuilding that are dependent and reliant on that," he said. The Trump administration should not be "adding to their costs for those because that's going to jeopardize our members' jobs."

Canadian officials and their U.S. counterparts have said in recent weeks the two sides are making progress toward a trade deal.

While the Carney government is seeking as much of a reduction in tariffs as possible, Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc has said Canadians should not expect a deal that brings zero tariffs .

Unions in the U.S., some of whom represent significant numbers of Canadian workers, are watching the talks closely and urging the Trump administration to shift its position.

Roxanne Brown, international president of the United Steelworkers (USW), signed a joint letter with Bryant this summer calling on the White House not to impose the threatened 50 per cent tariffs on some $28 billion worth of Canadian goods.

The international president of the United Steelworkers, Roxanne Brown, centre, is surrounded by union representatives during a Sept. 15 news conference in Laval, Que., addressing tariff and trade tensions between the U.S. and Canada. (Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press)

"We had great concerns about the impacts those tariffs were going to have on our members' jobs," Brown told CBC News. "We wanted to be on the record to really push back against those tariffs."

Trump went ahead with the additional tariffs, which apply to a range of Canadian products including wood products, alcohol, cheese and sporting goods.

When it comes to steel production, the USW supports tariffs on what Brown calls "bad actors," countries that unfairly subsidize their industry or engage in dumping of cheap steel.

"There should be a clear study into that dynamic between the United States and Canada. If it doesn't exist, the tariffs shouldn't exist," Brown said.

Trump says he's working on a 'fair' trade deal with Canada

Reaching interim U.S. trade agreement would kickstart new CUSMA talks, minister says

She says the environment between the Trump administration and Ottawa right now is "pretty combative" and her union has been asking the White House for months to take a more sensible, practical approach with its northern neighbour.

"That trading relationship has benefited both of our countries, it's benefited the jobs in both of our countries and for our union, that's a really important relationship to maintain," said Brown.

United Auto Workers president Shawn Fain delivers the keynote address at the annual national conference of the union's political arm, on Feb. 9 in Washington, D.C. (Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters)

One major union whose leadership has at times supported Trump's tariffs is the United Auto Workers (UAW). Its president, Shawn Fain, despite having urged his members to elect Democrats in 2024, strongly welcomed the Trump administration's initial sweeping tariffs, including those on Canada and Mexico.

"Tariffs are a powerful tool in the toolbox for undoing the injustice of anti-worker trade deals," the UAW said in a statement in March 2025. "We are glad to see an American president take aggressive action on ending the free trade disaster that has dropped like a bomb on the working class."

Fain and the UAW appeared to buy into Trump's argument that auto tariffs would bring good-paying jobs back to the U.S., and the White House communications team amplified his support .

In the past year and a half, after several Michigan leaders of the UAW publicly broke with their union president , Fain has pulled back somewhat on his full-throated backing of tariffs.

He campaigned in the midterms for Abdul El-Sayed, the winning Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Michigan, where tariffs on Canadian exports became a key election issue. In a webcast conversation with El-Sayed on Oct. 16, Fain insisted his support for tariffs has always been restricted to "strategic and targeted" ones.

"The unfortunate side of this is this administration has just managed to do blanket tariffs on everything and try to use it as political leverage," Fain said.

Ford vehicles are shown on the assembly line at the company's assembly plant in Louisville, Ky. U.S. President Donald Trump has threatened threat to raise tariffs on automobiles and auto parts from Canada to 50 per cent on Jan. 1. (Darron Cummings/The Associated Press)

The UAW did not respond to CBC's request for an interview this week.

Cathy Feingold, international director of the AFL-CIO, the largest federation of unions in the U.S., says the White House should be working with countries like Canada to address global trade challenges rather than punishing them.

"We completely oppose the chaotic nature in which the tariffs of the Trump administration have been imposed, especially on some of our closest allies and partners like Canada," Feingold told CBC News.

How will a resounding U.S. political shift impact the cross-border auto industry?

Where Trump goes now on the big 3: tariffs, Iran war, immigration

She says the AFL-CIO specifically opposes the 50 per cent tariffs imposed in August under Section 338 of the U.S. Tariff Act, the first time in nearly a century the section had been used.

"It's raised costs on both sides of the border. It disrupts cross-border industries. It's threatening union jobs on both side of the border," Feingold said.

She says she's hopeful the results of the midterms and the incoming Democratic control of Congress creates an opportunity for a shift toward trade policies that benefit workers in the U.S., Canada and elsewhere.

However, Trump has threatened to raise tariffs on automobiles and auto parts from Canada to 50 per cent on Jan. 1, a move that would put significant pressure on the bottom line of the three big Detroit-based automakers, Ford, General Motors and Stellantis.

Correspondent

Mike Crawley is a correspondent for CBC News, based in Washington. He began his career as a newspaper reporter in B.C., spent six years as a freelance journalist in various parts of Africa, then joined the CBC in 2005. Mike reported on Ontario politics for 15 years. He was born and raised in Saint John, N.B.

items.title: A Boston man won $1M US in the lottery. Days later, ICE arrested him
items.summary: Ariel Antonio Velasquez-Morales won $1 million US on a scratch ticket, the Massachusetts State Lottery announced Saturday. Three days later, he was arrested by immigration officials who said "his luck ran out."

scraped.title: A Boston man won $1M US in the lottery. Days later, ICE arrested him | CBC News
scraped.description: Ariel Antonio Velasquez-Morales won $1 million US on a scratch ticket, the Massachusetts State Lottery announced Saturday. Three days later, he was arrested by immigration officials who said "his luck ran out."
scraped.h1: A Boston man won $1M US in the lottery. Days later, ICE arrested him
scraped.body_text:
Ariel Antonio Velasquez-Morales held an oversized cheque for $1 million US and smiled in the photo posted Saturday by the Massachusetts State Lottery.

Local media described the Boston man as "all smiles," reporting that he planned to save and invest his winnings after matching 11 words on a $10 US scratch ticket. Lottery officials said it was the first puzzle he'd ever scratched.

A few days later, his photo was posted online again — but this time, by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), which said it had arrested the "illegal alien from El Salvador" on Tuesday. Now, Velasquez-Morales will remain in ICE custody until he's removed from the U.S., the agency said in a news release.

The ticket "ultimately led to his arrest," ICE said, without elaborating how. CBC News has reached out to ICE and not yet heard back. Velasquez-Morales does not yet appear on ICE's Online Detainee Locator System, where members of the public can search for people held in the agency's custody.

“Looks like his luck ran out,” said ICE public affairs assistant director Micah Bock in the news release.

On Nov. 24, ICE Boston arrested Ariel Antonio Velasquez-Morales, an illegal alien from El Salvador, during operations in East Boston, Mass. Velasquez-Morales entered the United States illegally on May 15, 2013. He was ordered removed by an immigration judge on April 24, 2014. https://t.co/YieIbY7afF

"Welcome to the ERO [enforcement and removal operations] Boston lottery! Where illegal aliens and sanctuary politicians are out of luck, and the law-abiding citizens of New England are always the winners!" ICE Boston posted on X.

It's unclear if Velasquez-Morales has legal representation. CBC News has reached out to several Boston-area immigration lawyers and not yet heard back.

A woman identifying herself as Velasquez-Morales's sister-in-law wrote on Facebook Wednesday asking for respect and empathy for him, his wife and children.

"There is a family waiting for him," she wrote in Spanish.

Another woman identifying herself as Velasquez-Morales's older sister commented on the same post, writing her wishes that he would soon be back home with his family.

CBC News has reached out to both women for comment and not yet heard back.

A photo of Ariel Velasquez-Morales posted by ICE in a new release on Nov. 25, announcing that ICE Boston had arrested the man a day prior. (U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement)

Velasquez-Morales illegally entered the U.S. in 2013 through the Texas border, according to ICE. An immigration judge ordered him removed in 2014, the press release noted, but "he illegally remained in the country."

While ICE posted on social media that "th e rights and privileges reserved for American citizens are for American citizens," state lotteries typically do not require citizenship or residency — if you meet the age requirement and are physically present in a participating jurisdiction when buying the ticket, you can play.

What happened at the Seattle airport? Outrage as ICE arrests man and daughter boarding flight

Kilmar Ábrego García, who faced U.S. deportation efforts and 'vindictive prosecution,' arrives in Spain

CBC News has reached out to the Massachusetts State Lottery and has not yet heard back. But its website help desk notes that anyone age 18 and up who is physically present in the state can buy lottery tickets at retail locations and win prizes. The Boston Globe reports that the lottery also doesn't require winners to have social security numbers, but that non-resident winners often face higher federal taxes on their winnings.

Some U.S. states allow lottery winners to remain anonymous no matter the amount, others depend on how much a person win, but many — including Massachusetts — do not let winners claim prizes anonymously.

"The Massachusetts State Lottery treats a winner’s name, town and prize as public information and releases them," explains the Massachusetts Legal Resources website.

'They're taking my dad:' Masked ICE agents arrest passengers at Seattle airport

"The lottery’s position, and the state’s, is that publicity is part of the game: It demonstrates that real people win, and it deters fraud in the claiming process."

Michael Baker, a Massachusetts attorney who works with lottery winners, told the Boston Globe that immigrants may not realize how much exposure winning the lottery can bring them.

"I’m sure people, when they play, they’re not expecting being at risk of being arrested," he told the media outlet.

Senior Writer & Editor

Natalie Stechyson has been a writer and editor at CBC News since 2021. She covers stories on social trends, families, gender, human interest, as well as general news. She's worked as a journalist since 2009, with stints at the Globe and Mail and Postmedia News, among others. Before joining CBC News, she was the parents editor at HuffPost Canada, where she won a silver Canadian Online Publishing Award for her work on pregnancy loss. items.title: Iranian journalist, Oscar-nominated screenwriter Mehdi Mahmoudian arrested in Tehran
items.summary: Rights groups are calling for the release of freelance journalist and Oscar-nominated screenwriter Mehdi Mahmoudian after Iranian authorities arrested him at his Tehran home on Wednesday, a day after he reported on an execution notice of two jailed protesters in Iran.

scraped.title: Oscar-nominated screenwriter, journalist Mehdi Mahmoudian arrested in Tehran | CBC News
scraped.description: Rights groups are calling for the release of freelance journalist and Oscar-nominated screenwriter Mehdi Mahmoudian after Iranian authorities arrested him at his Tehran home on Wednesday, a day after he reported on an execution notice of two jailed protesters in Iran.
scraped.h1: Iranian journalist, Oscar-nominated screenwriter Mehdi Mahmoudian arrested in Tehran
scraped.body_text:
Rights groups are calling for the release of freelance journalist and Oscar-nominated screenwriter Mehdi Mahmoudian after Iranian authorities arrested him at his Tehran home on Wednesday, a day after he reported on an execution notice of two jailed protesters in Iran.

Hosein Razzagh, a friend of Mahmoudian's and an Iranian activist based in Europe, told The Associated Press on Thursday that Mahmoudian was taken by security forces from his home.

The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) said in a statement on Thursday that a source close to the journalist told the organization that Mahmoudian's home was searched and his electronic devices were confiscated before he was detained. The source spoke to CPJ on condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal, it said.

A message posted on Mahmoudian's Telegram channel later on Thursday said he had been charged with anti-government "propaganda against the regime" and "spreading false information." His detention was also reported on Wednesday by reformist news outlet Emtedad.

A day before his arrest, Mahmoudian published an execution notice on his channel that two protesters jailed after the 2022 nationwide "Woman, Life, Freedom" protests were at risk of execution within 24 hours.

Mahmoudian posted later that day that according to a lawyer and family, the sentences had not been carried out.

Iran officials behind deadly Amini protest crackdown named

The 2022 protests were sparked by the death of 22-year-old Mahsa Amini after she was arrested by Iran's morality police over allegedly not wearing her headscarf correctly. Amnesty International said in a September report that authorities committed crimes against humanity in the monthslong crackdown on the protests that left hundreds of people dead and thousands detained.

Mahmoudian, who co-wrote the 2025 Iranian film It Was Just an Accident , which won the Palme d’Or at Cannes, has campaigned openly on behalf of jailed protesters and those at risk of execution in Iran, Razzagh said, adding that Iranian authorities "are extremely sensitive about execution cases."

There has been no official statement or public comment from Iranian authorities on his arrest.

The Oslo-based Iran Human Rights group has said at least 15 protesters have been executed in connection with the protests over Amini, with two of the executions being carried out in 2026.

During a brief telephone call with his family on Thursday, Mahmoudian said he had been transferred to Greater Tehran Prison, just outside of Iran's capital. He said that security forces had severely beaten him during his arrest, leaving visible injuries, the source told CPJ.

Reporters Without Borders (RSF) said Mahmoudian was also reportedly subjected to severe torture in detention, to the point of losing consciousness, according to confirmed reports it received.

"Journalism saves lives, and Mehdi Mahmoudian’s courage deserves to be celebrated. Instead, the journalist has been arrested, imprisoned and reportedly tortured by the very authorities he exposed," said Jonathan Dagher, head of RSF Middle East, in a statement on Thursday .

"RSF stands in full solidarity with the renowned journalist and filmmaker and calls for his immediate release. Publishing information in the public interest must never be treated as a crime.”

In recent months, the Iranian regime has resumed its wave of arrests targeting media professionals, RSF said.

Oscar-nominated director Jafar Panahi says he will return to Iran despite looming arrest

Iranian singer subjected to 74 lashes for performing without her hijab

Amnesty report says Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity in bloody 2022 protest crackdown

Razzagh told The Associated Press he last spoke with Mahmoudian by phone roughly between 2 to 3 a.m. on Wednesday about a death penalty case linked to the 2022 protests.

He said that Mahmoudian later didn't answer his phone, and that witnesses reported seeing more than a dozen armed agents raid his home.

The screenwriter and journalist has been repeatedly imprisoned for his work.

Mahmoudian was arrested earlier this year on Jan. 31 and subsequently released on Feb. 17, shortly before the Academy Awards, according to the CPJ.

His detention comes on the heels of Tehran's sentencing on Oct. 26 of his colleague and acclaimed director Jafar Panahi to five years and one month in prison. The Tehran court also ordered the confiscation of Panahi’s “movable and immovable assets."

Director Jafar Panahi poses on the red carpet at the Academy Awards in Hollywood on March 15. (Daniel Cole/Reuters)

Panahi, who directed and co-wrote It Was Just an Accident with Mahmoudian, returned to Iran in March after he had been previously convicted of “propaganda activities against the system.” Panahi has not been detained at this time, but his current whereabouts are unclear.

Panahi is among the most celebrated of contemporary Iranian directors and has continued making movies despite repeatedly being imprisoned, banned from travelling and put under house arrest by Iranian authorities over the past 20 years.

Mahmoudian and Panahi were among 17 Iranian activists, filmmakers and lawyers who signed a public statement issued on Jan. 28 condemning Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and the violent crackdown on protesters following mass anti-government protests in January.

Senior Writer

Sara Jabakhanji is a Toronto-based senior writer assigned to cover news developments in the Middle East. She has worked in CBC bureaus in Ottawa, London and Toronto. You can reach her at sara.jabakhanji@cbc.ca.

items.title: Minister says 3-day deadline for NT child protection consultation 'in error'
items.summary: The deadline for consultation on a second round of changes to Northern Territory child protection laws has been extended from three days to three weeks. Robyn Cahill says her department "forgot to change the date for consultation and that is being corrected as we speak".

scraped.title: Minister says 3-day deadline for NT child protection consultation 'in error'
scraped.description: The deadline for consultation on a second round of changes to Northern Territory child protection laws has been extended from three days to three weeks.
scraped.author: https://www.abc.net.au/news/olivana-lathouris/103566246
scraped.h1: Three-day consultation deadline for child protection changes 'in error', minister says, as timeframe extended
scraped.body_text:
Emergency

Backstory

Newsletters

中文新闻

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

TOK PISIN

By Olivana Lathouris

Topic: Children

Robyn Cahill says her department "forgot to change the date for consultation and that is being corrected as we speak". ( ABC News: Michael Donnelly )

The NT's child protection minister has extended the deadline for feedback on a consultation paper flagging more changes to child protection laws.

Organisations were initially given three business days to respond.

Following backlash over the timeframe, Robyn Cahill has said the deadline was a mistake, with submissions now due December 18.

The Northern Territory's child protection minister says a consultation paper that gave stakeholders just days to respond to proposed law changes was sent "in error", with the deadline for consultation now extended to three weeks.

But sector advocates say they need "months" to respond to complex proposed changes to child protection laws and they are "frustrated" at being repeatedly given limited consultation time.

The Northern Territory is considering further child protection changes that would limit judicial oversight of care arrangements and give child protection workers the ability to issue domestic violence orders, the ABC can reveal.

The consultation paper obtained by the ABC has revealed plans by the NT government to introduce a second round of reforms to child protection laws, just months after passing sweeping changes in July .

The paper includes 86 questions about 20 areas of reform including the length of protection orders, care plans, family visitation arrangements and domestic violence orders.

The ABC understands just a handful of organisations received the consultation paper.

They were given just three business days to provide submissions on the 43-page document after receiving an email from the Department of Children and Families on Tuesday night.

In the initial email sent to stakeholders, the department said there was "no wriggle room available for submissions" and flagged the department would be seeking cabinet endorsement for the changes "before the end of the year".

On Thursday, following backlash about the lack of sector consultation, Children and Families Minister Robyn Cahill told NT parliament the paper sent by her department had been circulated by mistake.

The NT government is planning to introduce a second round of reforms to child protection laws. ( ABC News: Michael Franchi )

Ms Cahill said the paper was originally due to be sent out in early November, but a decision was made to delay consultation due to an ongoing recruitment process for a permanent department chief executive.

"A decision was made that it would be best to wait given that decision was imminent," she said.

"So, when they sent it out, they forgot to change the date for consultation and that is being corrected as we speak."

A spokesperson for Ms Cahill said the deadline had been extended until December 18 but declined a request for an interview yesterday, citing a bomb threat targeting NT government ministers and bureaucrats.

The minister was later seen speaking with constituents at a public engagement event in the Smith Street Mall alongside other government members, including Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro.

The proposed changes, if introduced, would include limiting judicial oversight of care arrangements and giving child protection workers the ability to issue domestic violence orders.

Despite the now-extended timeline, legal organisations and children's advocates have said the consultation period still is not long enough to provide thorough feedback.

"The proposed changes are incredibly technical," Top End Women's Legal Service chief executive Caitlin Weatherby-Fell said.

The NT government was criticised over previous child protection reforms, including by sector representatives and Aboriginal organisations. ( ABC News: Olivana Lathouris )

Ms Weatherby-Fell said frontline services that were already struggling to keep up with caseloads were becoming "increasingly frustrated" by having limited time to provide feedback on important changes.

It follows the government being strongly criticised over the first set of child protection reforms , with sector representatives and Aboriginal organisations arguing they were not given an adequate opportunity to voice their concerns.

"As frontline services, we can't just drop our pens and erase ourselves from our clients," Ms Weatherby-Fell said.

"We continue to see increases on demand, year on year, for domestic violence-related help, for care and protection-related help, particularly after changes to the Care and Protection [of Children] Act earlier in the year."

Australia's national commissioner for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children and young people, Sue-Anne Hunter, said she was not invited to consult on the second round of reforms.

"I was emailed by a community organisation and that's the first time I saw it," she said.

"[I was] really surprised there are more amendments considering no one really agreed on the first amendments."

Sue-Anne Hunter says she was "really surprised" to see more amendments were in the pipeline. ( ABC News )

Ms Hunter said she was concerned about the prospect of some changes potentially being introduced without adequate scrutiny from the sector or Aboriginal voices.

"We're talking about children's lives," she said.

"We need to get this right because you just keep coming back to the table and making the same mistakes again and again."

items.title: 'Pigeon heaven' comes at a hefty price in WA
items.summary: A growing number of regional Western Australian communities are calling for a coordinated approach to control pigeons, as nesting birds cause costly damage to buildings and raise health concerns. Pigeons like to nest near solar panels where it's protected from the elements.

scraped.title: 'Pigeon heaven' comes at a hefty price in WA
scraped.description: A growing number of regional Western Australian communities are calling for a coordinated approach to control pigeons, as nesting birds cause costly damage to buildings and raise health concerns.
scraped.author: https://www.abc.net.au/listen/dana-hamilton/106487056
scraped.h1: Calls for control as pigeons damage, defecate and nest on buildings across WA
scraped.body_text:
Emergency

Backstory

Newsletters

中文新闻

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

TOK PISIN

ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt

Topic: Birds

Father Robert Cross says pigeons were costing the church between $10,000 and $15,000 per annum. ( ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis )

Anecdotal reports say pigeons are an increasing problem in regional towns such as Geraldton, Northam and Albany.

While causing hefty damage bills, pigeons also create a human health concern.

Business groups, councils and property owners are exploring collaborative control measures.

Increasing numbers of pigeons are defecating and nesting in public buildings across regional Western Australia, racking up damage bills and causing human health concerns.

In Geraldton, 420 kilometres north of Perth, the iconic St Francis Xavier Cathedral, nesting pigeons create an ongoing maintenance and damage bill of up to $15,000 a year.

"The gutters get blocked, the downpipes get blocked and it starts damaging the fabric of the cathedral," said Geraldton diocese director of heritage Robert Cross.

Father Cross said pigeons were causing similar issues in other buildings owned by the Catholic Church in Geraldton.

"They like heights, they like to look down on the rest of us," he said.

A pigeon sits on one of Geraldton cathedral's church bells. ( ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis )

Father Cross said any plan of attack needed to include the state's main grain handler, the CBH Group.

"It's really an issue that needs a coordinated approach by those people and places in Geraldton that are either creating a problem, or providing what we just say is pigeon heaven here on Earth," he said.

"Once upon a time you just go out and have a few shots at them and scare them off, but these days we've got all these safety regulations that make it so much more difficult to do something about the problem."

Pigeons feed at a Geraldton CBH site near the port. ( ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis )

City of Greater Geraldton mayor Jerry Clune agreed Geraldton's pigeon problem was growing due to 'so many feedstocks' being readily available.

"This time of the year of course there's so much grain, not (just) in huge stacks but on the roadside as well so, they're everywhere," he said.

"It becomes a health problem as well, the city are doing their best to control it but if it's not a community effort then those actions will be all in vain."

Pigeons eat the spilled grain coming from trucks during harvest time. ( ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis )

Mr Clune said the city had previously participated in a joint control program with CBH and the Mid West Ports Authority where pigeons were baited with contraceptive laced grain.

"I think CBH and the port have sort of given up on that, and I think the city will probably move in a similar direction, because there's so many other sources of grain that that is not the solution," he said.

"There's all sorts of ways (to control pigeons), you can anaesthetise them, you can get licensed shooters, you can trap them with a gas type thing.

"It is a community problem, and people who do have properties, then the onus relies with them to take control of what to do with those pigeons.

Jerry Clune says the city's pigeon problem is getting worse. ( ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis )

"Unfortunately around Geraldton we've got a lot of federation style buildings and they've got a lot of ledges and all that and it's perfect for pigeons.

"They just love those sort of buildings and consequently they tell all their mates to come and share the digs with them."

Business owners in Albany, 400km south of Perth, have complained of a spike in pigeon numbers this year with flocks of the bird visible in the CBD and near the port's grain terminal.

Earlier this week, reports of a man with a gun on a building in Albany was actually a pigeon exterminator.

Police issued a public notice after calls were made to emergency services after spotting a man with a firearm on top of a York Street liquor store.

Pigeons like to nest near solar panels where it's protected from the elements. ( ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis )

Albany police officer-in-charge Senior Sergeant Carlos Correia said the contractor had not advised authorities of his plans.

"[The contractor] didn't let anybody know and they've been told there is procedures to let people know so we don't scare our community when they see people on a roof with a firearm.

"More often than not they do it at night-time when they can't be seen."

Sergeant Correia thanked the public for being vigilant.

Pigeons are causing similar concerns in WA's Avon Valley, 95km north-east of Perth.

Northam Chamber of Commerce chief executive Theresa Lee said she had heard reports of pigeon 'debris' from roof spaces landing on desks in offices, and the chamber was attempting to lead a collaborative control program across Northam.

"We're looking at asset damage, the pigeons (are) affecting corrosion on metal roofing and structural elements due to the acidic nature of their droppings," she said.

Pigeons often nest on people's roofs creating noise and poo problems. ( ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis )

Ms Lee said the chamber was surveying all businesses to find out where pigeons are nesting across the community in a bid to create a more effective control program.

BirdLife Australia senior adviser Sean Dooley said pigeons were technically rock doves, and were not an ecological threat as they lived near humans.

"They're pretty much street kids really," he said.

"They need buildings and grain or bread or something to feed on, but they are remarkable birds, they've got this reputation as rats with wings and all that sort of stuff but they're incredibly intelligent birds and really adaptable.

"They're one of our oldest domesticated animals and they were initially bred for food but because they have this innate ability to find their way back to their nesting sites, they've been used for communication for centuries."

The ABC has repeatedly requested interviews with the CBH Group.

A 2018 planning document from CBH says pigeons are a "predominant problem in major centres such as ports and major depots" and details CBH's control of pigeons using a narcotic compound in a bait, and shooting.

Pigeons sit on top of the Geraldton cathedral. ( ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis )

Emergency

Backstory
