中文新闻

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

TOK PISIN

live

Topic: State and Territory Elections

The Victorian election is one day away, with the Coalition hoping to unseat a Labor government that has enjoyed three consecutive terms in power.

Yesterday, Liberal leader Jess Wilson revealed the Coalition would partly privatise the sewerage network, cull and delay various level crossing removals, and cancel the current government's plans to expand free kinder.

Follow our live coverage below:

By Richard Willingham

A plan to build new kindergartens in so-called "childcare deserts" would be scrapped by a Coalition government as part of its plan to cut spending.

The kinder deserts are areas identified in Victoria with a lack of kinder spots for families, so the state was going to build and operate some centres.

But hidden in Liberal leader Jess Wilson 's election costing is a half-a-billion-dollar cut to capital works for early childhood centres.

The Coalition is also saving another $400 million by not expanding access to free kinder to 30 hours a week. Families currently receive 15 hours a week of state-funded kinder.

The Coalition is set to undertake an Early Learning Structural Review to help identify gaps in the sector and assess infrastructure capacity.

It says it will ensure future early childhood facilities are built where there is genuine local need.

The Coalition is not convinced Labor's plans do that.

The ABC understands Labor's establishment of an early learning centre at Sunbury Secondary College (not Sunbury Primary School or by using existing places at existing non-government early learning centres) was a key reason for the opposition to include this area in its review.

By Mikaela Ortolan

Victoria's opposition unveiled major policies on kinder and the partial privatisation of public assets yesterday, just two days out from the election.

At the time, roughly 2 million Victorians had already cast their ballots.

Opposition Leader Jess Wilson has defended her decision to drop the detailed policies and costings, which you can read about below.

By Mikaela Ortolan

Good morning and welcome to our coverage of the Victorian state election campaign.

It's the final day of campaigning before election day.

Voting will officially close at 6pm tomorrow, Saturday , November 28 .

We'll bring you all the latest coverage of the day's events as they happen.

The bigger Netflix gets, the easier it is to miss stuff. This is true of all digital platforms, of course, but it’s especially true of Netflix of late, as the streaming service’s lineup now also includes a growing library of reality shows, live-programming , and even games . It makes it easy for some of the best shows to zoom right past you, unnoticed — which almost happened to me with Midnight Diner .

If you haven’t seen it, Midnight Diner is probably the most comforting thing available on Netflix. The show follows the patrons of a cozy little restaurant tucked away in the backstreets of Shinjuku, which is only open during the unusual hours of midnight to 7:00AM. This, in turn, attracts a unique blend of customers, who help each other out under the watchful eye of the shop’s owner (Kaoru Kobayashi), known only as “master.” The show aired for three seasons on Japanese TV, before being picked up by Netflix for a handful more under the subtitle Tokyo Stories .

What’s especially notable about the show’s return is the huge gap: season 2 of the Netflix iteration streamed in 2019, and it took seven years for it to come back. The break was so long that season 3’s first episode, which premiered in October, is about the restaurant’s struggles during the pandemic. There are a bunch of cute scenes of the diner’s regulars sneaking outside to check if the restaurant is open yet, and wondering if it will ever be able to. If nothing else, the break was a chance for the reliable master to finally take a vacation.

But once Midnight Diner ’s new season gets going, it’s right back to everything that made it beloved. Each episode uses a different dish as a way of exploring a particular story. An overworked manga artist imagines the life he missed out on over plates of spicy konjac, while a pair of old friends reconnect while munching on pork cutlet sandwiches. What’s remarkable about the show is the way it balances being a charming, comforting watch with exploring truly difficult and heartbreaking topics. It’s the combination of sweetness and sadness that makes it work so well. It’s as likely to make you laugh as it is to make you cry.

And unlike most Netflix series, the whole season isn’t streaming all at once. Instead, new episodes come out every Tuesday; so far six of a planned 10 episodes are available. It’s a welcome way to spend an evening, as the show’s slow pace and warm sense of humanity can feel like all-too rare traits in the current streaming landscape.

But the main reason I’m even writing about Midnight Diner ’s return is that it has been so easy to miss. There’s been next to no promotion for it — all I could find was a trailer on Netflix’s Japanese YouTube channel — and I only happened upon it accidentally after the initial premiere while browsing aimlessly through Netflix’s new releases. This, despite being someone who has watched and rewatched the previous seasons multiple times. You’d think I’d get a notification or something. Netflix has always been full of hidden gems, but now that it’s busier than ever, those gems are all the more hidden.

The Forerunner 265S may not be the newest or flashiest Garmin, but it’s one that I’ve always loved most in testing. For runners with smaller wrists, it fits nicely. The battery life is pretty good thanks in part to its OLED touchscreen. When I reviewed it a few years ago, I called it the Goldilocks of fitness watches at the time, and the only thing that bugged me was its price. But now that it’s down to $299.99 (a $150 discount off its MSRP) at Amazon and Best Buy for Black Friday, I can easily recommend it.

Garmin’s Forerunner 265S is identical to the standard 265, only it features a slightly better battery life and a smaller 42mm build for those with more petite wrists.

The neat thing about Garmins in general is that you really don’t need the latest models to get the most out of the company’s platform. Its watches tend to get firmware updates for several years after launch, which is how long the average Garmin user tends to hold on to theirs. This particular watch is best suited for folks who want something a bit slimmer and smaller, enjoy a pop of color, and want a little extra fitness tracking prowess — but don’t need the whole kit and caboodle that sends the price up by hundreds.

There are a few other Garmin models I like that are also on sale during Black Friday. I wish that I had 10 arms to fully vet every single last one, but alas. That said, here are some others that I have tested and recommend:

If you’re looking for a new laptop or a gift for the student in your life, you can save $100 on the MacBook Neo at several retailers, in both storage sizes and all four colors. The 256GB model is currently discounted to $599.99 at Amazon and Costco , while the 512GB model with Touch ID is available for $699.99 via the same retailers ( Amazon / Costco ). None of the retailers currently list an end date for the discount, which is the biggest price drop we’ve seen since Apple raised the laptop’s MSRP by $100 in July in response to the ongoing RAM crisis .

Apple’s budget-friendly MacBook leverages the A18 Pro processor, a chip originally found in the iPhone 16 Pro, to keep costs down. Both the 256GB and 512GB models feature 8GB of memory, and my colleague Antonio G. Di Benedetto was impressed by the vivid 13-inch screen and speakers, the latter of which are better than those in many cheap (and even midrange) Windows laptops. The Neo isn’t super performant, especially in terms of storage speed and total memory, but it’s great for everyday tasks, casual use, and students.

scraped.title: Ford unveils the GT41 as it hopes to win Le Mans again
scraped.description: Ford enters the World Endurance Championship in 2027 with the new prototype.
scraped.h1: Ford unveils the GT41 as it hopes to win Le Mans again
scraped.body_text:
Ford enters the World Endurance Championship in 2027 with the new prototype.

Sixty years ago, after two failed attempts, Ford won the 24 Hours of Le Mans with its GT40 race car. In the years since, the Blue Oval has been back to France more than a few times, with varying success. It could never replicate the GT40’s success winning overall, but it celebrated the 40th anniversary with a class win . Now it wants another shot at the really big trophy , and it debuted the car during the Detroit Lions-Chicago Bears football game today: meet the GT41.

“Revealing the Ford GT41 is a significant moment for everyone involved in this program,” said Dan Sayers, manager of Ford Racing’s Hypercar program. “It’s the result of an enormous amount of work across our engineering, design, and development teams and an important milestone on our journey towards 2027. We know the scale of the challenge ahead—the level of competition in Hypercar is incredibly high, and there are no shortcuts to success. Our focus has been on building the right foundations, bringing together the right people and making sure we learn as much as possible from every stage of development.”

Like many other entrants in the World Endurance Championship’s Hypercar class, Ford has chosen the rear-wheel-drive LMDh technical approach rather than building the GT41 entirely from scratch, as Ferrari and Aston Martin do with their cars. LMDh cars start with one of four approved carbon fiber chassis—in this case, Ford is working with Oreca, which has also partnered with Genesis and Acura.

The hybrid system and transmission are also standard parts. But Ford supplies the engine—a 5.4 L V8 based on the Mustang’s Coyote engine—as well as software to control the hybrid powertrain. A non-hybridized version of the Coyote has already been racing effectively under the hood of the Ford Mustang GT3.

The technical regulations also allow for more styling freedom than we often see in racing. The absolute amount of aerodynamic downforce is capped, as is the minimum drag, so OEMs are encouraged to use road car styling details to create a closer link between prototype and road car. I’ll probably need to spend more time looking at it to spot those road car cues, but I do see quite a few superficial similarities with the Genesis LMDh car, as well as the Ferrari Hypercar .

Despite being an American car brand, Ford doesn’t have plans as yet to enter IMSA’s WeatherTech championship, so don’t expect to see the GT41 next January racing at Daytona. Instead, it will take its first green flag in Qatar in March, the first of WEC’s nine races next season.

Ford should find it an extremely competitive championship. Although Peugeot and Alpine will not race next year, McLaren is also entering, alongside returning teams from Aston Martin, BMW, Cadillac, Genesis, Ferrari, and Toyota, which this year won Le Mans and the overall title, following three years of Ferrari domination.

Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

scraped.title: Draining peatlands is responsible for a few percent of our global warming
scraped.description: Detailed estimate going back to 1800 shows how much carbon is being liberated.
scraped.h1: Draining peatlands is responsible for a few percent of our global warming
scraped.body_text:
Detailed estimate going back to 1800 shows how much carbon is being liberated.

Much of the focus for human-caused climate change is on fossil fuels, which are creating most of our problems. But land use change is also a large component of the story, accounting for about one-third of total historical CO 2 emissions. Deforestation plays a major role here, but practices like draining wetlands also factor in. Exactly how much of our history of eliminating wetlands has contributed to warming is challenging to figure out. But thanks to new sources of data that measure emissions from today’s surviving wetlands, it’s possible to put a better number on it.

A new study led by Jevan Yu at MIT focuses on peatlands—environments like bogs and fens where organic matter accumulates into thick layers of material. Some 600 billion tons of carbon are held in these vast stores of peat, which is more than you can find in all the world’s living vegetation, the researchers note.

Because these areas are permanently inundated, any oxygen in the water is quickly used up, leaving the job of decaying all that organic matter to anaerobic bacteria that work much more slowly and don’t digest everything. So instead of seeing organic carbon turning into the CO 2 gas released by aerobic bacteria, in peatlands, a subset of it gradually turns into methane gas. Methane is an even more potent greenhouse gas than CO 2 itself and ultimately gets oxidized into CO 2 . That means there’s a little trade-off from peatlands—most of the carbon they have is kept out of the atmosphere, but the carbon that does escape does so as methane.

Many peatlands have been drained by digging ditches that let water flow out to repurpose the land for agriculture or other uses. That lowers the water level, supplying oxygen to the exposed peat and ringing the aerobic bacteria dinner bell. Methane emissions get turned down, and CO 2 emissions get turned way up.

The researchers used recent studies that measure gas emissions from peatlands to build a global model that estimated CO 2 and methane release as the water level drops. The two gases respond differently to a given drop in water level, and CO 2 in particular responds differently depending on where in the world the bog is located. Using reconstructions of water-level changes due to historical peatland drainage, the team ran their model starting in 1800.

The simplest way to represent the climate impact of both CO 2 and methane changes was to calculate the change in Earth’s energy budget—the strength of the greenhouse effect, in other words. They calculated the total effect in 2020 at about +83 milliwatts per square meter of the Earth’s surface from the CO 2 emissions, and about -9 milliwatts per square meter from the reduced methane emissions, for a total effect of +73 mW. That is 2.7 percent of the total human-caused change in Earth’s energy budget. (With the error bars on all these numbers, it’s 1.8–3.6 percent.)

Or to look at it another way, it means that around 4 percent of all the carbon that was buried in peatlands is now in the atmosphere.

Regionally, over half of the total CO 2 came from Europe, almost a quarter came from Southeast Asia, and only 14 percent came from North America. The timing is quite different, as well, with the contribution from Southeast Asia only jumping up in the last few decades.

Draining a peatland only starts the process of releasing carbon, though. So that means past land-use change will still be producing emissions in the future. To examine this, the researchers also ran their model forward to 2100.

If peatland water levels were simply held constant from 2020 on, the total change in Earth’s energy budget would nearly double, from 73 to 138 milliwatts per square meter by 2100. Moderate restoration of peatland water levels could reduce that growth, and ambitious restoration could even cause the effect to shrink slightly below its 2020 potency in their analysis. This is a process we can halt if we really want to.

But since rolling all the way back to the landscape of 1800 is unlikely, elevated emissions will continue for a long time. That makes this another part of the climate system where change plays out slowly, with long-term consequences.

Nature, 2026. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11339-0 ( About DOIs ).

scraped.title: From minimalist to maximalist: Ars staffers show off their home offices
scraped.description: Our home offices range from tasteful to "please explain yourself."
scraped.h1: From minimalist to maximalist: Ars staffers show off their home offices
scraped.body_text:
Our home offices range from tasteful to “please explain yourself.”

Ars Technica is a place that has always leaned into remote working. Since its beginnings in 1998, Ars has never had a single, central office—a setup that makes for a great commute to work, with little risk of getting stuck in traffic.

As Ars staffers step away from their desks for a few days to spend some time with family and friends, we wanted to give you a look inside our home offices. We’ve got all sorts of setups, tucked into basements, dens, spare bedrooms, apartment corners, and lofts. They run the gamut from minimalist “here’s my laptop and monitor” setups to “I really like collecting things.” Without any further ado, let’s dig in:

As an apartment dweller in New York City, I’ve usually set up my home work station in a small corner of my residence along with sometimes decamping for local cafes or coworking spaces. My current hodgepodge of equipment is probably on the minimal side compared to many members of the Ars team.

I’m usually multitasking on my basic monitor display and work laptop configuration, with the monitor sitting on a stack of several books (apologies in particular to Mary Beard’s excellent history of the Roman Republic, titled SPQR).

Accessories plugged into the work laptop include a simple Lekvey Ergonomic Mouse and a Logitech K380 keyboard that I’ve often brought along with me to public workspaces. Sometimes I’ll use the built-in Macbook Air keyboard, but I like having the laptop display elevated, whether I’m working at home or elsewhere.

My personal Apple M4 Macbook Air usually sits on the side, where I primarily use my old, battered pair of Sennheiser HD 518 headphones to listen to music during the work day.

I have a simple standing desk, but it’s not the easiest to change positions, so I wouldn’t recommend it for anyone who wants to adjust frequently. Whenever I’m sitting, I sometimes switch between a simple wooden chair from Ikea and a more ergonomic chair.

Aside from an assortment of coasters and a tea container turned pen holder, my desk also holds a painted dinosaur sculpture (courtesy of my young son) and two versions of the Spot It! Matching game (also for my son’s entertainment).

Last but not least, I have a pair of Powerblock dumbbells tucked under my work desk. I wouldn’t say they feature heavily in my work day, but they’re easily accessible if I have 15-20 minutes to spare.

Greetings from my basement hobbit hole! My desk sits across from a workbench area that was already here when we got the house. I have labeled drawers full of PC parts, tools, and cables accumulated over decades. The drawer organization was quite the upgrade over my previous solution of “chuck everything in unlabeled storage tubs.”

My current PC setup is an AceMagic W1 mini PC running Fedora, and a Blackview Intel N150 I keep on Windows for audio recording (PipeWire is fussy). The two are connected to my inputs and monitors via a KVM so I can switch back and forth at the press of a button.

The monitors are mismatched thrift finds. One is an HP, the other Sansui. The TV is a similar story—an old Samsung LCD that set me back $10 at the thrift store. I use it as a third monitor for watching PC streams. An Onn Android box is also connected, though it rarely earns its keep.

Below the TV sits a Lenovo ThinkSmart View, a repurposed B2B video-conference gadget modded to run LineageOS. It handles smart-home controls and tracks my solar production during the day. There’s also a Flashforge 5M printer in the corner, and the pegboard wall holds tools, Mega Man figures, and about 10 years’ worth of convention badges.

The back closet is the scary part: old consoles, spare drives, boards, and parts for every project I’ll get to “eventually.” The chair is a Dowinx gaming chair I grabbed on a Slickdeals whim—it’s fine, but I wouldn’t recommend it to anyone.

The rug-patterned Dude mousepad really ties the desk together, man.

I’m something of an outlier at Ars, in that I use Windows most days. I’m no great lover of Windows 11, but I still use it thanks to years of computing inertia. My machine is custom, built in early 2024 with a Raptor Lake Core i7 (that thankfully did not fall victim to the overvolting bug) and an RTX 4070 Ti. It has long been my preference to build my own PC for gaming and work to ensure easier repairs and upgrades. Although with the prices of components being what they are, I hope all these parts last a very long time.

The primary monitor on the bottom is an Alienware ultrawide OLED. I got it for gaming, but it’s also a nice productivity display that gives me lots of room to keep windows visible. Above that, I have an Asus ProArt LCD calibrated in sRGB for photography work. I’ll get to the keyboard, but I do want to point out my preferred mouse, a Logitech MX Vertical. I have carpal tunnel issues, and this thing has been a lifesaver.

I believe organizing my desk before taking the photo would be a form of lying, so rest assured this is what it looks like on an average day. I have a few organizers to keep phones and various accessories from getting scattered around my Uplift sit-stand desk (seen here in sitting mode), which I quite like. The chair is a Herman Miller Aeron, which I don’t like as much. It’s fine and has plenty of adjustments, but the mesh is very hard. You should only buy one on sale, and if you do, get a cushion.

Above the desk are some Star Trek cross-stitches, courtesy of my talented wife. The dangling ’90s-era computer components are a mobile I put together many years ago, featuring a neat Intel i486 DEC socket board and some SDRAM.

I’m not a particularly neat person. My natural state is to have two or three projects half-exploded all over every surface: piles of 3D-printed prototypes, spools of wire, a soldering iron, laser-cut acrylic for a pinball project, the packaging from something I recently opened and need to sort through. Those aren’t random examples; that’s the contents of my workbench behind me on the opposite wall of my office as I type this. It’s a bit of a mess.

To combat that tendency, I make a concerted effort to keep the desk where I spend so many hours of the day calm and a place where I can focus. It doesn’t always last! But I’m always at least striving for it, and what I find helps is having a very intentional design where everything has a place.

My desk surface is made from rubberwood butcher block, on Flexispot motorized legs. I recently picked up another rubberwood slab to build the cantilevered shelf. The supports neatly tuck away my M1 Max Mac Studio, which is still a great little workhorse with 64 gigs of RAM, and my Arturia audio interface, which I use to record line-in sources like synthesizers.

On the left is a task lamp and a pen holder with six discrete holes. This fits in with the intentional design part: I have to pick the six things I want handy, and I can’t just pack it with more and more stuff. Currently that’s my Apple Pencil, a Pentel mechanical pencil, an Olfa mini snap-off blade knife, and a selection of three Pigma Micron pens in different line widths.

The right side holds an Aiyima 10th anniversary hi-fi stack: A20 amp, D20 DAC, and T20 pre-amplifier. The speakers are SVS Ultra Evolution Nanos. They’re sitting on the latest version of some 3D-printed stands I’ve been designing. I print them with hollow legs and then fill them with concrete for mass and stability.

Since I know Ryan is going to flex on everyone with his keyboard collection, I have to try my best to keep up with my daily driver. It’s a Percent Canoe v2 case, running Holy Panda switches modified with 63 gram SPRiT springs for a slightly lighter touch, and GMK Bento keycaps. This was a pandemic build project, and it has served me well since.

I used to run multiple monitors, but I’ve found that I don’t focus as well with them and prefer a singular spot to pay attention to. I’m using an Apple Studio Display because I’m very picky about pixel density. I opted to order it without the stand so I can run it on an ergo arm.

When I built the shelf for my desk, I fabricated a mounting bracket for the arm out of schedule 40 steel pipe and a 3D-printed sleeve that sits in a pocket CNC’d out. Since it sits flush on the underside, I don’t have to use a clamp that would extend down into the space where I keep my Mac and audio interface.

When I need a secondary display, or I want to use my Apple Pencil in Photoshop or Illustrator, I use an iPad Pro. I used to have a dedicated Wacom monitor, but I find this much more convenient both in terms of space efficiency and ergonomics. If I’m not really leaning into hand drawing or lettering, I do most of my graphic work with a mouse, which is currently a Logitech MX Master 3S.

To wrap up the final items, the chair is an Aeron I bought new in 2003. I’ve had to repair it a few times over the years, but it’s either been things I consider wear items (wheels, armrests, gas cylinder) or Herman Miller has replaced under warranty. It was a big purchase for me at the time, but it’s ended up being a great investment. That’s Sophie draped over it, one of our four cats.

Tucked next to my desk, behind the subwoofer under the little side table, is my home server and networking gear. The server runs Unraid and is primarily used for my Jellyfin media collection and Home Assistant. Networking is a combination of Unifi and Eero, but at some point I’d like to ditch the Amazon gear and go fully native Unifi.

I spend a lot of time in my office. It’s not just a place to edit, write, and do other Ars-y things. It’s also my rehearsal space and a place to relax and unwind when I need some me-time. Long-time readers won’t be surprised to see Apple hardware front and center. I’ve been using Macs since college, and they’ve done alright by me ever since. My daily driver is a first-gen Mac Studio (M1 Max) with 64GB of RAM, which drives two Apple Studio Displays. As a long-time mouse hater, I use a Magic Trackpad along with my extended Apple keyboard. Underneath the desk is a UPS and a Thunderbolt disk enclosure that is one of my two backups.

The bookshelves are where my home networking gear lives. That includes a Synology DS920+ that backs up all of the computers in the house, serves up media, and runs my instance of Mealie . The Eero 6+ handles home networking, with everything in my office except my MacBook Pro connected via Ethernet. As much as I’d like to live a paperless existence, the HP printer-scanner-copier combo still gets some use. They’re difficult to see, but to the right of the G4 Cube (sadly inoperable) on top of the bookshelf sit an Apple TV and M2 Mac mini, which hook up to the 43-inch TV. My graphite iBook and eMate are now resigned to propping up bibs from races and other cycling events.

This is my office, which is the place where I am much of the time. The chair is a Herman Miller Embody and is one of the best things I’ve ever spent money on. The desk is a standy desk that I don’t stand at nearly often enough; the work PC is a Mac Studio; and the gaming PC is a frankenbox with a cockpit running Windows 10 LTSC (from my cold dead hands, etc., etc.). The Linux boxen are headless and are mostly banished to the closet.

The paintings (including the awesome Apollo 12 SCE-to-aux one) are all originals by the inimitable Stephen Quick , who does a hell of a job with commissions. What started as a funny idea about a Warhol-esque take on the many faces of Kurt Russel kinda turned over a couple of years into somewhat of a “these are some actors whose work I like” series. My buddies and I went to a lot of movies when we were teenagers, so the imagery sparks good memories for me.

The rest of the office has space stuff in it, especially the part behind where I was standing to do the pano sot. I’ve heard it said that when a man hits his 40s, he must choose between becoming obsessed with World War 2 history or smoking meats; I did kind of a variation on “World War 2” and fell deeply into historic human spaceflight. Apollo is kind of my jam, and some weekends you can even catch me docenting at Space Center Houston’s Saturn V exhibit! (Yeah, it’s maybe not as pretty as the exhibits at Marshall or KSC, but the JSC Saturn V is the only one made of flight stages end to end!)

Welcome to the mess of wires, monitors, and handheld fidgets that is my loft desk. Let’s take a quick tour along with the rest of my gaming cave/mid-life crisis Mario collection that lives right by it.

My office setup is probably a lot simpler—basic?—than most of my Ars colleagues. I use an adjustable wood-top desk that allows me to stand or sit while I work. I do almost all of my writing and editing on a MacBook Air, and I have a spare available in case I need it. Sometimes I travel with both MacBooks so I can use one for writing and the other for monitoring a rocket launch, press conference, or other event. I also work a lot from my porch, where I can enjoy the fresh air and quiet mornings on our ranch in rural Texas.

An iMac and a second monitor stand behind the laptops. I generally use them to watch conferences, rocket launch livestreams, weather radar, or live news. It just depends on what’s happening any given day. One of the things I love about the space beat is there’s something happening nearly every day, and it’s possible to cover much of it from home. There are often multiple things happening the same day, so the dual-screen setup becomes especially handy then. For example, I can use one monitor to watch what SpaceX is doing at Starbase, Texas, and another to watch a rocket launch in Florida. I use a ring light behind my desk for TV interviews or podcast appearances.

Absent from my desk is my large collection of space swag stowed away in storage boxes. Perhaps I will bring it out to add to my workspace for a future Ars Staff Source. For now, I use a mouse pad from the European Space Agency that I’ve had for at least 15 years. The mouse pad features ESA’s astronomy missions that were in development or operations at the time. All of the missions have now launched, and some have long been decommissioned. It’s a good reminder of how long it takes to design, develop, build, and launch science missions. Anyone who says this stuff is easy is being dishonest.

This image is a bit misleading, in that it implies I work on the pictured PC (RTX 4070, Ryzen 5 3600X, 32GB RAM) and sit at my desk while doing so. That’s occasionally true, but more often, I can be found wandering around my apartment with my M4 MacBook Air during work hours. I don’t even sit at my desk to game much anymore—on the off chance that I’m playing a game the Steam Deck can’t handle natively, I’ll stream it from my PC to my Steam Deck using Moonlight and Apollo ( previously Moonlight and Sunshine ).

You may also notice that my desk, from a company called Uplift, is adjustable. As it turns out, I don’t enjoy standing while working, so the ability to loft my tabletop skyward has been chiefly deployed in the service of making it easier to retrieve something I’ve dropped down there.

At night, my desk often moonlights as a craft area; I swap out my keyboard (a Wobkey Rainy75) for a cutting mat, and I’m ready to build some Gundam, assemble a book nook, or tackle a crochet pattern (a few amigurumi are scattered around my desk to keep me company). You can see some of my supplies on the left, but I have other stuff stashed in drawers and various containers that I can bring to my desk as needed.

So sure, I do work here sometimes.

My wife Anna and I rent an apartment in Chicago, and we’ve chosen the city life over, well, space. As such, my 10-by-10-foot office space serves multiple functions. I use it primarily for work, but since Anna and I are both big gamers and she is often camped out with the PlayStation 5 in the living room, I have my own gaming setup in the office. It’s cramped, but it works!

I do editing, news hits, and most other work during the day, but I’m a night owl at heart and find that I can only do heavy writing—like on longer feature articles—at night, so I’m picturing both the daytime and nighttime view here. I have a collection of Govee lights (Govee Hexa panels, several RGB Edison bulbs, and a Star Light Aurora galaxy projector) to max out the vibes for those nighttime focus (and gaming) sessions.

We moved into this place in the dead of the pandemic, and I bought most of the stuff in this office during that year or shortly afterward, so it’s a very 2020–2021-coded array of hardware.

The desk is a Secretlab Magnus Pro, and the chair is a Steelcase Gesture. I love the desk, but I have mixed feelings about the chair. I don’t like the material of the Herman Miller Aeron, but people kept telling me to buy an ergonomic chair for long-term back health, so I bought the other one everyone recommends. To be frank, I’m never fully comfortable in it, though, and wish I had just said “life is short” and bought something comfy and bad for me!

The main machine is a 14-inch MacBook Pro with an M1 Max, 64GB of RAM, and a 2TB hard drive—still holding strong after five years. I also have an Alienware Aurora R10—hear me out—prebuilt gaming desktop with a Ryzen 9 5900X and an RTX 3080. When I bought it, it was during the COVID-times GPU shortage, and there was absolutely no other way to get the GPU I wanted. The system is loud, hot, and hard to work with; I want very much to replace it with something custom, but the need has not yet arisen. I tend to hold on to stuff until it literally stops working.

As for monitors, the center monitor is a 27-inch, 1440p, 240 Hz OLED Asus XG27AQDMGZ. The left and right monitors are both 27-inch 4K, 60 Hz IPS Dell U2720Qs. I’ve got a pair of Audioengine A2+ speakers, plus a Blue Yeti X, a Logitech Lighta Glow, and the good ol’ Logitech C920 for video and voice calls.

Then there’s input: a Keychron K1 Pro keyboard, a Razer Orochi V2 mouse, and a Sony DualSense controller. I’ve got a Belkin charging station for my iPhone 17 Pro, AirPods Pro, and Apple Watch Series 7, plus AirPods Max on a headphone hanger on the front of the desk. The CalDigit E5 Thunderbolt hub is doing a lot of work here!

I feel fortunate to have a job that allows me to occasionally apply my lifelong love affair with video games. My favorite game of all time is The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim ( Morrowind is a close second), and I like Bethesda games in general. I’ve got a working (but mostly useless) Fallout Pip-Boy, which ought to count for something! I also have a few other Skyrim knickknacks hanging about. And if you’re a Star Trek: The Next Generation viewer, you might have already noticed the desk mat.

I do enjoy playing games at my desk sometimes, but after I sit at the computer all day, I often want to be somewhere else when winding down. So pictured here is the other half of the room. The leather armchair I use for console gaming is paired with a leather ottoman (the colors don’t match because, again, COVID-era supply limitations).

I have an LG C1 OLED TV with a PlayStation 5 Pro, a PlayStation 3 that is backward-compatible with PlayStation 1 and 2 games, a Nintendo Switch I barely touch, and three Analogue FPGA retro consoles: the Super Nt, Mega Sg, and 3D.

It’s a tiny room to spend so much time in, but after almost seven years in this apartment, it certainly feels like home!

Nvidia is under pressure to do things differently, and a new WSJ report shows how far that’s going.

According to the Journal, Nvidia has told manufacturing partners, including Dell and Super Micro, to hit pause on server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia for an unspecified period as it assesses whether its regional partners are meeting U.S. export requirements.

The central, still-unproven claim in the Nvidia scandal is that Alice Huang, a former executive at the data-center company Megaspeed, is a Chinese spy. She had an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who abruptly resigned on Nov. 12 after acknowledging it and was just as abruptly reinstated on Monday of this week.

What’s publicly known is murkier than the headlines suggest. U.S. intelligence has reportedly tracked Alice Huang’s contact with an officer of China’s spy agency, but officials haven’t offered public evidence that she was commissioned to target Nvidia’s chief. In the past week, after President Trump successfully pushed to bring Jensen Huang back, the administration has played down the allegations it once circulated internally. Whether that reflects new intelligence or political pressure is the big question.

Undisputed reporting shows the claim emerged from the White House itself . It first appeared in a highly classified memo written in March under the oversight of Secretary of State Marco Rubio and circulated to White House officials ahead of Trump’s trip to China in May. The memo formed the partial basis for the New York Times’ initial reporting on the scandal, published Oct. 29 and its existence was first reported on Nov. 8 .

The memo did not definitively say, according to the Wall Street Journal, that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. CNN, by contrast, has reported that the memo concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset.

What’s better established is that Alice Huang was in touch with Chinese intelligence. The Ministry of State Security (MSS) is Beijing’s civilian spy agency, responsible for both foreign intelligence and domestic counterintelligence. Last weekend, the Times, citing people with knowledge of U.S. intelligence reports, reported that Huang was in contact with an MSS officer from the spring of 2025 until this fall , a period that overlaps her relationship with Jensen Huang. (The Chinese government has called the spy claims a “smear,” and Megaspeed says Huang left the company in August 2025 and that its business is legitimate.)

Top Trump officials have nonetheless all but discredited the espionage claims, along with the suggestion that Nvidia fell prey to spying or foreign influence.

Attorney General Todd Blanche, who was Trump’s personal defense lawyer before taking over the Justice Department, told journalists on Tuesday: “I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen.” On the same day, Trump said a pardon was an option for Jensen Huang but that he did not think one would be needed. Senior intelligence officials reportedly told Congress that the government apparently has no actual evidence that the MSS directed Alice Huang to pursue an affair with Jensen Huang.

None of those statements necessarily exonerates Alice Huang as an intelligence agent. Instead, they support the alternate theory that the Chinese government didn’t tell her to begin the affair and that Jensen Huang broke no law by having it. Not being directed to have an affair isn’t the same as not being a spy, though.

From a certain angle, the circumstantial evidence surrounding Alice Huang looks quite suspicious. She was a top executive at a company investigated for illicitly channeling Nvidia chips to China, and her husband, Kang Wei, is said to have even closer ties to the MSS, with some sources saying he worked for the agency.

The timing of the government’s reversal is at the heart of the matter. Trump has said he lobbied the board “directly and indirectly” to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, so it wouldn’t be surprising if officials who serve at his pleasure were recasting the case in terms that satisfy his agenda. That wouldn’t necessarily make their assessments wrong. But unless new intelligence has actually resolved the question, and none has been publicly identified as yet, that backdrop is critical to keep in mind. CBS has also reported that Rubio, whose office oversaw the original memo, has privately voiced concerns about aspects of Jensen Huang’s return.

Doubts persist elsewhere, too. Earlier this month, CNN reported that the intelligence community was still working to understand Alice Huang’s relationship with Jensen Huang and that the intelligence collected on her to date does not prove she was acting as a spy for Beijing. After a briefing by top intelligence officials earlier this month, Rep. Jim Himes (D-Conn.), the incoming chair of the House Intelligence Committee, said he was unsure whether she was a spy or a “ useful idiot .” And this week, the Wall Street Journal pointed out that under Chinese leader Xi Jinping, top corporate executives routinely maintain ties to the country’s intelligence service without being formally deputized as assets.

The crush of conflicting claims, most from anonymous government sources, obviously leaves large questions unanswered as to what actually transpired. Some of those questions that naturally spring to mind:

There are answers to all of these questions, of course, but when the public will get them is anybody’s guess. Jensen Huang is due to appear before the Senate Banking Committee next week, and by the look from the statements of some of its members , he’s likely in for a rough ride. Unfortunately, congressional hearings, particularly public ones, rarely unearth secrets that haven’t already been disclosed.

After 20 years of existence, X, the social network formerly known as Twitter, has finally added parental controls for teenagers, giving parents and guardians a way to manage what their kids see and interact with on the platform. But unlike most platforms’ implementation of such controls, X is putting its own spin on the system by giving teens a say in the matter.

The company said accounts belonging to 13-to-17-year-olds will be set to “protected mode” by default, meaning they won’t be able to see sensitive content, and won’t be served targeted ads. However, X is allowing teenagers to retain a measure of control over their accounts, letting them see what restrictions were made to their accounts. Parents and guardians will also not be able to read their teens’ private messages, see search or viewing history, or post as their teen.

The controls let parents see how much time their teen spends on X per week, set daily limits, require their approval for new followers, limit feed recommendations and videos to already followed accounts, filter specific words, turn off sensitive media, specify who can send their teen DMs, and see who they are messaging.

The controls arrive months after X came under fire for a lack of controls preventing the platform’s AI chatbot from being used to generate sexualized images of children and women . The social network has also long been rife with child sexual abuse material , misinformation , AI bots, and openly lets users post porn .

X has generally not been a platform aimed at teenagers, but that doesn’t mean they don’t use the platform. A 2024 study found that nearly a third of Gen Alpha kids have an X account. The platform itself requires users to be at least 13 years old, though that’s not a high bar given the kind of content on the platform.

“Parents want practical tools, and teens deserve room to grow. With Parental Controls on X, families can set the guardrails that fit their home, while teens keep ownership of their accounts and can see every change. Striking that balance is vital and what we set out to build.” Michael O’Herlihy, head of safety at X, wrote in a blog post.

items.title: Trump demands probe into ‘record setting error’ after third-quarter GDP data gets massive revision higher
items.summary: President Donald Trump on Thursday deemed the latest gross domestic product revision a mistake, claiming that it should be "immediately investigated."

scraped.title: Trump demands probe into ‘record setting error’ after third-quarter GDP data gets massive revision higher
scraped.description: President Donald Trump on Thursday deemed the latest gross domestic product revision a mistake, claiming that it should be "immediately investigated."
scraped.author: Sean Conlon,Steve Liesman
scraped.h1: Trump demands probe into ‘record setting error’ after third-quarter GDP data gets massive revision higher
scraped.body_text:
President Donald Trump on Thursday falsely deemed the latest gross domestic product revision a mistake, claiming that it should be "immediately investigated."

Data released Wednesday from the Commerce Department revealed that the U.S. economy exhibited much stronger growth for the third quarter than initially estimated, showing that real GDP grew at a 4.3% annualized rate . That was revised upward from the department's advance estimate of 3.4%.

That revision was a "RECORD SETTING ERROR," Trump said in a Truth Social post , suggesting that the initial release could have influenced the outcome of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections , where Democrats flipped both chambers of Congress and even multiple governorships.

"I would like to wish a Happy Thanksgiving to even those who issued fake Economic Numbers, just prior to the Election, and corrected them yesterday, three weeks late, showing that the GDP was actually 4.3%, versus 3.4%, A RECORD SETTING ERROR, and one so grave that it should be immediately investigated," Trump wrote.

However, the difference between the advance estimate and the figure in the second release is far from being an all-time record. It was the largest revision since the 1.2 percentage point revision seen in the second quarter of 2020.

On an absolute basis, the latest revision was tied for 16th among all revisions from the advance estimate to the second release since 1990. It also tied four other quarters with a similar 0.9 percentage point difference — and was approximately double the average revision of 0.43 percentage points for all 147 quarters.

The upward revision shows Trump's policies are "delivering results" that defy expectations, White House spokesman Matthew Middleton told CNBC.

Revisions to U.S. economic numbers are not out of the ordinary . Initial reports count on partial survey data and early estimates. Those data are later updated with more survey responses — which sometimes leads to changes from the initial reports.

GDP data is revised repeatedly over a five year period. By the time the final revision is done, the average absolute error from the second release to the final is 1.14 percentage points.

The advance estimate for Q3 U.S. GDP, which came just days before Election Day in early November, was still better than the figure economists had expected at the time. It also showed a significant step-up in growth from the second quarter.

Because that was a strong showing for the economy, some on Wall Street consider this week's revision to be a confirmation of the economy's recent growth trend.

Jim Baird of Plante Moran Financial Advisors said immediately following the release that it "reinforces an increasingly familiar tension" that the economy is "performing quite well, but its resilience also gives the Fed an even stronger case for further rate hikes."

"The economy isn't merely hanging in there. It continues to demonstrate considerable resilience, with consumers spending, businesses investing and few signs that restrictive monetary policy is creating significant cracks in the broader expansion," the firm's chief investment officer said.

Traders are currently pricing in a nearly 100% chance of a hike at the Federal Open Market Committee's December meeting, per the CME FedWatch tool . They're also anticipating an additional hike in January.

— CNBC's Jeff Cox and Fred Imbert contributed reporting

items.title: Semiconductor chips are the new oil. Here's why
items.summary: Semiconductor exports overtook oil and gas for the first time in 2026, as the AI boom fueled chip demand.

scraped.title: Semiconductor chips are the new oil. Here's why
scraped.description: Semiconductor exports overtook oil and gas for the first time in 2026, as the AI boom fueled chip demand.
scraped.author: Deena Zaidi
scraped.h1: Semiconductor chips are the new oil. Here's why
scraped.body_text:
In this article

The artificial intelligence boom has pushed semiconductors past oil and gas in global export value for the first time, according to a Deutsche Bank analysis of International Trade Centre data .

Yet the milestone arrives at an awkward moment, just as investors reassess the outlook for artificial intelligence spending and drive down the price of semiconductor stocks. Last week, before Monday's breathtaking reversal, semiconductor stocks suffered their worst weekly loss in a quarter century, with the PHLX Semiconductor Index (SOX) plunging nearly 11% last Friday alone, capping a more than 17% weekly decline.

Nvidia soared more than 31% Monday after the leading maker of artificial intelligence chips had fallen for a seventh straight week, plunging 46% during that stretch. Then it fell again, dropping almost 10% on Tuesday and Wednesday. Advanced Micro Devices tumbled 20% in two days last Thursday and Friday. Micron Technology sank 27% over the seven days ended last Friday.

"For decades we've talked about the petrodollar. Perhaps increasingly we need to think about the chip dollar," Jim Reid, global head of macro and thematic research at Deutsche Bank wrote in a report this month.

Semiconductor exports overtook oil and gas for the first time during the January-March quarter of 2026, reaching about $1.61 trillion, compared with $1.53 trillion for oil and gas, the report said, using four-quarter rolling totals.

The gap widened in the second quarter, when semiconductor exports totaled about $1.60 trillion and oil and gas exports reached about $1.47 trillion. Disruptions to oil supplies through the Strait of Hormuz after the Iran war helped widen the gap. Daily oil flows through the Strait collapsed nearly 77%, to 4.9 million barrels in the second quarter of 2026 from 21.6 million barrels in the fourth quarter of 2025, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration .

Yet the demand for semiconductors has proven insatiable in the face of soaring data center construction, boosting global trade in the increasingly scarce AI component. Hundreds of billions of dollars of orders for graphics processing units and data centers aim at providing AI computing power, Rothschild & Co. Redburn wrote in a report last Thursday.

"Compute will be the new commodity fueling this transformation on a global scale," Rothschild analyst Cara Thomson said.

The shift toward chips has macroeconomic implications just as the explosion in oil trade did in the 1970s.

Oil-exporting countries historically recycled much of their surpluses into the purchase of U.S. Treasuries and other bonds, helping finance U.S. deficits and underpin demand for other government debt.

Reid at Deutsche Bank said that since semiconductor-surplus countries in Asia are more closely tied to U.S. tech companies, some chip-export earnings could flow back into U.S. technology stocks, startups and data centers, further helping to finance the AI investment cycle.

The changing dynamics in global trade could also tilt the mix of global financial flows, Reid said. "So welcome to the chip-dollar era: potentially more growth, more excitement, more volatility, and structurally higher yields" in corporate and government debt.

items.summary: ETF Action founding partner Mike Akins and GraniteShares CEO Will Rhind react to Nvidia's sharp losses and latest comeback.

scraped.title: Buyer beware? Nvidia's volatile swings expose risks of single-stock ETFs
scraped.description: ETF Action founding partner Mike Akins and GraniteShares CEO Will Rhind react to Nvidia's sharp losses and latest comeback.
scraped.author: Julian Torres,Stephanie Landsman
scraped.h1: ETF Edge
scraped.body_text:
In this article

Nvidia 's latest bout of volatility is highlighting risks tied to single-stock exchange-traded funds.

Among the hardest hit: the GraniteShares 2x Short NVDA Daily ETF (NVD) . The fund sank 63% on Monday after Jensen Huang got reinstated as the chip giant's CEO. Meanwhile, the firm's 2x Long NVDA ETF (NVDL) soared nearly 62% on the same day.

ETF Action founding partner Mike Akins joined " ETF Edge " as Nvidia shares soared 31% during Monday's session, wiping a large portion of the losses from the days following Huang's resignation . Shares cooled on Tuesday and Wednesday, however.

"Historically speaking, we do not see these types of large drawdowns followed by huge drives up in a healthy market," Akins said on Monday. "It usually tends to be when you're in a recession or in a bear market territory, which we're not technically in for the broader market, but we are in for this AI trade."

But it may not be time to go cold turkey on single-stock funds.

"[Leveraged ETFs are] definitely a retail trading vehicle… I think it's OK to have a little fun trying to trade that," Akins added. "I'm certain there are people that are better at trading these than others. But on the whole, timing the market is very, very hard."

GraniteShares founder and CEO Will Rhind also joined "ETF Edge" on Monday as Nvidia single-stock short ETFs overshadowed his firm's new Anthropic launches: The 2x Short Anthropic Daily ETF (ANS) and the 2x Long Anthropic Daily ETF (AIL) .

"We thought this was going to be the biggest news event of the day with Anthropic the first leveraged ETFs going live," he said. "I can tell you this is like a sideshow compared to what we're seeing with Nvidia."

Rhind suggests Nvidia's wild swings aren't dampening enthusiasm for single-stock ETFs.

"As long as there's enthusiasm in the underlying name… people will want to trade it and most likely want to trade it with leverage either on the long on the short side," added Rhind.

" Fast Money " tackled the risks tied to ETFs that are tied to single stocks, too.

"If this is somehow part of a portfolio, [then] that is a dangerous game to be playing," trader Guy Adami said on Monday .

Karen Finerman also addressed the strategy's downsides.

"Leverage is always the thing that kills. It's always leverage," said Finerman, co-founder and CEO of Metropolitan Capital Advisors, in the same interview. "You can survive anything but leverage."

As of Wednesday's close, the GraniteShares 2x Short NVDA Daily ETF plunged 55% so far this week while the GraniteShares 2x Long NVDA Daily ETF is up 31%.

scraped.body_text:

FIFA was the victim of a cyberattack that saw hackers gain access to what soccer’s world governing body describes as a “limited set of personal and business information,” it said Thursday.

“FIFA is working closely with the relevant authorities, including law enforcement,” the organization said in a statement sent to The Associated Press.

FIFA didn’t say when the cyberattack took place, or the precise nature of the hacked information.

Last week, a group calling itself the Handsome Boy Hacking Club posted a screenshot on X of what it claimed were FIFA files. Three days later, it appeared to take credit for the hack when responding to a post that said more than 12 gigabytes of internal documents had been leaked.

“FIFA condemns in the strongest possible terms the unlawful acquisition and publication of information, particularly personal data,” the governing body said in its statement. “Such actions constitute a serious and unacceptable violation of privacy and can have significant consequences for the individuals concerned.”

The breach comes at a time when FIFA and its president, Gianni Infantino, is under scrutiny after his foiled, secretive plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

Infantino is also trying to extend his 11-year presidency of FIFA to 2031. He is the favorite when the election is held on March 18, with Kohzo Tashima of Japan and Philippe Diallo of France the other candidates.

scraped.title: Wang Fuk Court survivors mourn 168 victims on anniv. of tragic blaze
scraped.description: Former Wang Fuk Court residents were among a stream of mourners filtering into a park facing the charred housing estate on Thursday, as they marked a year since a deadly blaze ripped through their homes and killed 168 people.
scraped.author: Hans Tse
scraped.h1: In Pictures: ‘Utterly exhausting’ – Wang Fuk Court survivors mourn 168 victims on first anniversary of tragic blaze
scraped.body_text:
Hong Kong Free Press HKFP

Hong Kong news, breaking updates – 100% Independent, impartial, non-profit

Former Wang Fuk Court residents were among a stream of mourners filtering into a park facing the charred housing estate on Thursday, as they marked a year since a deadly blaze ripped through their homes and killed 168 people.

Some of them had lost loved ones in the tragedy while others were displaced by the blaze that broke out on November 26 last year. Wang Fuk Court was home to 1,984 households and close to 5,000 residents before the fire hit.

The inferno claimed the lives of four people from the Lee household: the elderly mother, an older brother, his 15-month-old daughter, and their domestic worker. They were survived by the elderly father, younger brother Lee Chun-ho, and his sister-in-law.

See also: Wang Fuk Court Fire tragedy: Full list of victims

Lee Chun-ho and his elderly father arrived at the makeshift memorial site filled with floral tributes on Thursday afternoon. The younger Lee was seen sobbing after placing a bouquet on the ground.

Phyllis Lo, who lost her mother, and Yip Ka-kui, whose wife Pak Sui-lin died in the blaze, also appeared at the Kwong Fuk Sitting-out Area near the scorched complex in the afternoon to pay their respects.

See also: Hongkongers mourn Tai Po fire victims on first anniversary as some lament lack of official memorial

Au, an ex-resident of the complex’s Wang Tai House who asked to be identified only by her surname, told HKFP that she had worried that acts of mourning might be disrupted following government warnings that all memorial events must be lawful on the anniversary of the blaze.

But Au said she was relieved to see people paying tribute in an orderly manner and that the mood was calm at the park. “This has allowed me to quietly remember our 168 neighbours,” she added in Cantonese.

The authorities said an official mourning event would not be held.

Au described the past year as “utterly exhausting,” saying residents had to handle urgent administrative matters relating to the fire every single day.

“Over the past year, everything I did every day revolved around three words: Wang Fuk Court,” she said, adding that she felt her life had been paused due to the tragedy.

Still, she said she felt a sense of solace after seeing fellow residents on Thursday, noting that survivors have become a vital source of comfort for one another since the tragedy.

Dorz Cheung, another resident, left work early on Thursday to return to Tai Po. The 34-year-old said he was emotional when he awoke on the anniversary, and that it had been hard to work throughout the day.

He laid a floral tribute and prayed while facing the housing complex.

“I haven’t prayed in a long time… I can’t help but pray to the Lord for an easier path for all of us [Wang Fuk Court residents],” he said. “I hope the deceased can rest in peace and look after us, from wherever they are now.”

scraped.title: China warns Australia-Philippines defence deal to fuel 'tensions'
scraped.description: China denounced a defence pact between Australia and the Philippines on Thursday, arguing it would "exacerbate tensions" in a region crisscrossed by competing territorial claims and vowing to "safeguard" its rights.
scraped.author: AFP
scraped.h1: China warns Australia-Philippines defence deal to fuel ‘tensions’
scraped.body_text:
Hong Kong Free Press HKFP

Hong Kong news, breaking updates – 100% Independent, impartial, non-profit

China denounced a defence pact between Australia and the Philippines on Thursday, arguing it would “exacerbate tensions” in a region crisscrossed by competing territorial claims and vowing to “safeguard” its rights.

The agreement between Canberra and Manila, struck this month during a visit to the Philippine capital by Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, updates a decades-old memorandum.

The countries have steadily increased defence cooperation in recent years, including joint maritime patrols in the strategically vital South China Sea.

Beijing claims most of the South China Sea despite an international ruling that its assertion has no legal basis. US ally the Philippines has been engaged in years of confrontations with China over disputed areas of the waterway.

See also: China ‘loves peace’ but could ‘easily win’ confrontation with Philippines – ambassador

“Certain Philippine politicians, driven by their selfish interests, are spreading false narratives about China, constantly engaging in provocations and stirring up trouble,” Chinese defence ministry spokesman Chen Xi told a news conference on Thursday when asked about the deal.

Those individuals are “attempting to enlist the backing of forces from outside the region to embolden themselves and create disturbances in the South China Sea”, he said.

“This will only exacerbate tensions and undermine regional stability.”

If faced with infringements or provocations, China will “take necessary measures to respond firmly”, Chen warned, in order to “resolutely thwart any attempts to plunge the South China Sea into chaos”.

The defence deal between Australia and the Philippines involves enhanced maritime activities, sharing of information and defence infrastructure development as key elements, according to Canberra.

scraped.title: Ex-lawmaker gets 120 hours of community service for drink driving
scraped.description: Former lawmaker William Wong has been sentenced to 120 hours of community service and fined HK$6,000 after he pleaded guilty to drink driving and three other traffic offences.
scraped.author: Irene Chan
scraped.h1: Ex-lawmaker William Wong sentenced to 120 hours of community service, fined HK$6k over drink-driving crash
scraped.body_text:
Hong Kong Free Press HKFP

Hong Kong news, breaking updates – 100% Independent, impartial, non-profit

Former lawmaker William Wong has been sentenced to 120 hours of community service and fined HK$6,000 after he pleaded guilty to drink driving and three other traffic offences.

Wong appeared at Shatin Magistrates’ Courts on Thursday morning for sentencing, local media reported . Taking into account Wong’s early guilty plea to drink driving and the fact that his previous drink-driving offence took place more than a decade ago, the magistrate sentenced him to 120 hours of community service and disqualified him from driving for one year.

Wong was also ordered to attend a driving improvement course at his own expense during the final three months of the disqualification period.

Wong also pleaded guilty to three other charges: careless driving, failing to stop after an accident, and failing to report an accident, for which he was fined HK$2,000 each.

The 66-year-old, then a legislator, was arrested on suspicion of drink driving and three other offences linked to a car accident on the Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) campus in July.

Police said Wong hit two parked cars outside a CUHK residential hall that evening. He left the scene after the accident but later returned for an investigation, during which he failed a breathalyser test.

Wong was an engineering professor at CUHK and associate dean of the Department of Systems Engineering and Engineering Management.

He resigned from the Legislative Council and his job at CUHK after the arrest, apologising for bringing “trouble” to society.

Wong was elected to the Legislative Council in 2022 via a by-election to fill four vacancies in the lawmaking body. The by-election was a small-circle vote in which only members of the Election Committee, a body composed of political elites, could vote.

He was re-elected during the Legislative Council elections in 2025.

In Hong Kong, drink driving carries a maximum penalty of a HK$25,000 fine and three years in prison.

Seen through a net on a school ground in Sikar, Rajasthan, two children hold hands — mirroring how young girls get trapped in the net of child marriage, tradition and family pressure, long before they get a chance to grow up.., in Sikar Rajasthan. | Photo Credit: Sushil Kumar Verma

Nandini (name changed), 16, who lives in Rajasthan’s Sikar, had mapped out her future: finish school, go to college, and get a job to be financially independent. Her family, however, had other plans. Last month, they fixed her wedding without her consent. But the Class 12 student refused to surrender her dreams. She picked up her father’s mobile phone and called the 24x7 child helpline, 1098.

Over the next few days, Nandini called the helpline more than six times, using whatever phone she could lay her hands on. Sometimes, she pretended she wanted to speak to her prospective groom; at other times, she sought to contact her friends. But each call carried an urgent message: wedding preparations were under way, guests were being invited, and the date was drawing closer. Help!

Each time, the call was connecting to the District Child Protection Office. “She had asked us not to contact her. She said she would call whenever she got a chance. Her first call came just three days before the wedding,” recalls Gargi Sharma, District Child Protection Officer.

With barely 72 hours to act, the team secured an injunction order from the court and stopped the wedding. The family was taken by surprise when officials arrived, suspecting that a neighbour had tipped them off. They never imagined that the quiet schoolgirl in their midst had been orchestrating her own rescue. Her identity as the whistleblower remained a secret.

The Sikar administration prevented 29 child marriages in 2024 and 10 in 2025. “In 2026, we have received information about 21 cases so far,” Sharma says. But there are many Nandinis, especially in India’s villages, who do not have the education or the agency to say no to child marriage.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) may transform the way Arabic is learned and used, but human emotions and traditional values remain beyond the reach of technology, an international conference on the Arabic language held at Anvarul Islam Arabic College, Kuniyil, observed on Thursday.

The two-day conference, titled ‘Digital humanities: reimagining Arabic language and literature’, was organised by the Arabic department of the college in association with Calicut University’s Arabic department, Kerala State Higher Education Council, and Arab Union of Internet Writers.

Liyaqat Ali, deputy director of collegiate education, inaugurated the conference on Wednesday. College Principal K. Mohammed Fawaz presided over the function.

Liyaqat Ali, deputy director of collegiate education, inaugurating an international conference on Arabic at Anvarul Islam Arabic College, Kuniyil, on Wednesday. | Photo Credit: SAKEER HUSSAIN

Arabic scholars Sumayya Ibrahim Abu Thailath from Palestine, Najeeb Ali Mulkhath from Yemen, Simi K. Salim, K. Ali Noufal, I.P. Abdul Salam, C.M. Sabir Navas, K.A. Nasser, P. Firoz, M.K. Ameer Swalahi, Shakir Babu Kuniyil, and K.P. Abdul Haleem Thangal spoke.

E.T. Mohammed Basheer, MP, inaugurated the valedictory function on Thursday. He highlighted the growing global significance of the Arabic language in an increasingly interconnected world.

Scholars Mujeeb Nellikkuth, Ali Jafar, Mohammed Aman K., P. Sulaiman and C. Abdul Wahab spoke.

scraped.title: Concrete Floods Walls and an Elevated East River Park Now Protect a Swath of Lower Manhattan - Inside Climate News
scraped.description: Inspired by rising sea levels and Hurricane Sandy’s epic flooding in 2012, the $1.4 billion system of walls, berms and movable floodgates is designed to hold back 18.5-foot storm surges.
scraped.author: By Alissa de Chassey
scraped.h1: Concrete Floods Walls and an Elevated East River Park Now Protect a Swath of Lower Manhattan
scraped.body_text:

The most critical parts of the East Side Coastal Resiliency Project’s flood protection system may be the ones New Yorkers will never see.

In the new John V. Lindsay East River Park in lower Manhattan, engineers have been working on an ambitious challenge: protecting the park and surrounding neighborhoods from coastal flooding.

Beneath a 2-foot-thick concrete wall designed to hold back coastal flooding, steel structures extend deep underground, anchoring the barrier and helping prevent water from finding a way underneath it.

Depending on the location, engineers supported the wall with steel sheets driven into the ground or large underground pipes. The latter were used in areas where existing utility lines prevented the installation of a continuous barrier, explained Eric Ilijevich, a director at the city’s Department of Design and Construction.

But keeping floodwater from flowing over the wall is only part of the challenge. Water can also seep through the soil beneath it. To prevent this, engineers installed underground barriers using a technique called jet grouting, which involves injecting cement-based material into the ground to seal gaps.

The greatest danger is not seepage during a single storm, but the cumulative damage caused by repeated flooding. Over time, water moving through the soil could erode the ground supporting the wall, potentially undermining the entire structure.

The system, nearing completion, is designed to protect against flooding up to 16.5 feet above sea level, but engineers built in an additional two feet of protection, bringing it to 18.5 feet in case the team “was wrong in their projection,” said Joseph G. Lione, associate commissioner for coastal resiliency at the Department of Design and Construction of New York City.

The East Side Coastal Resiliency Project , which extends from East 25th Street along the East River to Montgomery Street, between the Williamsburg and Manhattan Bridges, was developed in response to the devastation caused by Hurricane Sandy in 2012, when a storm surge flooded large parts of Lower Manhattan, including the neighborhoods surrounding East River Park. The disaster exposed the vulnerability of the city’s waterfront communities to coastal flooding, a threat expected to grow as sea level rises.

A view of East River Park in Lower Manhattan in October, where newly renovated sections have reopened to the public while construction continues as part of the East Side Coastal Resiliency project. Credit: Alissa de Chassey/Inside Climate News

The $1.45 billion project aims to protect approximately 110,000 New Yorkers on Manhattan’s East Side from coastal flooding. It involves raising sections of East River Park by 8 to 10 feet and installing a system of floodwalls, berms and movable floodgates along the waterfront on either side of the elevated park.

Construction began in 2020 and is expected to be completed in 2027. Right now, only the northern section of the park is still under construction. “We’ve successfully completed over $1 billion” in construction, said Lione.

More than half of the park has now reopened to the public. Lione said the city was required to keep at least 41 percent of the park open throughout construction.

“They did a good job at keeping the park open,” said Wendy Brawer, a member of the Community Advisory Group and director of Green Map System, a sustainability nonprofit.

Raising the park has also improved accessibility by bringing it roughly to street level, as the city built bridges for better pedestrian access from the Lower East Side. “If the water rises, it will go on the steps; the park is now too high to be flooded,” said Lione.

The rebuilt park will also feature a continuous bike lane, “which the community really wants,” said Lione.

The project also relies on an extensive flood-protection system, much of it hidden beneath the rebuilt park.

The East Side Coastal Resiliency Project first took shape twelve years ago, in 2014.

But in 2018, the city announced a major redesign that would require raising and rebuilding much of East River Park. The decision sparked fierce opposition from residents and environmental activists, who opposed the destruction of mature trees and the prolonged loss of access to one of the neighborhood’s few green spaces during construction. “It was difficult to start with activists a few years ago,” Lione remembers.

Despite protests and legal challenges, construction began near East 25th Street, at the northern end of the project, before reaching East River Park in December 2021. “Now, we have very little pushback,” said Lione. “People understood what it was for.”

But opposition to the project has not disappeared.

“We still exist,” said Pat Arnow, co-founder of the East River Park Action, one of the major community advocacy groups that has opposed the city’s redesign of the park since 2018.

Arnow is no longer calling for a different flood-protection plan, although she maintains that “they could have provided the same amount of flood protection without destroying the entire park.”

For East River Park Action, the main concern is now the lack of shade in the rebuilt park following the removal of mature trees. The newly planted trees are still small, offering little protection from the sun. A few umbrellas provide some shade, but large stretches of the park remain exposed, with concrete surfaces absorbing heat.

“Those little umbrellas don’t do too much,” Arnow said. Brawer estimates that it will take 40 years for the new trees to provide comparable benefits.

New York City plans to plant 2,000 trees, said Lione. So far, the construction team planted about 600.

Lione said many of the removed trees were in poor condition because of exposure to saltwater from the East River. This is something Arnow believes is not true: “We have proof that they were growing,” she said.

Amy Burkoff is a retired biology professor at the City College of New York. But a few years ago, her job was “to document biodiversity in the park,” she said.

After understanding that the city’s redesign would require extensive tree removal, she worked with one of her students to measure what’s called the diameter at breast height, a standard forestry measurement for tracking tree growth. They compared their 2021 measurements with those recorded in 2015.

Burkoff and the student used the city’s own 2015 tree inventory, published as an appendix to the project’s environmental impact statement. Of the 28 trees they were able to compare, most had grown between 2015 and 2021, with an average increase in trunk diameter of slightly more than two inches, Burkoff said. “There is no evidence that these trees are sick and dying,” she said. “In my humble opinion, that was a lie.”

Ilijevich said that even the original design would have required removing 700 trees. He acknowledged that the city had failed to clearly explain the scale of the planned tree removal and why engineers believed alternative approaches would not provide the desired level of flood protection. “We hadn’t communicated the extent to which we were going to do a significant amount of tree removal, even with that original plan,” he said. The city is now planting more than 50 tree species, prioritizing native varieties and those better suited to future environmental conditions. Ilijevich said this diversity will make the park more resilient over time.

Brawer believes the redesign should have given greater consideration to rising temperatures and extreme summer heat. For her, accessibility goes beyond simply being able to enter the park. “If you can’t use the park because it’s too hot, I would call that inaccessible,” she says.

The demolition of a historic fireboat house was another source of concern for advocacy groups. House to the Lower East Side Ecology Center, which had been deemed eligible for historic designation, it had to be destroyed.

“They’ve already been out of their home since December of 2021,” said Arnow.

The foundation below the house was damaged, which forced the team to demolish it. “It was not a decision we made lightly. We did extensive consideration to try to preserve it or relocate it, and it just did not seem cost-reasonable,” said Ilijevich.

The city plans to build a replacement facility for the Lower East Side Ecology Center.

Some Lower East Side residents continue to question the city’s approach. They argue that the original park helped absorb floodwater during storms, including Hurricane Sandy. Ilijevich, however, argued that raising the park was necessary to protect surrounding neighborhoods from coastal flooding. “You have to think about infiltration rates and flow rates,” he says. Addressing the argument that the original park could absorb floodwater, “that’s not a realistic assessment of what happens during a coastal storm event. The park could absorb some of the energy, but it could not absorb the massive flow of flood water that I think people in their minds think.”

Both Ilijevich and Lione expect construction to be completed in 2027.

scraped.title: In a fertility advance, engineered molecular glue stabilizes chromosomes in aging eggs
scraped.description: Work in mice aims to reduce aneuploidy, the leading cause of pregnancy loss, and could one day improve IVF results for older women.
scraped.author: Megan Molteni
scraped.h1: In a fertility advance, engineered molecular glue stabilizes chromosomes in aging eggs
scraped.body_text:
Home
