Norman Rockwell’s Thanksgiving painting is classic Americana. Less well-known about the painting: it was commissioned as a depiction of FDR’s “Freedom From Want” and accompanied by a socialist’s essay on the working class as the “creators of abundance.”

Norman Rockwell’s iconic Thanksgiving painting was commissioned to be an embodiment of the “Freedom From Want” of FDR’s Four Freedoms. (Norman Rockwell / National Archives and Records Administration)

Our winter issue is out soon. Subscribe today to get your copy in our first mailing.

A n older woman, still wearing her apron from all her work in the kitchen, brings a large turkey to a table set with cranberry sauce and fruit and full of family, friends, and neighbors, who are smiling, talking, enjoying one another’s company. Her husband stands beside her at the head of the table, surveying the scene with pride.

The 1943 Norman Rockwell oil painting has become perhaps the most iconic and ubiquitous image of Thanksgiving in our modern era. It looks like a classic piece of kitschy, complacent Americana. Yet the image has a surprising political history. With so many in America going hungry this year, it’s a good time to remember that the painting was commissioned in honor of Franklin Delano Roosevelt’s bold call for “Freedom from Want” and released with a much bolder critique of New Deal America for failing to deliver that freedom to everyone.

“Freedom from Want” was one of the “Four Freedoms,” values set forth in FDR’s 1941 message to Congress on the need for continued US involvement in World War II, which the US would officially enter eleven months later. In our post–Ronald Reagan world, the very idea sounds revolutionary, especially since FDR said he was describing “the kind of world attainable in our own time and generation.” He argued the entire project of America’s domestic order was an ongoing “peaceful revolution.”

The Four Freedoms speech didn’t make much of an impression on the American public when FDR first delivered it. Two years later, the war underway, The Saturday Evening Post commissioned Rockwell to illustrate each of the Four Freedoms, and the artist delivered this image of an abundant Thanksgiving feast to represent “Freedom from Want.”

Along with the illustrations, the Post assigned essays to accompany them. “Freedom from Want” was assigned to Carlos Bulosan, a Filipino socialist activist, trade unionist, and writer. Bulosan was born in the Philippines to a peasant family, did not receive a formal education beyond third grade, and grew up picking coconuts and selling them to wholesalers to pay his older brothers’ school fees. He came to the United States at seventeen and worked in a fish cannery in Alaska, eventually becoming organizer and an elected official with the longshoreman’s union. In Washington and California, he worked as a dishwasher, a farm laborer, and in other low-wage jobs.

Despite his life’s hardships, he spent many hours in public libraries. Once, during a two-year battle with tuberculosis, he claimed to have read a book a day, including the works of Karl Marx and Walt Whitman. During this same bedridden period in the late 1930s, he began writing, contributing to publications like The New Yorker and Harper’s Bazaar — and The Saturday Evening Post .

Bulosan embraced the “Freedom from Want” assignment with a paean to America’s working class, whom he called “the creators of abundance.” His description of that class is rich and expansive:

If you want to know what we are, look upon the farms or upon the hard pavements of the city. . . . We cut timbers in Oregon just as the wild flowers blossom in Maine. We are multitudes in Pennsylvania mines, in Alaskan canneries. We are millions from Puget Sound to Florida. In violent factories, crowded tenements, teeming cities. . . . We are factory hands, field hands, mill hands. . . . We are the living dream of dead men. We are the living spirit of free men.

He emphasized the working class’s role in driving history forward, seeing that class as the engine of progress, not only through its labor but through its political struggles:

We are bleeding where clubs are smashing heads, where bayonets are gleaming. We are fighting where the bullet is crashing upon armorless citizens, where the tear gas is choking unprotected children. Under the lynch trees, amidst hysterical mobs.

Bulosan celebrates the progress of such struggles, including the right to organize unions. Yet because of the barbarities and inequalities of capitalism, Americans were still suffering deprivation:

We are not really free unless we use what we produce. So long as the fruit of our labor is denied us, so long will want manifest itself in a world of slaves. It is only when we have plenty to eat — plenty of everything — that we begin to understand what freedom means. . . . Our march to freedom is not complete unless want is annihilated.

Bulosan’s writing is heavy with disappointment that this vision hadn’t already been realized, emphasizing that the New Deal hadn’t gone far enough. Yet with an end to hunger, he wrote, democracy could be fully realized. He imagined a polity of plenty:

When we have enough to eat . . . then we have the time and ability to read and think and discuss things. Then we are not merely living but also becoming a creative part of life. It is only then that we become a growing part of democracy.

Rockwell’s painting was originally titled Freedom from Want , though since then, reflecting how this political context has been lost to history, it’s also been called I’ll Be Home for Christmas or simply The Thanksgiving Picture . As many observers have noted, the people around the table are enjoying their time together and are not looking at the turkey; the guests have the luxury of taking the food for granted as they revel in one another’s company.

Although Rockwell reportedly worried that his painting didn’t match Bulosan’s radical essay, it’s not hard to see how it does: both envision an America in which the conditions of plentiful comfort support a robust and lively social world. Just about everyone in America would recognize this Thanksgiving painting, but the socialist demand for food abundance that accompanied it has been forgotten.

That demand is more timely than ever. The cost of a typical Thanksgiving feast for ten this year has increased by 6 percent since last year, according to the American Farm Bureau.

And if you live in a neighborhood with a food pantry, as I do, you are probably seeing long lines around the block. With the increase in grocery prices and millions thrown off the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) by the Trump administration’s work requirements, food banks are seeing even more hungry people than during the pandemic years, with a dramatic increase in first-time visitors. Damningly, the Trump administration has discontinued the US Department of Agriculture’s annual household food security survey, but the New York Federal Reserve, in a national survey earlier this year, found what it called a “ remarkable ” increase in food insecurity from 2025 to 2026, especially in lower-income households and in households with young children. The New York Fed noted at the time that food insecurity was diminishing Americans’ confidence in the future; it seems certain that this increase in hardship contributed to the recent election results.

As so many go hungry in America, even as we elect more leaders in FDR’s tradition, Bulosan’s exhortation to American workers calls to us to push beyond the frame of what seems possible under US capitalism, to make the promises of its democracy real by feeding everyone.

“What do we want?” Bulosan asked, invoking the beginning of a timeless protest call and response:

We want to share the promises and fruits of American life. We want to be free from fear and hunger.

If you want to know what we are — we are marching!

Liza Featherstone is a columnist for Jacobin , a freelance journalist, and the author of Selling Women Short: The Landmark Battle for Workers’ Rights at Wal-Mart .

scraped.title: A Federal Judge Blocks the FCC's Review of ABC's Licenses, Saying It Likely Violates the First Amendment
scraped.description: The FCC "may not retaliate against or punish" broadcasters "for disfavored speech," U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan says.
scraped.author: Jacob Sullum
scraped.h1: A Federal Judge Blocks the FCC's Review of ABC's Licenses, Saying It Likely Violates the First Amendment
scraped.body_text:
Log In

Create new account

First Amendment

Jacob Sullum | 11.26.2026 4:00 PM

A federal judge on Wednesday ordered a halt to an unprecedented early review of the broadcast licenses held by ABC-owned stations, saying it posed an "existential threat" that was apt to have a chilling effect on the TV network's constitutionallly protected editorial decisions. Loren AliKhan, a Joe Biden appointee on the U.S. District for the District of Columbia, issued a preliminary injunction after concluding that ABC is likely to prevail in its claim that the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) violated the First Amendment by retaliating against the stations for speech that offended President Donald Trump and FCC Chairman Brendan Carr.

"Given the extreme, indeed existential, nature of the possible penalty Plaintiffs face—loss of their broadcast licenses—the court concludes that early license renewal proceedings create a risk sufficient to chill a broadcaster of ordinary firmness," AliKhan writes . "No one doubts that the Commission may enforce the law in the manner it sees fit. But in doing so, Defendants may not retaliate against or punish Plaintiffs and other broadcast license holders for disfavored speech."

AliKhan "saw the FCC's attempts to punish ABC for what they are: a campaign of intimidation and retaliation against speech that displeases Donald Trump," Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at the Freedom of the Press Foundation, said in an emailed press release. "The First Amendment does not allow government officials to appoint themselves the journalism or comedy police. The Constitution recognizes that even good-faith government actors cannot adjudicate journalistic merits without letting political agendas cloud their judgment, and Brendan Carr is far from a good-faith actor."

Last April, the FCC announced that it was reviewing the licenses of all eight TV stations owned by ABC: WABC in New York, KABC in Los Angeles, WLS in Chicago, WPVI in Philadelphia, KTRK in Houston, KGO in San Francisco, WTVD in Durham, North Carolina, and KFSN in Fresno, California. That announcement came years before the licenses ordinarily would be up for review. The FCC had not invoked its early-review authority in more than half a century, and it had never before simultaneously reviewed all the licenses held by one network's company-owned stations.

The official justification for the FCC investigation was the concern that Disney, which owns ABC, had violated the agency's "equal employment opportunity regulations" by engaging in discrimination under the banner of "diversity, equity, and inclusion" (DEI). But Carr made it clear that the review would also consider the broader question of whether ABC's stations were complying with their vague statutory obligation to operate in "the public interest"—a standard he thinks precludes programming decisions that he deems biased against the president.

The context of the license review showed that Carr's concerns extended far beyond the "invidious forms of DEI discrimination" he perceived. For nearly a decade, Trump has been threatening to revoke broadcast licenses in response to news coverage he views as unfair and unbalanced, frequently complaining about ABC specifically.

On September 11, 2024, the day after Trump's presidential debate with Democratic nominee Kamala Harris, which was moderated by ABC News, he complained that it was "a rigged deal" and condemned ABC as "the most dishonest news organization," adding that "they ought to take away [ABC's] license for the way" it had conducted the debate. The month after the debate, Trump reiterated that "ABC should lose its license" because of "what they've done." Shortly after taking office as the FCC's Trump-appointed chairman, Carr reopened an investigation of the charge that ABC's fact checking during the debate qualified as "broadcast news distortion"—a claim the agency had previously deemed groundless.

"ABC & NBC FAKE NEWS" are "two of the worst and most biased networks in history" because they "give me 97% BAD STORIES," Trump complained on Truth Social in August 2025. "THEY ARE SIMPLY AN ARM OF THE DEMOCRAT PARTY AND SHOULD, ACCORDING TO MANY, HAVE THEIR LICENSES REVOKED BY THE FCC. I would be totally in favor of that because they are so biased and untruthful, an actual threat to our Democracy!!!"

Trump reiterated that threat an hour later. ABC and NBC are "two of the absolute worst and most biased networks anywhere in the World," and they "should lose their Licenses for their unfair coverage of Republicans and/or Conservatives," he said . "Crooked 'journalism' should not be rewarded, it should be terminated!!!"

The following month, late-night comedian Jimmy Kimmel delivered a monologue on his ABC talk show in which he erroneously suggested that conservative activist Charlie Kirk's assassin was a Trump supporter. Two days later, Carr publicly threatened ABC stations with fines or license revocation if they failed to punish Kimmel for his ill-informed but constitutionally protected remarks. ABC and its affiliates immediately fell in line by suspending Kimmel's show for a week—the punishment that Carr had recommended.

Trump was unsatisfied by that outcome. "I can't believe ABC Fake News gave Jimmy Kimmel his job back," he said . "I think we're going to test ABC out on this."

The FCC "should look into the license of NBC, which shows almost exclusively positive Democrat content," Trump wrote on Truth Social in October 2025. "Likewise, ABC Fake News—About the same thing, 97% negative to Republicans!"

At a press conference that November, Trump re-upped his complaint. "I think the license should be taken away from ABC because your news is so fake and it's so wrong," he told Mary Bruce, the network's chief White House correspondent. "And we have a great commissioner, the chairman, who should look at that because I think when you come in and when you're 97 percent negative to Trump, and then Trump wins the election in a landslide, that means obviously your news is not credible and you're not credible as a reporter."

The next day, the White House issued a press release , headlined "ABC 'News' Is Fake News," averring that "ABC 'News' is not journalism—it's a Democrat spin operation masquerading as a broadcast network." The White House said "the network's longstanding commitment to hoaxes, character assassinations, and outright fiction targeting only one side of the political aisle is a deliberate deception to wage war on President Trump and the millions of Americans who elected him to multiple terms."

Trump followed that up with another Truth Social post four days later. "ABC & NBC, in particular, are a disaster—A VIRTUAL ARM OF THE DEMOCRAT PARTY," he said . "They should be viewed as an illegal campaign [of] the Radical Left. NO EXPANSION OF THE FAKE NEWS NETWORKS. If anything, make them SMALLER!"

Trump revisited that theme in December. "If Network NEWSCASTS, and their Late Night Shows, are almost 100% Negative to President Donald J. Trump, MAGA, and the Republican Party, shouldn't their very valuable Broadcast Licenses be terminated?" he wrote . "I say, YES!"

A month later, the FCC launched an investigation of the ABC talk show The View , casting doubt on its longstanding exemption from the agency's "equal time" rule, without which interviews with political candidates would be legally perilous. "For years," Carr complained on X in January, "legacy TV networks assumed that their late night & daytime talk shows qualify as 'bona fide news' programs—even when motivated by purely partisan political purposes. Today, the FCC reminded them of their obligation to provide all candidates with equal opportunities."

Trump had frequently criticized The View , and Carr shared his antipathy to the show. "Once President Trump has exposed these media gatekeepers and smashed this facade, there's a lot of consequences," Carr remarked in July 2025. "I think the consequences of that aren't quite finished. And look, The View 's got a lot of challenges there."

Last April, Kimmel offended the president again, this time by making a joke alluding to Trump's age and his wife's feelings about their marriage. Trump condemned that "really shocking" bit on Truth Social, saying, "Jimmy Kimmel should be immediately fired by Disney and ABC." The FCC announced its early review of ABC licenses the very next day.

In July, ABC and NBC declined to air a primetime speech by Trump. Those decisions were unremarkable given a long line of similar judgment calls by TV networks under administrations of both parties. But Trump was outraged .

"NBC and ABC fake news have both said that they would not cover this speech," Trump said during the address, which included dubious claims about election fraud. "They knew what it was about" but decided not to broadcast it "because of the fact that they don't like the topic, because they know how corrupt our system is and they don't want to reveal it," he averred. "They and others in the media are part of a plot." He added that "fraud like this should mean a revocation of their licenses."

Carr lent support to that suggestion at a press conference the following week. "When you have the president of the United States standing inside the White House delivering an important speech, I think that's something that broadcasters should be carrying," he said . He added that "Disney's decision there" would be one of the "points raised" during the ABC license review.

"The decision by broadcasters to carry or not carry the speech is something that is likely to be raised by petitioners that are seeking to have the FCC not renew the license for the Disney ABC stations," Carr explained in a subsequent interview. "We are looking into this question itself about the decision to air programming or not."

Carr, in short, seems to share Trump's understanding of ABC's "public interest" obligations, which the president thinks the network has violated by fact-checking him, covering him in a way he does not like, declining to give him the attention he thinks he deserves, and airing speech that irks him, including criticism and jokes at his expense. In light of Trump's anti-ABC rants and the FCC chairman's evident agreement with his beef, it is not surprising that AliKhan saw merit in the network's argument that the commission's threat to put its stations out of business was motivated by a desire to punish conduct protected by the First Amendment. That history reveals the ABC proceedings as part of Trump's broader attempt to weaponize the FCC against his opponents.

The ABC license review is "more intrusive, burdensome and extreme than anything I observed as a chairman," Mark Fowler, who chaired the FCC during the Reagan administration, said in a declaration supporting the network's lawsuit. "The blatant interplay between presidential complaints respecting ABC's broadcast content and subsequent [FCC] punitive actions," he added, "define[s] the Chairman as a biased political operative with a personal stake and bias in this case's outcome. Never in its history has the agency ever acted so corruptly and unlawfully to intrude on broadcasters' First Amendment rights."

The threat of license revocation, AliKhan notes, already has had an impact on ABC's programming decisions. In response to Carr's "equal time" investigation, ABC said , it "must now evaluate any invitation to a political candidate for its potential consequences, including whether it might later be cited by the Commission as a basis for non-renewal in the Stations' impending license renewal proceedings." The View 's producers started avoiding interviews with political candidates and even began eschewing clips of politicians that might provoke FCC scrutiny. Kimmel's show likewise decided not to air an interview with James Talarico, then a U.S. Senate candidate, which was instead shown on YouTube.

"The impact of the FCC's censorship spree has not been limited to ABC or other outlets Carr has pursued directly," Stern said. "He has put broadcasters on notice that if their coverage provokes a Truth Social tantrum, the FCC may deem hurting the president's feelings contrary to the 'public interest' and come after them with bogus investigations. Outlets that Carr has intimidated can breathe a little easier. The lesson to learn from this ruling is don't cave to Carr or any other anti-speech bullies in this administration. Instead, take them to court—the judiciary is on to them, and they lose regularly."

scraped.title: Second District Court Rules Against Trump's New Birthright Citizenship Executive Order
scraped.description: Judge Christopher Cooper of the District of DC ruled the order is illegal, and issued a class action injunction blocking it.
scraped.body_text:
Log In

Create new account

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Donald Trump

Judge Christopher Cooper of the District of DC ruled the order is illegal, and issued a class action injunction blocking it.

Ilya Somin | 11.26.2026 10:20 AM

Yesterday, in the case of Nathan v. Trump , federal district Judge Christopher Cooper of the District of DC issued a ruling against Trump's new executive order restricting birthright citizenship. The ruling is very similar to an earlier September decision by Judge Boardman of the District of Maryland. The one difference is that the class action injunction in Nathan covers a class that literally consists of all children illegally deprived of birthright citizenship under the new order, whereas the class in the Maryland case is slightly narrower.

I previously wrote about Trump's new executive order seeking to deny birthright citizenship to various classes of children born on US soil, and noted the first legal challenges to it . As I pointed out then, almost every part of the new order is at odds with the Supreme Court's recent ruling in Trump v. Barbara , which struck down Trump's executive order denying birthright citizenship to children of undocumented immigrants born in the United States, and those born to non-citizen parents here on temporary visas. The Fourteenth Amendment guarantees citizenship to all children "born or naturalized in the United States, and subject to the jurisdiction thereof." In Barbara , the Supreme Court majority made clear that "subject to the jurisdiction thereof" includes children of all persons who are subject to and required to obey US law.

Judge Cooper rightly concludes that nearly all the various classes of children barred from birthright citizenship by the new order are in fact protected by the reasoning of Barbara and other Supreme Court precedents, because they and their parents are clearly subject to US law, and required to obey it:

Earlier this year, the Supreme Court struck down President Trump's Executive Order 14160, which purported to deny citizenship to children born to parents temporarily or unlawfully present in the country. Those children, like "nearly all children born in the United States," the Court explained, are "citizens at birth" because they are born "subject to American law." Trump v. Barbara , 609 U.S. 719, 734–37, 740–41 (2026). Barbara reaffirmed that birthright citizenship extends to all but three narrow categories of children, each long understood to be beyond the Nation's governing authority at birth: children of foreign officials enjoying full diplomatic immunity, children of enemy forces in hostile occupation of U.S. territory, and children born aboard foreign public ships.

Yet Barbara's ink had scarcely dried when the President issued a second executive order—Executive Order 14418, at issue here—directing federal agencies to withhold recognition of citizenship from additional categories of U.S.-born children with noncitizen parents. Among those now targeted are children whose parents work for foreign governments or international organizations but lack diplomatic immunity, children born through commercial surrogacy arrangements, and children with a parent suspected of membership in certain gangs or terrorist organizations. As the Supreme Court has made clear, however, the President cannot carve out new exceptions to birthright citizenship for children born within the United States and subject to its laws. The Court will therefore certify a class consisting of children who are or will be unlawfully denied citizenship under the Order. And it will preliminarily enjoin the Government from enforcing the Order against members of that class.

As explained in my original August post on the new executive order, that order covers four groups almost all of whose members are clearly subject to US law:

Children of "alien enemies," defined as those where at least one of two non-citizen parents is a "designated Foreign Terrorist Organization under 8 U.S.C. 1189 or Specially Designated Global Terrorist, consistent with the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, 50 U.S.C. 1701 et seq ., and Executive Order 13224 of September 23, 2001 (Blocking Property and Prohibiting Transactions With Persons Who Commit, Threaten to Commit, or Support Terrorism)."

Children born to at least one non-citizen parent who is a "foreign government employee" or employed by an "international organization that possess[es] international-organization immunity."

Children where "either parent" has engaged in "birth tourist" transactions of various kinds (deliberately seeking to give birth in the US so the child would get birthright citizenship).

Children "born in a territory or territorial waters of the United States where citizenship is not conferred by Federal statute." …[T]his only applies to children born in American Samoa, the one populated overseas US territory to whose residents Congress has not conferred citizenship by statute….

As I explained more fully in my August post , all of the children in these four categories are obviously subject to US law, with the exception of those born to foreign diplomats who have diplomatic immunity. This latter group is already excluded from birthright citizenship. In that post, I also explained why the analogy between "alien enemies" (as defined in the order) and children of members of an invading army occupying US territory fails.

Judge Cooper's opinion analyzes all four categories thoroughly and effectively. He's particularly strong on the case of children of "alien enemies," a category which - he explains - the Trump order defines far more broadly than is justified by legal precedent, and which in any case does not include anyone not "subject to the jurisdiction" of the United States, because all such people are under US control and required to obey US law when on American soil. That differentiates them from the historically recognized exception for children of enemy troops in "hostile occupation" of US territory during a war. The US does not have effective jurisdiction over territory occupied by a hostile enemy army. But the last time any such thing occurred was during World War II, when the Japanese occupied a number of US island possessions in the Pacific.

I noted some additional problems with Trump's "alien enemies" carveout in my August post about the second birthright citizenship order:

Finally, the [order is wrong about] children of "alien enemies," defined…. as members of various designated "terrorist" entities. If they enter the United States, they are subject to US law. That's why they can be prosecuted for any crimes they commit on US soil - including acts of terrorism!

Members of these groups may be bad people. Some have committed horrendous crimes. But that is no reason to visit the sins of the parents upon the children. If a murderer or a rapist has a child born on US soil, the child is entitled to birthright citizenship, notwithstanding the reprehensible behavior of the parents. The same logic applies here.

It is also worth noting that the "foreign terrorist organization" (FTO) designation has been slapped onto various groups that are not actually terrorists in the ordinary meaning of the word, most notably groups engaged in smuggling illegal drugs.

Trump may be trying to use the "alien enemy" designation here to analogize these children to children of members of an invading army, born at a time and place where the invaders have seized control of US territory, thereby preventing the exercise of US "jurisdiction." Trump v. Barbara reaffirms the longstanding view that such children are excluded from birthright citizenship, because born in an area where US jurisdiction does not (at the time) meaningfully apply.

But FTOs have not, in fact, "invaded" or occupied any part of the United States. Thus, US jurisdiction still applies. Therefore, children of members these organizations are not analogous to children born to members of an occupying foreign army. No part of the United States has actually been invaded and occupied since the Japanese seized various US territories in the Pacific during World War II.

In my article, " Immigration is Not Invasion ….," I explain in much more detail why the activities of drug dealers do not qualify as an "invasion," why an FTO designation cannot change that reality, and why courts should not defer to the president's claims that an "invasion" has occurred.

Ilya Somin is Visiting Professor of Law at the University of Virginia, Professor of Law at George Mason University, Simon Chair in Constitutional Studies at the Cato Institute, and author of Free to Move: Foot Voting, Migration, and Political Freedom, Democracy and Political Ignorance: Why Smaller Government is Smarter , and The Grasping Hand: Kelo v. City of New London and the Limits of Eminent Domain .

scraped.title: Terror at 10,000 meters: What a bumpy flight in Argentina taught me about deregulation
scraped.description: Without airline deregulation, maybe I would have paid more to a state monopoly for the same near-death experience.
scraped.author: Christian Britschgi
scraped.h1: Terror at 10,000 Meters: What a Bumpy Flight in Argentina Taught Me About Deregulation
scraped.body_text:
Log In

Create new account

Travel

Christian Britschgi | From the December 2026 issue

The December 2026 issue of Reason explores Argentine President Javier Milei's accomplishments and what is yet to be done.

Even before we aborted our first attempted landing in the southern mountain town, I knew our flight was in trouble. High winds had been tossing our plane around like a fluttering leaf. Up and down the cabin, passengers were vomiting into the aisles.

To my left, one of my travel companions was whispering prayers to himself at an increasingly frantic pace. In the middle seat, I was thumbing through rosary beads as fast as my trembling fingers would allow. To my right, my other travel companion had a more stoic reaction. "The one time my domestic flight in Argentina leaves on time," he said, shaking his head.

The point of the trip was to take in the beauty of Bariloche, a popular lakeside tourist destination nestled in the Patagonian Andes along the Chilean border. Recent deregulation of Argentina's domestic airline market ensured it was practical and affordable to fly there from Buenos Aires, where we'd been staying since we'd arrived in the country. Weather permitting, we'd even go skiing.

Unfortunately, the weather wasn't even permitting us to land.

I am not generally a nervous flyer. The rational part of my brain reminds me of how safe air travel is in the United States, and that's usually enough to calm the reptilian jitters I feel during normal levels of turbulence. But I was not in the United States, and these were not normal levels of turbulence. Worse still, the airline we'd voluntarily opted to fly on was a budget carrier whose ability to offer our bumpy flight was made possible by the government's liberalization of the industry. For the entirety of my professional career, I had been cheering on the cause of deregulation. Now, here I was praying that a cut-rate profit-seeking carrier would keep my fellow passengers and me safe during exceptionally challenging flight conditions.

With every bounce and dip, I became more convinced that I would realize my biggest fear of dying an ironic death.

For decades, Argentina's aviation industry had been dominated by the state-owned and state-protected national carrier Aerolíneas Argentinas. The airline began life under President Juan Perón in 1950. For decades, it cruised along as an overstaffed, monopoly-protected enterprise under a variety of civilian and military regimes. In 1990, the government attempted to improve the state's balance sheet by privatizing the airline. But the carrier still suffered year after year of losses, despite continued state protection from competitors.

Renationalization in 2008 did not improve Aerolíneas Argentinas' financial situation. Instead, it made the government's fiscal situation worse. State subsidies to the renationalized airline totaled $8 billion by 2021 . The state-owned carrier also developed a reputation for unreliability. While official on-time rates remained high, many travelers to Argentina are familiar with the national carrier's drastic changes to departure times, and even changes to which airport a flight was leaving from.

The privileges Aerolíneas Argentinas enjoyed in Argentina came at the cost of competing airlines and passengers generally. Between 2019 and 2022, 17 airlines ceased operations in the country. Companies such as LATAM Airlines, which tried to compete with Aerolíneas Argentinas, left in large part due to government restrictions and union conflicts. Prices were high and service quality was low.

When Javier Milei won the presidency, the airline was identified as a prime candidate for privatization.

That has not happened. But Milei's deregulation of the nation's airline industry does appear to have been beneficial for Aerolíneas Argentinas and the flying public as a whole. The airline slashed unprofitable routes and trimmed staff. In 2025, it posted its first operating profit since the 2008 nationalization.

Milei's " open skies " policy, which liberalized prices and allowed more foreign carriers to offer service between Argentine cities, saw the number of flights offered rise. In 2025, a record 50.6 million passengers flew to, from, and within Argentina.

My plane eventually landed safely, but we then had to wait an hour for our bags to be unloaded, giving me time to reflect on the policy implications of my traumatic experience. Without the lower prices and wider availability of flights created by deregulation, perhaps I would have stayed on the ground and avoided the terrifying flight altogether? Or maybe, in a more statist world, I would have paid more to a state monopoly for the same near-death experience?

The rosary that remained clutched in my still-trembling hands suggested a third possibility. Perhaps there was no policy takeaway here: Perhaps weather is just weather, and our prayers are heard under a variety of regulatory regimes.

We opted to fly a competing airline on our departure from Bariloche. I reasoned that it would be at least as safe as the carrier we flew in on. God's grace is infinite. Unlike the Argentine government, He could afford to protect more than one airline.

scraped.title: It’s Still Important to Release the Epstein Files
scraped.description: Americans deserve to know the truth.
scraped.author: Luke Nicastro
scraped.body_text:
Americans deserve to know the truth.

As the recent election blowout demonstrates, many Americans are upset with their political leaders, especially because of the wars and their consequences, such as high fuel costs, food inflation, and the like. Americans are becoming acutely aware there is a malign influence over the policies of our political elites which appear to be unconcerned about the needs of the citizens. An increasing number of people feel that, no matter who or what they vote for, nothing changes. This growing disconnect between the will of the voters and the policies pursued in Washington raises important questions about who exercises influence over our political leaders and how that influence is maintained.

Time has exposed a conspicuous pattern that there are people who experience extraordinary financial success due to special inside access and knowledge. Jeffrey Epstein appeared to have been a beneficiary of, and a conduit for special access to, an unusual degree of wealth and power. He and his associates also appear to have been involved in disgusting and illegal behavior which could have been and could still be used to blackmail powerful people.

The Epstein operation appeared to follow a pattern which mimicked the initiation process used by the criminal underworld. Street gangs and the Mafia often require an aspiring member to commit a felony to join. The gang could destroy the new member by revealing their felony to the authorities, thus assuring loyalty. Participation in the trafficking and abuse of under-age girls and boys is an easy hook to attract ambitious and powerful opportunists, who seek illicit pleasure while grasping for more influence, power, and wealth.

Those who appeared to be part of Epstein’s circle in America have largely avoided negative consequences for their disgusting and potentially illegal behavior, even though there are scores of victims who have been ignored by the authorities for decades. Epstein himself was the perfect example. Decades ago, prosecutors submitted evidence that he abused more than 30 girls. Yet Epstein, who was able to call on his influential friends in government and finance, went an astonishing length of time before even being charged. And unsurprisingly, the victims were kicked to the curb. These repulsive abuses are still unaddressed because the Justice Department has willfully hidden millions of files and refused to expose the perpetrators, while “accidentally” exposing a number of the victims.

With the recently submitted bipartisan Epstein Files Transparency Act II (H.R. 9694), Reps. Thomas Massie (R-KY), Ro Khanna (D-CA), and others are seeking through legislation to neutralize the trickery the Department of Justice has been employing to block the release of the millions of files still withheld from the public.

The revelation of the remaining Epstein Files will hopefully provide us all a look at who is part of the ring of bad actors. This additional information should produce a clearer and better understanding of this grievous problem, and hopefully the tools and awareness to break the cycle of abuse and corruption.

After our recent and historic electoral rejection, both parties in Congress ignored the message and reelected the same bought-and-paid-for leadership, which has maintained the tired, out-of-touch policies. No matter what the electorate does, there appears to be a continuity of agenda that is rarely derailed. We end up continuing profligate spending on never-ending wars at the expense of America. Our families are suffering, our health care is not creating good outcomes for many, the middle class is rapidly unraveling, we have serious drug issues, our cities are decaying, schools are floundering, civil society is fraying, our manufacturing base is eroding, but unsurprisingly there are always many billions of dollars for our gold-plated military to pursue foreign wars. Most tragically, these wars fail to achieve their stated goals, nor do they provide any benefit for America. Not to mention all the American citizens killed and maimed (both physically and mentally) by these wars. Or the millions of innocent foreigners killed and violated.

It is time we start to expose these bad actors and their enablers in an effort to neutralize their dark influence. The people so far connected to Epstein can’t be the only ones. There are probably many more abusers and bad actors following the same model. It is time to expose them. What we have seen is a start, but the rest could be much worse, or the government wouldn’t have put so much effort into suppressing the information. Look at how much effort and money was leveraged to defeat Massie in his primary this past spring. Those implicated by the files are not casually concerned about their contents. The Epstein Class is terrified of the damage that could be caused by these revelations.

The American people deserve to understand the forces shaping their government’s decisions, particularly those involving war and peace. Whether Epstein's network exercised any influence over those decisions remains an unanswered question. Full disclosure, consistent with the protection of victims, is an essential step toward establishing the truth and restoring public confidence in our political institutions.

George D. O’Neill, Jr., is a member of the board of directors of the American Ideas Institute, which publishes The American Conservative , and an artist who lives in rural Florida.

This is not a paywall!

Your support helps us continue our mission of providing thoughtful, independent journalism. With your contribution, we can maintain our commitment to principled reporting on the issues that matter most.

scraped.title: Two Cheers for the Puritans
scraped.description: This Thanksgiving, spare a thought for the grim Calvinists who made our country possible.
scraped.author: Jude Russo
scraped.body_text:
This Thanksgiving, spare a thought for the grim Calvinists who made our country possible.

It is unfortunate but undeniable that there are no great Thanksgiving movies. Alone among our great national celebrations, Turkey Day is bereft of an adequate cinematic accompaniment. (Yes, I’m aware of the horribly unfunny and overrated Planes, Trains and Automobiles .)

In view of this lack, I decided this year to experiment a little, ultimately landing on Cromwell , the 1970 epic featuring Richard Harris in the titular role and Alec Guinness as King Charles I. It’s a fun flick, even if it often departs from the historical record; the battle scenes are excellent, and Guinness gives a splendid portrayal of the high-minded yet sensitive Charles. And it’s seasonally appropriate, as black-frocked, buckle-hatted Puritans constitute the motive force behind the film’s action.

For our own Pilgrims were Puritans, as every schoolboy knows. Cromwell himself even contemplated emigrating to Massachusetts, and might have done so had his war gone differently.

But what, anyway, is (or was) a Puritan? H.L. Mencken famously defined the persuasion as “the haunting feeling that someone, somewhere, may be happy.” More soberly, though perhaps less accurately, they were reformed Protestants who first emerged in the Elizabethan era. They sought to purify of Romish influence that great, shambling compromise known as the Church of England—hence “Puritans”—and, despite the monolithic way in which we speak of them today, they were by no means homogeneous.

Those of their number who first settled New England’s rocky shores, for example, were part of a “congregationalist” or “separatist” minority who held, contra most Puritans, that there should be no national church, instead entrusting autonomy to every individual congregation. (The majority of their coreligionists instead wanted a more organized state establishment, something like that of Presbyterian Scotland).

But all Puritans agreed on the basics. They opposed ritual and most hierarchy (bishops & co. had to go). They were Calvinist in theology, and tended to take the individual rather than the community as their unit of analysis. They wanted to abolish the saints and the many wonderful feast-days that still adorned the English calendar, replacing these with a relentless focus on the sabbath. They emphasized the reading of Scripture and preaching—which last was particularly alarming to conservative stalwarts. (“There should be more praying and less preaching,” the royalist Duke of Newcastle pronounced , “for much preaching breeds faction.”)

In class terms, they were for (and of) the rising, largely urban bourgeoisie, their worldview being peculiarly conducive to capitalist accumulation. Politically, they aligned with Parliament against the king. And although they sought the warrant of antiquity for their beliefs, professing to take their religion straight from the Bible and their insistence on parliamentary prerogative from the medieval and Anglo-Saxon past, they were in fact radical innovators.

The Puritans were the makers of England’s civil war, which used to be called by some the “Puritan Revolution,” and of that great democratic experiment which collapsed into regicide and dictatorship before it could really get going. Theirs was a doctrine, one historian tells us , “which gave men courage to fight tenaciously, if necessary alone. It supplied a superb morale.” From their revolution came—eventually—modern capitalism, the mass press, political liberalism, even the notion of civic consciousness . (Here I should note that, had I lived in those heady times, I would as a papist perforce have enlisted on the other side. But, fair-minded modern that I am, I can appreciate much of what they left us.)

It is a legacy that arguably includes the United States itself. In his magisterial Ideological Origins of the American Revolution , the late Bernard Bailyn adduced the “political and social theories of New England Puritanism” and the “radical social and political thought of the English Civil War” as two of our Revolution’s most important ideological wellsprings (the others being the republican literature of classical antiquity and Enlightenment philosophy).

This debt is illustrated by a wonderful episode that occurred during John Adams’ and Thomas Jefferson’s diplomatic missions in Europe—the former to the Court of St. James, the latter to Versailles—when the two Founders had an opportunity to tour the English countryside together. Among the stops were the battlefields of Edgehill and Worcester, where the forces of king and parliament had clashed nearly a century and a half before. As Adams relates :

Edgehill and Worcester were curious and interesting to us, as Scenes where Freemen had fought for their Rights. The People in the Neighbourhood, appeared so ignorant and careless at Worcester that I was provoked and asked, “And do Englishmen so soon forget the Ground where Liberty was fought for? Tell your Neighbours and your Children that this is holy Ground, much holier than that on which your Churches stand. All England should come in Pilgrimage to this Hill, once a Year.”

His Rotundity overdid it, perhaps, but a large measure of gratitude is clearly owed to the dour men who won those victories.

Nor should we forget their confreres on the other side of the Atlantic, who largely kept out of the fray. At the same time that the Roundheads were completing their final destruction of the Cavaliers, the early New Englander Thomas Shepard was writing his A Defence of the Answer , a now forgotten work that contains one of the most stirring and peculiarly American expressions of thankfulness ever penned. “What shall we say,” Shepard asked ,

of the singular providence of God bringing so many shiploads of His people through so many dangers, as upon eagles’ wings, with so much safety from year to year? The fatherly care of our God in feeding and clothing so many in a wilderness, giving such healthfulness and great increase of posterity? What shall we say of the work itself of the kingdom of Christ? And in the form of a commonwealth erected in a wilderness, and in so few years brought to that state scarce the like can be seen in any of our English colonies in the richest places of this America after many more years standing? That the Lord hath carried the spirits of so many of His people through all their toilsome labor, wants, difficulties, losses, etc., with such a measure of cheerfulness and contention?

Happy Thanksgiving, all.

Before joining the magazine, he spent nearly a decade working on defense and foreign policy in both government and industry, most recently as National Security Advisor to U.S. Senator Josh Hawley. He has also worked at the Congressional Research Service, the Department of the Navy, the National Defense University, and several defense contractors.

items.summary: Under President Clinton, the U.S.-led West set the stage for the Ukraine War. The post Europe Is Wrong to Dismiss Russian Demands for Common Security appeared first on The American Conservative. Russia Europe Is Wrong to Dismiss Russian Demands for Common Security Under President Clinton, the U.S.-led West set the stage for the Ukraine War. Credit: Alexandros Michailidis/Shutterstock With direct talks between the United States, Russia, and Ukraine resuscitated, a seemingly new item is dominat...

scraped.title: Europe Is Wrong to Dismiss Russian Demands for Common Security
scraped.description: Under President Clinton, the U.S.-led West set the stage for the Ukraine War.
scraped.author: Jude Russo
scraped.body_text:
Under President Clinton, the U.S.-led West set the stage for the Ukraine War.

With direct talks between the United States, Russia, and Ukraine resuscitated, a seemingly new item is dominating the discussion. In previous rounds, media attention had focused narrowly on two items: 1) security guarantees for Ukraine, possibly including NATO membership, and 2) Ukraine’s territorial integrity.

But as the latest round opened in Abu Dhabi on November 10, Moscow made it clear that “one way or another, the settlement in Ukraine will be linked to a new security architecture on the European continent. These are two component parts, and neither can exist without the other,” in the words of the Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov.

Washington then signaled that the Americans were on the same page. The U.S. envoy Jared Kushner announced that discussions would include “the need for a broader European security architecture.” President Donald Trump told reporters that the agreement being negotiated would “involve all of Europe.”

Much of Europe reacted with apoplectic rage. Russia should not be rewarded for their aggression with a new sphere of influence, European leaders said. There is no need for a new security architecture in Europe, they insisted , as NATO already provides a European security architecture. The problem, they added, is that Russia took a hammer to European security. Kaja Kallas , the European Union high representative of foreign affairs and security policy, and António Costa , the European Council president, led the charge in this rhetorical campaign.

These European claims are wrong. NATO is not a European security architecture. Russia (and a host of other countries) are part of Europe, but not part of NATO. The U.S. (and Canada and most of Turkey) are in NATO, but not in Europe. NATO expansion after the Cold War moved the line that divided Europe further east, encompassing neighbors of Russia while excluding Russia. NATO’s eastward expansion laid a foundation not for security, but for conflict.

In a 2007 speech to the Munich Conference on Security Policy, Putin asked, “Against whom is this expansion intended?” NATO, he pointed out, is a military alliance. Old assurances that NATO was merely “defensive” died in 1999 with NATO’s new Strategic Concept . NATO’s heart had been the Article 5 pledge among members to defend against “an armed attack against one or more” of its members. The new strategic concept, for the first time, removed the defensive restriction, declaring that the arrangements “also enable NATO's forces to carry out non-Article 5 crisis response operations.”

It must also be pointed out that it was not Russia who first destroyed the security architecture and brought war to Europe. It was NATO, led by the U.S. under President Bill Clinton, with the 1999 bombing of Serbia without a UN Security Council resolution. It was NATO that first violated the sovereignty of a nation with its 38,000 bombing missions over Yugoslavia. After the Cold war, it was NATO that most flagrantly violated the territorial integrity of a European nation when it sliced Kosovo off of Yugoslavia.

Clinton had repeatedly assured Russia’s President Boris Yeltsin that NATO expansion was not aimed at Russia and was not a threat. Yet in attacking Yugoslavia, NATO bombed a historic Russian ally mere weeks after the accession of Poland, Hungary, and the Czech Republic in the first violation of NATO’s promise not to expand east. Russia is now guilty of violating the sovereignty and territorial integrity of a European nation, but it was not the first to do so in the post–Cold War period.

Not only should European leaders be more open to including discussion of a broader European security architecture in the Russia–Ukraine peace talks, they should not be acting shocked or surprised. Its inclusion has been the refrain, not just of Putin, but of every Russian leader since the close of the Soviet Union.

In December 2021, weeks before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Putin demanded negotiations on the broader security architecture, reminding the U.S. and NATO of their post–Cold War promise and their assurances under the NATO-Russia Founding Act . Moscow demanded that NATO had to “refrain from any further enlargement of NATO, including the accession of Ukraine” and that NATO “shall not deploy military forces and weaponry” on the territory of any country that joined NATO after the May 1997 signing of the NATO-Russia Founding Act .

It was not the first time Putin had called for a European security architecture that respected Russian concerns. Two decades ago, in his 2007 Munich speech, Putin stressed the need to “seriously think about the architecture of global security.” He insisted that “NATO expansion does not have any relation with… ensuring security in Europe. On the contrary, it represents a serious provocation.” He called on “responsible and independent partners” to “work together in constructing a fair and democratic world order that would ensure security and prosperity not only for a select few, but for all.”

Putin was not the first. At the close of the Cold War, Mikhail Gorbachev, the last leader of the Soviet Union, proposed a security architecture free from lines dividing Russia and the West. President George H.W. Bush seemingly supported the idea, but Clinton nevertheless deepened the divide and moved it further east. It was that missed opportunity that paved the road to the Ukraine War. As early as 1989, Gorbachev had spoken of the chance for “one Europe.” He declared Europe “our common home” and spoke of “Europe from the Atlantic to the Urals.” Gorbachev envisioned a European security architecture in which each country, including Russia, would be an equal partner, free from blocs and hegemons.

After Gorbachev, Yeltsin would pick up the mantle. At an explosive turning point in 1994, at a summit in Budapest, Yeltsin repeated Moscow’s rejection of NATO enlargement and warned that Ukraine must never be permitted to enter NATO. He warned of a coming “cold peace.” Arguing that Russia and NATO are “no longer adversaries” but “partners,” he said that a new security architecture must “not create new divisions, but promote European unity.”

The next year, a frustrated and angry Yeltsin would ask Clinton, “How do you think it looks to us if one bloc continues to exist while the Warsaw Pact has been abolished? It’s a new form of encirclement if the Cold War bloc expands right up to the borders of Russia.” He would then tell Clinton that, instead, “We need a new structure for pan-European security.”

In 2008, Russian leaders were still issuing the same pleas. In his Draft Treaty on European Security , President Dmitry Medvedev envisioned a pan-Euro-Atlantic and Eurasian security treaty in which no nation could strengthen its own security at the cost of another’s. He proposed a wider Article 5–like commitment, inviting all nations “from Vancouver to Vladivostok.”

European leaders have the right to reject a new, inclusive security architecture. But they are wrong to insist an adequate European security structure already exists, and they are wrong to pretend that it was Russia alone, or first, who undermined the post-Cold War order in Europe. And they are being disingenuous when they feign surprise that Moscow should now reiterate its longstanding demands for inclusive security. If a lasting peace is to come to Europe, then the architecture of its security will need to include all of Europe.

Ted Snider is a contributing editor for The American Conservative . He is also a frequent contributor to Responsible Statecraft and other outlets.

scraped.title: Hegseth's 'hunt and kill' message draws mixed reception in LatAm
scraped.description: The defense secretary sealed some new security deals last week, but the limits of military cooperation were clear
scraped.h1: Hegseth's 'hunt and kill' message draws mixed reception in LatAm
scraped.body_text:
The defense secretary sealed some new security deals last week, but the limits of military cooperation were clear

During a whirlwind trip through Latin America last week, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth traveled to Bogota and vowed to “hunt and kill” people he labeled “narcoterrorists.”

Colombia’s foreign minister made clear that joint military operations on Colombia soil would require congressional approval. That exchange captured the lesson of the trip: while many governments in the region welcome U.S. assistance in countering transnational criminal organizations, few have publicly embraced Hegseth’s approach of using military forces to “kill” versus “capture” suspected traffickers.

And, while Hegseth returned with new defense agreements, the details of those agreements show the limits of which governments are willing to cooperate and how far they are willing to go in the Pentagon’s renewed “war” on drugs.

Hegseth began his travels into the region with an unannounced stop in Venezuela , where he signed a binational defense agreement with Venezuelan’s Minister of Defense General Gonzalez Lopez, with Venezuela’s Acting President Delcy Rodriguez watching. Gonzalez Lopez has been under U.S. sanctions since 2015 for human rights abuses during this time as head of Venezuela’s intelligence service.

Hegseth called Venezuela a “compliant security partner,” and its leaders openly welcomed closer military cooperation in public. But even compliant Caracas left the question open of allowing U.S. forces to conduct combat operations on-the-ground in the country. The Venezuelan Defense Ministry has stated renewed cooperation can only exist with respect for Venezuelan sovereignty and preservation of Venezuelan military command and control over its own force . Delcy Rodriguez and Gonzalez Lopez, as well as Cabello Rondon and Padrino Lopez, may be less of security ‘partners’ that the U.S. wants, particularly without coercive and transactional military and economic leverage.

Next, Hegseth flew to Colombia, where he donated a used, older model, C-130H , primarily as a replacement for a similar model aircraft Colombia lost in a crash just eight months prior. It was a nice gesture, but didn’t increase Colombia’s capacity beyond where it was earlier this year. What he really hoped to secure was Colombia’s agreement for joint U.S.-Colombia operations on the ground in the country. This didn’t happen; instead, Colombia’s foreign minister Bula Escobar said such a move would require congressional approval . Perhaps a lesson for Hegseth… in a democracy, the long-term commitment of the military to combat operations is the responsibility of the democratically elected legislature, not a minister, and not even just a president.

Then, it was off to Ecuador. A country in which U.S. Special Operations Forces have already been engaged in on-the-ground combat operations, without full public disclosure to the U.S. Congress. The Pentagon itself confirmed “joint maritime interdictions and combined kinetic operations” by U.S. and Ecuadorian military forces.

On September 24th, the Government of Ecuador, in fact the president of Ecuador himself, released public images of U.S. Marine Special Operations Command forces on-the-objective, potentially firing their weapons at the target building while approaching it and then later in the room where arrests were made , during Ecuadorian counter-drug raids. While the White House notified Congress on March 9 of a joint strike conducted three days earlier, no specific War Powers Resolution report to Congress has yet occurred for either the September 24 operation nor U.S. operational support near the objective on August 7.

Next up was Honduras, where the biggest news was a joint U.S.-Honduran declaration on National Defense Areas , with the potential to militarize Honduras’ borders. What is not clear is why the U.S. needed to sign onto an agreement with Honduras on how Honduras categorizes its own internal territory. Also uncertain is an actual designation of such NDAs, as no specific locations or boundaries were announced , and Honduras has not announced the actual authorities military forces would be granted in these areas.

All the while, back in Washington, select members of the Organization of American States (OAS) met to discuss activating the Rio Treaty in response to the Hemispheric threat posed by transnational criminal organizations. In Washington, the OAS members discussed Article 6, which calls for consultation of members on other threats to peace in the hemisphere. In a vote of 14-2 (with Brazil and Uruguay against, and The Bahamas abstaining), the OAS countries agreed to convene their foreign ministers within 75 days to address transnational drug trafficking and terrorism to consider diplomatic and/or legal measures to address the threat .

The vote explicitly called for non-military measures, and neither endorsed past military action (including U.S. strikes on suspected drug boats) nor authorized future military operations. After the vote, the U.S. assistant secretary of State for the Western Hemisphere applauded the move, commenting on the path towards “inflicting sanctions and other consequences on the narcoterrorist organizations” . Such statements should be watched carefully, because “other consequences” under this week’s OAS Rio Treaty proposal does not include military action.

To top off the week, the Mexican Military captured Meza Flores , the leader of the Beltran Leyva organization who oversaw criminal operations in northern Sinaloa State . Mexico’s press release after the operations was unusually transparent, naming the special operations force involved in the operation, and citing the operation as a result of “coordination between intelligence agencies of the Secretariat of National Defense and the U.S.” in accordance with the existing bilateral cooperation framework. Mexico has been clear about not allowing U.S. combat forces to operate within its country.

Overall, the week showed governments across the Western Hemisphere are willing to work with the Trump Administration to counter transnational organized crime, but most will do so on their terms, particularly regarding actions within their own territories . The Western Hemisphere doesn’t belong to the U.S.; Washington should be reminded it must work by, with, and through sovereign nation states, and under the democratic authorities of its own country and legislature, if it aims to succeed in efforts to counter transnational threats.

Meanwhile, Hegseth took away the wrong lesson from his visit. During his travels, he and other senior Pentagon officials have publicly pledged to “hunt” and “kill” narcotics traffickers: “Narco terrorists should die, not be caught and released.” But this potentially illegal tactic is not embraced equally across the region, and is in fact countered by several of the most powerful countries in the region.

Mexican President Sheinbaum has pointed to existing protocols for intercepting vessels and arresting suspects, rejected proposed U.S. drone strikes inside Mexico, and made clear her expectations for Mexican security forces: execute arrest warrants issued by judges. Brazilian President Lula said authorities should bring suspects to trial and let courts determine their involvement in illicit trafficking.

It is especially true that most countries of the region don’t want U.S. military forces in their sovereign territory “hunting” and “killing.” Sharing intelligence, logistically supporting operations, and sending U.S. troops into combat are three different decisions; agreement on one implies little about a nation’s agreement on the others.

scraped.title: Are US aircraft carriers becoming $22 billion liabilities?
scraped.description: Spending more than $150 billion on carriers over the next 30 years might make sense in a world where a carrier’s offensive punch goes largely unchallenged
scraped.h1: Are US aircraft carriers becoming $22 billion liabilities?
scraped.body_text:
Spending more than $150 billion on carriers over the next 30 years might make sense in a world where a carrier’s offensive punch goes largely unchallenged

The Bunker appears originally at the Project on Government Oversight and is republished here with permission.

Armchair admirals like to quote presidents demanding to know “where are the carriers?” when trouble erupts somewhere around the world. That’s why there was a wave of stories last week when the U.S. carrier presence near Iran jumped from two to three. It was “a dramatic show of military might as President Donald Trump keeps his options open for next steps in the Iran war,” the Associated Press reported November 16. Two days later, when one of the carriers left the region, not so much. What had been a “dramatic show of military might” on Monday turned into a mere “shuffling of aircraft carriers in the Middle East” by Wednesday, the AP said .

Such high-seas tracking should come as no surprise. Crow’s nests and watchstanders have been replaced by satellites and websites . There are even websites dedicated to locating the U.S. Navy’s 11 aircraft carriers. These steel-hulled behemoths have been heralded as “4.5 acres of sovereign U.S. territory.” But they’re steadily becoming a 4.5-acre bull’s-eye.

If, as the AP says, the Navy is “shuffling” its carriers, it is a very expensive deck. A new projection by the Congressional Budget Office says the Navy’s next seven carriers will cost $22 billion each (planes not included ). That’s “much higher” than the $15.3 billion price tag contained in the Navy’s most recent 2025 projection (WARNING — MATH AHEAD: some of that 44% increase is due to inflation, because the higher current cost uses what dollars are worth in 2026; the prior estimate was calculated in 2024 dollars).

Spending more than $150 billion on carriers over the next 30 years might make sense in a world where a carrier’s offensive punch goes largely unchallenged. But that is changing — more accurate missiles are keeping carriers further way, beyond those missiles’ lethal range. And an ever-growing share of a carrier battle group is dedicated to defending the carrier itself from attack .

Just when does a $22 billion asset become a $22 billion liability?

A winged messenger from history Carrier pigeons ( Columba livia domestica , in Latin) may have a lesson for the Navy’s aircraft carriers ( Navis aeroplanorum , more or less): Know when your time is up. The Navy, which had been using the birds since the 1880s for communication (via a tube fastened to a leg), went on to employ them for World War II sub-hunting missions, or when radio silence was needed so foes couldn’t detect electronic transmissions. But improved wireless communications, including encryption, ended the carrier pigeon’s military career after World War II. That’s when U.S. Navy aircraft carriers began ruling the seas. The carrier pigeon served the nation well for about 70 years; the aircraft carrier has now spent as many years plying the world’s oceans. But its time is running out, too. One of those veteran carrier pigeons should fly into the Pentagon and deliver a message to Admiral Daryl Caudle, the chief of naval operations. An enlisted aide — of course — would remove the rolled-up message from the aluminum tube and read: “You gave up the carrier pigeon flock when it was time. Now is time to give up the aircraft carrier fleet .” Increasingly accurate, fast, and numerous carrier killers — ranging from barrages of sophisticated Chinese ballistic missiles to far simpler Iranian drones — make clear that the flattops’ days are numbered . As hard as it is for Navy buffs like The Bunker to admit, the sun is setting on these commanding but increasingly vulnerable symbols of American industrial intrepidity and U.S. military might. But will the Navy — and the nation — make the right choice? The problem actually is rooted — like so many national nightmares — on Capitol Hill. That’s because U.S. law requires the U.S. Navy to keep 11 aircraft carriers in its fleet. Having Congress dictate such force structure requirements makes about as much sense as a real-estate developer from Queens telling the Navy what kind of catapults it should use to launch its carrier-based aircraft… “Full speed reverse, Captain!” The above-mentioned Congressional Budget Office report says its “estimates of costs for Ford -class carriers do not include effects of potential changes to their design.” That’s a tart jab at Admiral (j.g.) Trump, who has insisted new carriers return to steam-launched catapults to put their planes into the air, instead of the more advanced electromagnetic versions. After a troubled start , the electric model makes a lot more sense . The change would no doubt cost billions and delay the carriers’ delivery by years. Congress made clear last week that Trump’s dream of replacing electro-magnetic catapults on the sea service’s new 1,100-foot-long carriers will remain just that. “Returning to steam is a non-starter, and everybody needs to understand that,” Senator Roger Wicker (R-MS), chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, told Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao during Cao’s November 17 nomination hearing to assume the post permanently. At that same session, Senator Tim Kaine (D-VA) told Cao that during Kaine’s recent visit to the USS Gerald R. Ford , the only carrier with electro-magnetic catapults, its crew was “ very complimentary ” toward the new hardware. “Just because the president directed it,” Kaine added , “I do hope you’ll consider the experience of those who’ve been operating these launches on the Ford … before you decide to go down a path that will be more expensive and also less capable.” The day before, the Senate Appropriations Committee warned (PDF) that changing catapults “would result in many billions of dollars in additional costs and many years in program schedule delays.” But bigger isn’t always better. Smaller is smarter There is a pro-big-carrier mindset in the Navy and its suppliers that believes these vessels can fend for themselves in future conflicts. That may be true for relatively minor-league skirmishes, like the current one with Iran. But a future clash with China would be a whole ‘nother thing . Instead of dozens of missiles, there could be hundreds, draining a carrier’s defenses. And disabling a carrier — keeping it from launching its warplanes — is just as militarily significant as destroying one. This is not a new debate. “The U.S. view of carrier invulnerability is a perilous assumption,” John Patch, a retired Navy commander, wrote in 2010. “If 9/11 taught Washington anything, it clearly demonstrated that fortress America was vulnerable in ways its citizens and defenders never imagined.” It’s a safe bet U.S. carriers would have to stay far enough away from a foe like China that their relatively short-legged fighters would be defanged . Beijing is now building its fourth carrier , with more likely to come. That’s led some to argue that the U.S. military should attack this growing Chinese fleet just like China plans to attack U.S. carriers. “The goal is to make China’s carrier program a costly liability rather than a winning advantage,” said an August report from the Center for Strategic and International Studies. Thankfully, from the Chinese perspective, the U.S. Navy has already achieved that goal. That’s why the Navy should begin funneling at least some of that $154 billion slated for future big-top carriers to smaller, less costly — less targetable — drone carriers. Spreading out U.S. naval firepower — distributed maritime operations , as the service calls it — is a Navy promise. But it can’t be a Navy priority because of the service’s continuing fealty to its flattops. A French defense contractor has proposed such a ship, and China — of course — is already developing one . The U.S. Navy is more interested in preserving the — if you’ll pardon the phrase — sunk costs of its existing and proposed carrier fleet. It’s limiting its ambition to developing drones that will share deck space with human-flown pilots aboard those humungous vessels. “It’s just tradition, the industrial base and some other old and musty arguments” that keep the U.S. Navy building the big carriers, former Pentagon deep thinker Thomas Barnett told The Bunker 15 years ago. “We should scale back our carrier design to something much cheaper and simpler. Think of mother ships launching waves of cheap drones — that would actually be more frightening and intimidating.” That would scare the Chinese. Not to mention hidebound Navy admirals and their sclerotic shipyards . Here’s what has caught The Bunker's eye recently → Carsenal of democracy The Pentagon is discussing deals with General Motors and Ford to help mass produce drones, the Wall Street Journal’s Sharon Terlep and Heather Somerville reported November 24. → Bombs away! Veteran Pentagon reporter Thomas E. Ricks reviewed three books that detail the promise — and peril — of air power, in the New York Times November 19. → Not how a democracy is supposed to act The Defense Department has gone to great lengths to hide information about the war with Iran, Missy Ryan wrote in The Atlantic November 22. Ford , the only carrier with electro-magnetic catapults, its crew was “ very complimentary ” toward the new hardware. “Just because the president directed it,” Kaine added , “I do hope you’ll consider the experience of those who’ve been operating these launches on the Ford … before you decide to go down a path that will be more expensive and also less capable.” The day before, the Senate Appropriations Committee warned (PDF) that changing catapults “would result in many billions of dollars in additional costs and many years in program schedule delays.”

But bigger isn’t always better.

There is a pro-big-carrier mindset in the Navy and its suppliers that believes these vessels can fend for themselves in future conflicts. That may be true for relatively minor-league skirmishes, like the current one with Iran. But a future clash with China would be a whole ‘nother thing . Instead of dozens of missiles, there could be hundreds, draining a carrier’s defenses. And disabling a carrier — keeping it from launching its warplanes — is just as militarily significant as destroying one.

This is not a new debate. “The U.S. view of carrier invulnerability is a perilous assumption,” John Patch, a retired Navy commander, wrote in 2010. “If 9/11 taught Washington anything, it clearly demonstrated that fortress America was vulnerable in ways its citizens and defenders never imagined.” It’s a safe bet U.S. carriers would have to stay far enough away from a foe like China that their relatively short-legged fighters would be defanged .

Beijing is now building its fourth carrier , with more likely to come. That’s led some to argue that the U.S. military should attack this growing Chinese fleet just like China plans to attack U.S. carriers. “The goal is to make China’s carrier program a costly liability rather than a winning advantage,” said an August report from the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

Thankfully, from the Chinese perspective, the U.S. Navy has already achieved that goal.

That’s why the Navy should begin funneling at least some of that $154 billion slated for future big-top carriers to smaller, less costly — less targetable — drone carriers. Spreading out U.S. naval firepower — distributed maritime operations , as the service calls it — is a Navy promise. But it can’t be a Navy priority because of the service’s continuing fealty to its flattops.

A French defense contractor has proposed such a ship, and China — of course — is already developing one . The U.S. Navy is more interested in preserving the — if you’ll pardon the phrase — sunk costs of its existing and proposed carrier fleet. It’s limiting its ambition to developing drones that will share deck space with human-flown pilots aboard those humungous vessels.

“It’s just tradition, the industrial base and some other old and musty arguments” that keep the U.S. Navy building the big carriers, former Pentagon deep thinker Thomas Barnett told The Bunker 15 years ago. “We should scale back our carrier design to something much cheaper and simpler. Think of mother ships launching waves of cheap drones — that would actually be more frightening and intimidating.”

That would scare the Chinese. Not to mention hidebound Navy admirals and their sclerotic shipyards .

→ Carsenal of democracy

The Pentagon is discussing deals with General Motors and Ford to help mass produce drones, the Wall Street Journal’s Sharon Terlep and Heather Somerville reported November 24.

→ Bombs away!

Veteran Pentagon reporter Thomas E. Ricks reviewed three books that detail the promise — and peril — of air power, in the New York Times November 19.

→ Not how a democracy is supposed to act

The Defense Department has gone to great lengths to hide information about the war with Iran, Missy Ryan wrote in The Atlantic November 22. The Pentagon declined to comment.
