items.title: If You Don’t Know Why You Should Be Grateful, Ask A Farmer
items.summary: The harvest is completely dependent on our work ethic, learning from experience, and Almighty God's protection and care.

scraped.title: If You Don't Know Why You Should Be Grateful, Ask A Farmer
scraped.description: The harvest is completely dependent on our work ethic, learning from experience, and Almighty God's protection and care.
scraped.author: Joy Pullmann
scraped.h1: If You Don’t Know Why You Should Be Grateful, Ask A Farmer
scraped.body_text:
The harvest is completely dependent on our work ethic, learning from experience, and Almighty God’s protection and care.

At a central Wisconsin free u-pick this harvest season, the bean and cabbage fields looked like flowers swarming with human bees, all eagerly doing work we’re told “Americans don’t do.”

“Look how many beans I have already,” a preschooler told his toddler sister. He turned to his mother, who picked in a flowered purple nursing dress as the baby sat nearby, sucking her lip in a wagon. “Mommy, look how many beans I have.”

“We’re going to do a lot of freezing this year, ’cause you love beans in the winter time, don’t you?” his mother replied. Twenty feet away, their pigtailed big sister picked in pink shorts and a Daisies Girl Scout vest. The vest must have been new, because it was blank and crisp.

Girl Scout Daisies are kindergarteners or first graders. At the Farm+Food Exploration Center , where the family was picking that day, Girl Scouts can earn up to 11 patches and badges. My farming family and their friends helped build the center, which opened just three years ago. It’s a gift from family farmers and other philanthropists to their community and country — a gift celebrating hard work and the gratitude you learn from sustaining yourself and others through it.

A few attendees looked like this u-pick involved more walking than they’ll do all month. Some were rolled out to the fields in wheelchairs or Gators to snag volunteer-picked produce. An older woman asked a crew-cutted football player if he’d help her pick corn. “Of course,” he replied. As they walked off to the field, he asked cheerily, “How’s your day going?”

One wheelchair-bound woman brought her golden retriever and standard poodle, who sense asthma attacks before she can. Her kids loaded her chair with produce. One field away, a footballer helped a petite elderly woman whack off a cabbage with a drywall blade, reportedly the tool du jour.

Our family has a black and white photo of a baby sitting on a now antique tractor, beaming. It could be any of my aunts, uncles, grandparents, great-aunts, great-uncles, or their neighbors, and that’s why we all argue about who it really is.

In my grandparents’ day, if people weren’t farmers themselves, they were usually connected closely to someone who was. They — and often their shoulders and calves — witnessed the sunup to sundown labor it took to keep three squares on everyone’s tables.

Many more people spent summers baling or harvests detasseling corn for seed companies or Augusts through Octobers seasonal potato grading and pea picking. They knew not just the aromatic smell of a dairy but the sandy roughness of a cow’s tongue, that cow pies don’t compost so well as horse douvers (my dad’s term), the smell of grain bins on dad when he returns home white as cornflour after a 3 a.m. emergency, and most of all just how hard it is to earn your daily loaf.

That deep cultural memory is all but gone now. Just 1 percent of Americans work on farms today. Every honest job is worthy of honor, but farming cultivates gratitude in a way that earning one’s living in a climate-controlled room tapping at a screen with an endless steaming mug of anything you want at your desk does not.

Farming is one of the few jobs in our ethereal age that requires constant interaction with physical reality. The real factor might make “dirty” jobs the best jobs. My dad says constant interaction with physical realities that are often completely outside your control teaches gratitude, humility, and above all human dependence on the Almighty. Neither you or I, after all, can make it rain. Without rain, we all die. And Who made the rain to water the earth?

The more people live in virtual unreality, the less we viscerally understand about physical reality. That’s an unexamined side effect of offshoring and global supply chains. People used to making just about anything in the world show up on their doorsteps within three days so long as they have the right credit card limit are less able to grasp the many immovable limits of human existence. Our sexes are fixed. Many things about our health, dispositions, and abilities are fixed. Our family is given to us, we don’t choose them.

If you’re a farmer, the harvest — and thus your entire livelihood — is dependent on Almighty God’s protection every day from predators, diseases, hail, drought, and even too much sunshine. What’s true for farmers is true for all of us, the Holy Bible teaches.

None of us can by our own will guarantee our next breath or heartbeat. All Elon Musk’s money cannot make his soul live forever. Every person is dependent on God like newborn babies are dependent on their mothers and fathers. And every good thing we have we receive from His hand.

This people closer to the elements often understand more deeply than those of us who work with words, spreadsheets, ones, and zeroes. That’s why farming events like Becknology Days are full of Bible verses and the fifth-generation family that owns Beck’s Hybrids, America’s third-largest seed company, keeps a chaplain for staff.

When we receive gifts from God we do not deserve — like food, air, sunlight, water, and children — in a well-ordered person it will prompt a deep desire to go and do likewise. And thus generosity is the first word that comes to mind when I think of that side of my family.

Farmers are the kind of people who bring in the harvest for a family whose father was just lost in an accident, on top of needing to work 24/7 to bring in their own. They are the kind of people like a rancher we didn’t know from Adam who showed up when my family’s borrowed RV choked on an offramp in nowhere, Wyoming. Not only did he own a giant truck, he kept straps in that bad boy big enough to tow our camper to the nearest campground. And he was willing to put himself at the service of stranded strangers for nothing but a smile and a handshake.

America makes fewer of these people now. We can debate why another day. Today, we are focusing on what is good, and expressing gratitude for it. That is what Thanksgiving is for. It is a time to give, reflect on what we’ve been given, and return thanks for it to our Creator.

The thanksgiving attitude of compulsive generosity is why my family and their farming friends created the Farm+Food Center, which is a hard-to-summarize hybrid between a children’s museum, an ag expo, and a community event hub. There, even people who have no farming connections can experience modern American farming culture, science, and fun.

They can see how bugs adore cabbage. They can watch a tractor sift potatoes out of the ground whole, like magic. They can pick free sweet corn and green beans. They can get dirt on their shoes and sunshine on their skin. And if they want more contact with realities that turn hearts towards eternity, they can sign up for classes, volunteering, and even apprenticeships and jobs.

The family with four children ages first grade and younger walked away from that August u-pick with two five-pound mesh bags full of green beans, one full of cabbage, and one full of potatoes. It surrounded the baby’s carseat inside their canvas wagon. Those hard-working tots are not only going to eat green beans in the wintertime, now they know how green beans grow, and what it feels like to pick each one with your own hands.

items.title: This Free New Curriculum Can Revive Love Of Western Civilization Among American Kids
items.summary: Our hope is that schools will start teaching Western civilization once again.

scraped.title: Free New Curriculum Can Revive Love Of Western Civilization
scraped.description: A new curriculum offered at no cost can help schools and parents revive study of Western civilization and the powerful lessons it teaches.
scraped.author: Eric Coykendall
scraped.h1: This Free New Curriculum Can Revive Love Of Western Civilization Among American Kids
scraped.body_text:
Our hope is that schools will start teaching Western civilization once again.

Fully celebrating Thanksgiving Day in America requires a lesson in history and ideas that was once common but has grown increasingly rare, especially among our nation’s schoolchildren.

Who were the Pilgrims? Why did they and other European settlers risk their lives crossing the Atlantic? American students increasingly do not know the answers to those questions. While they learn a little American history, they learn next to nothing about the Western and European history from which it grew.

For decades, Western civilization has been gradually pushed aside as a subject in public schools. As far back as 1998, according to the U.S. Department of Education, just 9 percent of high-school graduates had taken a course in Western history or civilization. Since then, that statistic has not improved. Over the past three decades, the emphasis on standardized testing in reading and mathematics has squeezed out history instruction further. Between 1999 and 2016, elementary schools lost nearly an hour of social studies instruction each week.

Restoring this narrative, historical education is the purpose of The Golden Thread , a new series of Western civilization textbooks published by Encounter Books, together with a curriculum developed by Hillsdale College.

At Hillsdale College, we work with a network of almost a hundred K-12 schools around the country as well as our own: Hillsdale Academy is a private K-12 school adjacent to the Hillsdale College campus. We provide resources at no cost to help schools in our network. We develop curriculum and train their teachers, leaders, and boards. We have a strong interest in good curriculum being available for those schools.

When Encounter Books approached us a few years ago about creating a new set of Western civilization texts, we were thrilled. Our schools never stopped teaching Western civilization, but access to good textbooks had dried up.

But a textbook is only a starting point. Most teachers want lesson plans, model tests and quizzes, and other resources that will help inform their teaching. To this end, we created The Golden Thread Curriculum to accompany the two-volume Golden Thread textbooks — themselves published by Encounter Books and written by the distinguished historians James Hankins and Allen Guelzo. Hillsdale has developed the accompanying curriculum to support teachers as they bring these books into the classroom.

The curriculum helps teachers trace the “golden thread” of Western civilization from the Greeks to the Romans, through Christianity, the early Middle Ages, the Renaissance, the Reformation, the Enlightenment, and beyond. This golden thread includes major ideas that inform us as Americans, that certainly informed our founding, and that inform how we relate to one another in politics, philosophy, religion, art, music, trade, and so much more.

All of these supporting materials are available free of charge at goldenthreadcurriculum.com .

Our hope is that, by building these materials, we will create new demand among schools — that schools will start teaching Western civilization once again. Public school students in Michigan , for instance, may learn about the history of Thanksgiving in an American history class, but they never study it as a chapter in a continuous history of their inherited, Western tradition. The prescribed sequence for high school instead favors “world history,” which sounds like a broad opportunity to teach both Western history and a variety of other histories, but has been a Trojan Horse for overturning meaningful engagement with our own tradition.

“World history” is too broad a subject to teach in much detail at the secondary level, and this lack of detail or narrative is its most salient feature. Rather than engaging with unique and powerful stories of individuals bearing some connection to our students, world history is directed by a multiplicity of impersonal forces, best described at the level of statistics, trends, and, of course, group grievances.

To teach Western civilization properly, we trace its narrative history. We look at the individual stories and ask: Why did these people act this way? Why did they decide to move their families across a hostile ocean and risk life on an unexplored continent? We put ourselves in their situations to be formed by their experiences.

We do so for reasons both prudential and moral. By studying the narrative of Western civilization, we consider real people dealing with real circumstances and making decisions with moral import. How do their decisions inform us? Are they examples we should follow? How do their beliefs, ideas, and institutions inform our own? To know them is to know something important about ourselves.

Private schools and charter schools have more flexibility to give their students better intellectual fare than meager “world history” standards like those on offer in Michigan. Reinvesting in Western civilization curriculum in those settings is a no-brainer. The state of Idaho has recently reformed its world history standards in favor of honoring our own tradition, and other states should follow suit. For the many homeschool parents all over the country looking for good resources, I would recommend this curriculum to them as well. Even teachers who can’t use the entire curriculum right away can benefit from much of the background to inform their teaching.

Thanksgiving is an ideal time to reflect not only on our personal blessings, but on the people in the past who made our way of life possible. Americans share in a debt of gratitude to our ancestors and to the land and tradition that calls us to something higher than ourselves. Reading The Golden Thread and teaching the accompanying curriculum from Hillsdale College is an excellent place to start learning about that debt.

items.title: Johnny Depp Gives Us An Ebenezer Scrooge Without Redemption
items.summary: In Ti West's Ebenezer, the Ghosts do not care what happens to Scrooge. There is no light, no warmth, no real hope.

scraped.title: Johnny Depp Gives Us An 'Ebenezer' Scrooge Without Redemption
scraped.description: In Ti West's 'Ebenezer,' the Ghosts do not care what happens to Scrooge. There is no light, no warmth, no real hope.
scraped.author: Nathan Stone
scraped.h1: Johnny Depp Gives Us An Ebenezer Scrooge Without Redemption
scraped.body_text:
In Ti West’s Ebenezer , the Ghosts do not care what happens to Scrooge. There is no light, no warmth, no real hope.

Fun fact: since 1901 , there have been dozens, if not hundreds , of adaptations of Charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol made, including from cultural heavyweights like Mickey Mouse, the Muppets, and Looney Tunes. In addition to film and TV renditions, the story has also in spired operas, stage plays (including one entirely in Klingon ), radio plays, ballets, and comics. It’s a glutted field to play in. Not that another version can’t be made. It’s just that anyone who takes up the challenge needs to figure out how to be original enough to separate his version from the rest of the pack while still being faithful to the source material.

Ti West, best known for directing horror movies like 2022’s X and 2024’s MaXXXine , takes two swings at originality in his version, just titled, Ebenezer . The first is his star. Ebenezer marks Johnny Depp’s “first major Hollywood feature” since his 2022 trial with his #MeToo ex-wife, Amber Heard. There is no question that Depp is a brilliant actor. And he does look like the classic depictions of Ebenezer Scrooge — thin, stooped, wizened, a man eaten hollow from the inside out. He even gets a few great moments; the best is his screaming at his younger self who has just thrown away his relationship with Belle, the woman he loved. “Go after her!” Depp shouts. “If you do not, you will regret it for the rest of your life.” And when his younger self, of course, does not, Scrooge’s Depp runs out shouting Belle’s name. It is a powerful moment.

Unfortunately, Depp, for most of the film, is on autopilot, mixing all the cliches associated with Ebenezer Scrooge with yet another watered down knock-off of Captain Jack Sparrow. Depp scowls and mutters and snarls as so many Scrooges before him have while, periodically, engaging in “comedic” behavior, like raising the window cover of his office door to shout “Humbug!” multiple times at his nephew, Fred. Compare that to George C. Scott, for example, who played his Scrooge as a man who believes himself the only man wise to the con of Christmas . Here, there is too much quirkiness and no depth. Quirky Jack Sparrow worked in Pirates of the Caribbean because the entire world, with its sea monsters, undead pirates, and curses, was, itself, quirky. The same element is a black sheep in a story that ultimately is supposed to be about redemption.

West’s second swing is leaning into familiar territory and making Ebenezer a horror film. On paper, it makes a certain amount of sense . Even with the holiday setting, A Christmas Carol is a story that combines existential horror (a man haunted by actual ghosts) and psychological terror (a man being forced to confront his past and future). A horror leaning version could work and some of West’s additions here do work. Having Jacob Marley’s chains actively squeeze him, turning the chains into pythons instead of just dead weight is very effective. But for every step forward, there are four steps back. Some, like turning the other chained spirits into a zombie horde hunting Scrooge, are the equivalent of packing peanuts — annoying; there but with no weight. Others completely screw up Dickens’ story, with the Christmas Ghosts being the biggest sinners.

Beauty and terror can be mixed; the angels of the Bible do it all the time. But, here, West has gone with full horror that, like Depp’s performance, are by this point cliched. The Ghost of Christmas Past is a dead bride, complete with protruding spine and dead milk eyes. The Ghost of Christmas Present, besides being race-swapped, is a skeleton beneath his robe. These aesthetic changes would have been jarring but tolerable if the Ghosts still acted like themselves. In the book, the Ghosts haunt Scrooge to save him. His reclamation is the only reason why they appear. This doesn’t mean they treat him with kid gloves. Christmas Past not only makes him relive the mistakes of his past but then shows him what those mistakes have cost him. Christmas Present literally tells him that “in the sight of Heaven” he might be “more worthless and less fit to live” than millions like Tiny Tim. But the point is to shock Scrooge out of his old ways.

In Ebenezer , the Ghosts do not care what happens to Scrooge. Christmas Past treats her time with Scrooge as a robotic therapy session. Christmas Present is a glutton who literally yells at Scrooge that he doesn’t care what happens to him; showing Scrooge the present is just his job description. Gone is the light that comes from the Past; gone is the merry giant of Christmas Present who blesses Christmas dinners with incense. There is no light, no warmth, no real hope.

This is not surprising because West’s whole adaption is inverted. Watching the movie puts you on Scrooge’s side because you see how full of conmen, thieves, ingrates, and evil the world is. A blind beggar shows Scrooge that his malady is faked. Fezziwig, Scrooge’s first boss (“as hard and as ruthless as a rose petal”) is murdered by someone Fezziwig tried to help. Mr. Topper, a friend of Scrooge’s nephew, Fred, schemes with the founders of a charity to swindle Fred. Now West could have leaned into this angle, acknowledging that charitable giving, ultimately, rests on faith. Scrooge’s arc would then have been a rebirth of his faith. That would have been original and respectful of the source material. But he doesn’t, instead just playing through the motions of “Scrooge needs to learn not to be selfish,” for the umpteenth time. But this clashes with the world which West paints in very fine detail. Why shouldn’t Scrooge be selfish when the world actively wants to hurt him and everyone else?

It’s this dissonance that makes it impossible for Scrooge to be transformed by the Ghosts. He’s changed — he smiles more and treats Bob Cratchit better and gives a beggar his watch. But there is no indication that he has been reclaimed. No explosion of joy . No “back payments” made for the poor and needy. No prize turkey for the Cratchits (he buys a goose for Fred and his wife.) This is what ultimately ruins West’s adaption — it’s hollow man syndrome. If there is no sense that Scrooge was saved, there is no point in sitting through two hours just to see Johnny Depp go from “Humbug!” to “Merry Christmas,” especially with ticket prices what they are. Instead, find a version of A Christmas Carol you enjoy. With plenty to choose from, there has to be at least one.

scraped.description: ‘I am aging out of my chance to have a child,’ writes a 43-year-old woman who has never met the right guy. ‘I don’t know how to handle these emotions.’ Abigail Shrier weighs in.
scraped.author: Abigail Shrier
scraped.body_text:
Happy Thanksgiving, one and all! Freya here, the editor of Tough Love. I imagine a lot of you are in a turkey coma, surrounded by people you adore, feeling unutterably grateful—but I know some of you are not. That’s because, in the last few weeks, I’ve noticed an overwhelming theme in the letters Abigail has received: A lot of readers have asked her, “Why don’t I have a boyfriend yet?”

The question has come from women—and a couple of gay men—everywhere from the nation’s capital to the capital of Arkansas; most of them are in their early 30s, but since the dawn of the column, the same question has been asked by a 23-year-old in Arizona and a 52-year-old in Virginia. Nobody’s too young to feel lonely, or too old to date. But for everyone, there’s something about the holidays—when work is on pause and friends are scattered to the four corners of the earth—that makes you take a long, hard look at your life, and what’s missing.

Into that void steps Abigail, with a letter to a 43-year-old woman who’s always the bridesmaid, never the bride, and believes: “I am doomed to be a swinging single for the rest of my life.”

Abigail’s reply is a lament that we live in an age where it’s fashionable to pretend we can do without love. (It’s also a taste of what’s to come in Abigail’s next book, The Plot Against Love, which you can preorder now.) But it’s also, most importantly, a case for not giving up on the pursuit of love—because the prize is worth it. “If you found someone tomorrow, you could spend 50 years together,” writes Abigail. Enjoy! —Freya Sanders

Hi Abigail,

I don’t know if I have a problem, but here goes: The last of my unmarried, uncoupled, child-free friends is getting married this year. I am thrilled for her and happy to be involved in the wedding plans. However, it is stirring up what I call the “always a bridesmaid” blues: not envy, exactly, but an ache that I haven’t found what she has found. The fact that I am aging out of my chance to have a child is also bothering me a lot.

All of this, I know, is normal. But when I confide my feelings to friends, they mostly seem surprised. Despite years of listening to my dating stories, they somehow assumed that I had chosen not to get married and not to have children. I have always wanted to become a wife and mother—but they think the desire is new, spurred by age (which I find insulting) or because my friend is getting married. Maybe they got the wrong impression because I decided that I was going to live a full and happy and interesting life while looking for someone. Some of my friends allowed dating to consume them, and I was trying to avoid that.

So now I am struggling with two emotions: the despairing feeling that I am doomed to be a swinging single for the rest of my life (a great state for some, but not my preference) and the feeling that I’ve been abandoned by my friends, who somehow refuse to believe that all along I’ve wanted what they have. They now say things like, “You are dealing with the consequences of your choices.” Most of these are people who met their spouses by chance and many married in a whirlwind, but are now framing it as a sensible compromise that they made.

I don’t know how to handle these emotions beyond smiling in public and crying with Ben & Jerry’s in private. Any advice would be gratefully received.

—Mandy, 43

Mandy,

Almost a decade ago, I was introduced to a well-known Silicon Valley figure to whom I took an immediate dislike. We were chatting informally—this was not an interview, he made clear—but of course, it became one. I found myself pressing him on what we might lose as social media drew us into its quicksand. He rose to the defense of big tech with increasing irritability, as I needled him with social media’s human costs. I couldn’t stop myself, but neither could he.

At some point, he seemed to lose patience with me. “Look, do I know my neighbors? No, I don’t. Maybe I’m missing out,” he said, or something close to it, not sounding like he thought he was missing out. “But social media allows me to stay in touch with my closest friends all over the world.” That’s what he cared about. Not some neighbor he didn’t choose and might not even like.

Ross Douthat. Abigail Shrier. Douglas Murray. Niall Ferguson. Coleman Hughes. Caitlin Flanagan. Nellie Bowles. Arthur Brooks. Kat Rosenfield. Tyler Cowen. The voices you trust, all in one place.

Subscribe

That part of the conversation stayed with me. Because what he seemed to be saying was essentially this: I have the people I need. I don’t need a relationship with my neighbor.

As soon as we parted ways, I kicked myself for not having asked the most important follow-up question:

scraped.title: What We’re Grateful For
scraped.description: This Thanksgiving, Free Press staff and contributors count their blessings.
scraped.author: The Free Press
scraped.body_text:
This year, America celebrated 250 years since its founding. There were fireworks and parades, but of all the traditions this country has handed down, one of the best may be the one that arrives today: a day set aside, by Abraham Lincoln’s proclamation, to say thank you. This has also been a year in which much has felt uncertain—politically, technologically, economically—and everything seemed to speed up. Maybe that’s why, when we asked our Free Press staff and contributors what they’re grateful for, so many of their answers came back to slowing down and focusing on what’s right in front of us: new babies, a diner that doesn’t deliver, grandparents down the block. Others cast a much wider net and said they were grateful for a country that, at 250, still has its best days ahead of it.

Before we get to the responses, we want to express our collective gratitude for you, Free Press subscribers. You make everything we do possible. And if you’re not yet a paid subscriber, there’s no better time to join. Right now you can get 25 percent off your first year. Already a subscriber? You can give the gift of The Free Press at the same discount.

Get 25% Off

Happy Thanksgiving. —The Editors

As AI becomes more powerful and the headlines scarier, I’ve found myself grasping for the basics. I’m grateful for long, lazy meals at home, and my new hobby, which is hand-built pottery, which I’m terrible at, but you can’t touch your phone when it’s covered in clay. Every week, for a few hours, I gather with strangers, mostly women, and we all slap mud around while listening to jazz. It’s absolutely delightful, even though I have been told that my pieces give the impression that I am part of a court-ordered rehabilitation program.

Speaking of women, I’m grateful to all the ones in my life—cousins to co-workers—who show up as friends, mentors, and sounding boards. Lucky is a girl who has a big sister, and I have three. Plus, a very funny and fiercely loyal sister-in-law. Finally, always, my parents.

It’s impossible to answer the question “what am I most grateful for” both honestly and interestingly. The short answer is my wife, our daughters, their health, and the roof over our heads. But, important as all of that may be to me, it’s probably not that interesting to you. So here’s something a little further down my gratitude list this Thanksgiving: the American Republic.

scraped.title: The reality of Rejoin
scraped.author: Peter Mandelson
scraped.h1: The reality of Rejoin The EU will not rewrite its rules
scraped.body_text:
Mandelson spent four years as an EU commissioner. (JG Fox)

Mandelson spent four years as an EU commissioner. (JG Fox)

No one would open a complex negotiation with the European Commission for fun, or for want of anything better to do. For sure, Britain’s relationship with the EU is an important subject affecting the country’s core economic, defense, migration and energy policies, and Andy Burnham is asking legitimate questions about where the relationship goes in future.

But be under no illusion. The Brussels officials whose job it will be to negotiate any change in the relationship are tough and resolute for a reason: their single purpose on behalf of the member states is to protect the unity and indestructibility of the EU against all comers, including Brexit Britain, should it be necessary, eliminating risk of dilution, distraction or damage to the edifice of rules that keeps it running.

Among the key officials are those drawn from the trade directorate, which I headed as EU Trade Commissioner between 2004 and 2008, so I know well of whom I speak. I used to call them my “Taliban”: clever, talented people who are there to take a higher, almost religious, view of the EU’s core interests and who are deeply committed to the collective welfare of the member states. They are not intransigent, but nor are they about to undergo a British-induced Damascene conversion.

We can get a taste of what approach they will take by looking at Switzerland, whose latest deep single-market access agreement with the EU was signed this year, but whose negotiation began 12 years ago, in 2014. In fact, I remember receiving regular updates of the original challenging bilateral meetings even before then, back when I was a commissioner. Why has the process been so bumpy and protracted? Because, while rejecting full membership, Switzerland wanted access to the single market as well as retaining considerable control over its own laws, institutions and policies. This is anathema to the Commission. Had Switzerland opted for full membership, rather than its hybrid approach, the negotiation would have been far simpler and less painful, which is something the British government will now have in mind.

When conducting this sort of external negotiation, the Commission’s power derives from a key feature of its role more broadly. Its job is to arbitrate between the competing interests of the member states and, once an internal bargain is reached, it becomes the custodian of that bargain. Having brokered fragile compromises and trade-offs within its own side, the Commission will then do its utmost to stop disunity breaking out or the mandate being chiseled away. It has to keep its member states happy; so, when external negotiating partners complain about surprise ambushes by the Commission, these are often last minute bids made to keep the bloc united — as we saw recently over university tuition fees in Burnham’s reset agreement.

I point all this out not to be discouraging about the challenge of reversing or ameliorating Brexit. After all, if Ukraine can make progress negotiating with Brussels while keeping the Russian Army at bay, then so can we. But the British Government needs to have its eyes wide open as it considers any radical reframing of its relationship with the EU. Certainly, rejoining, which the Prime Minister has not ruled out, would require the sort of mega-deal which makes the recent reset look like a walk in the park. It is by no means an impossible task but its dimensions need to be clearly understood.

So, in practical terms, what would this entail?

Politically, if the Government decides that fundamentally changing the UK-EU relationship is desirable and viable, it requires the permission of the British people to do so at the next general election. Prefacing this with informal brainstorming with the EU is a good idea because it will clarify the options available. The public’s definitive verdict would then await a post-negotiation referendum, as Burnham has now clarified.

Throughout, the Prime Minister in particular, but also the Foreign Secretary, Chancellor and other ministers, will need to demonstrate considerable conviction and persuasiveness about why we need to roll back Brexit. The EU will want to know that the Government’s heart really is in a new beginning and that it can secure clear public backing for it.

An equivocal or wafer-thin public endorsement at the election would greatly worry the EU and make them question whether a multi-year negotiation would be worth the candle. The passions of 2016 are unlikely to be felt again, however, until the negotiation bears fruit. Before then, as we have already seen, the subject is more likely to be greeted with a public shrug or even a sigh, which will be disappointing for the Stay Out campaign, and for Nigel Farage, who probably thinks he is set to remake his political career on the back of a reinvigorated Brexit argument.

Should a mandate be won, though, the journey begins. Whitehall would need to divert from other pressing tasks, starting with increasing the number of its best policy officials, so as to match the knowledge and professional skills of the Commission. Given the Government’s other major priorities — for example, the Neets rollout, the design of new universal social care, long-term welfare reform and the defense overhaul — the implications of this for Whitehall’s human resources should not be underestimated. At the moment, it has the quantity of officials, but not necessarily enough with the weight and experience they would need to deal with Brussels.

Then, once a negotiation is underway, it will require a great deal of high-level ministerial attention over an extended period of time. The Commission will have its own mandate, obtained after lengthy EU internal discussion, but the British side will want to frame and influence the dynamic of the negotiation as much as it can, especially if it wants to broaden the discussion to EU reform. When I negotiated as the EU’s trade commissioner, I would give a lot of day-to-day latitude to my lead officials but there are many interventions that only a minister can make at the political level.

Personal relationships matter, and given that any negotiation between the UK and the EU will be an asymmetrical one, personal chemistry and impact will count for even more on our side. The EU will treat Britain as demandeur because we need the outcome we are seeking more than they do. I am not saying they will be indifferent to the result, and we are not supplicants — the Government must be careful not to give this impression — but the Commission will always ultimately be at an advantage, given the EU’s size and power.

If we are heading for anything like re-entry to the single market, with or without membership of the EU itself, the Government will need to contend with three main Commission negotiating parameters.

First, derogations from single market rules will not be allowed apart from where member states exceptionally allow themselves some slack — so cherry-picking or special perks will not be available for Britain. This does not matter in the large areas of trade where we are already aligned with the EU. It also does not mean joining the eurozone or Schengen where routine passport and border checks have been removed; but in every other respect, including free movement of people, the presumption will be that Britain fully respects the rules of the club it wants to use.

Second, Britain will have to pay properly for the privilege of participation in the single market, whether as an EU member or not. It is difficult to see what case Britain could make for renewing its original rebate, since the EU needs the money.

Third, Britain will not be allowed competitive or regulatory advantages over EU producers, farmers and retailers. This will perhaps be the most strict and complex of all the Commission’s conditions. Inevitably, it will apply to every sector and market, and to all technologies and services. For if Brexit has resulted in Britain benefiting from any market difference or technological edge, the Commission will seek a leveling of the playing field.

The biggest, but not sole, sensitivities for Britain will concern the regulation of our financial services sector and of AI. We currently have major competitive advantages in both: the former because of the City’s deep, historical, integrated capital market, and the latter because of Britain’s new regulatory attractiveness to start-up and scaling technology companies.

By Dominic Cummings

Some EU member states, on the other hand, seem envious, even resentful, of the City, and others are ready to take up arms against US tech firms. There is currently a prevailing taste for measures that will limit AI. While Britain rightly emphasizes the need for safety, security and trust in AI, we are clearly beating the EU as a premier location for tech investment. Just as the City of London is a global financial center which the EU could see as an asset, there are three principal centers for AI in the world, and London’s King’s Cross is one of them after Palo Alto and Shenzhen. It would be unthinkable for the Government to jeopardize this position, and it would be equally absurd for the Commission to expect us to do so for the sake of leveling the single market playing field. In reality, I would not expect them to ask for this.

If the Government were simply contemplating reducing trade frictions by joining the EU’s customs union, and losing the benefits (such as they are) of retaining an independent national trade policy, we would take on many EU rules but the level playing field would be less onerous. Negotiating access to the single market, however, without re-joining the EU, would mean embracing all the rules without having a vote on them — in effect, Britain would become a regulatory satellite of the EU.

This would inevitably raise huge business, public and political objections. It is why, should the Government decide that the status quo is unacceptable, ministers will be more likely to opt to re-enter the EU and become, once again, influential co-authors of the rules that bind us in every sector of the economy.

Is there any chance of a “best-of-both worlds” option? One in which Britain rejoins a different kind of EU, with more regulatory agility and geared more towards economic vitality?

We all remember David Cameron’s failure to “reform it from within” prior to the 2016 referendum. But his attempt was made too late, on the hoof, and it focused on the sensitive subject of migration. He thought that squaring a few heads of government over dinner would suffice. But his asks were not welcomed, particularly by Angela Merkel. I suspect the Burnham approach would be broader, better planned, advanced over a longer period of time and, consequently, taken more seriously — including by the Commission who, historically, have given a lot of attention to British policymakers and regulators.

A lot has changed since 2016 (including Merkel’s retirement), and growing public dissatisfaction is challenging the member-state complacency that was so much in evidence back then.

By Wolfgang Münchau

There are many in the EU who think that business and market regulation is far too restrictive and, in effect, anti-growth. There are also farsighted member state governments who see AI as an important source of productivity and growth and favor its development. The Draghi report presented to the Commission a few years ago actually attributed the extensive destruction of European businesses to the legal and regulatory burden imposed on them by EU law. Some reform has followed, and the Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, who was the author of much of the law-making, is now driving its revision.

So, while making radical reform a condition for Britain rejoining the EU is not practical, pursuing an understanding about the need for a range of key reforms in parallel is realistic, given the sympathy for fresh thinking that now exists in member states.

An interesting question, however, is whether a more populist and nationalist direction in the EU, following political change in France and Germany and other key member states such as Italy and Spain, would create a more favorable climate for reform, including on free movement. Or whether it would just create incoherence and chaos. I would not discount this shift — making the EU more receptive to Britain’s case for change. But a Le Pen government in France is an unknown — it could spur reform and reinvention or trigger turmoil and potential rupture.

If you think, as I do, that the EU is going to be forced into a lot of serious re-examination of its modus operandi in coming years for geopolitical reasons, given the rise of China and other economic powers, as well as the adjustment by the US of its position in the world, Britain’s re-engagement is timely.

There has always been a gap between elite opinion in Europe and the views of the public street but, if anything, this gap is narrowing. The street is making its views strongly felt electorally in all member states, including in all the larger ones — and it can no longer be safely ignored.

Today’s EU is not the same as the one we left in January 2020. Some argue this will create a less fertile environment for Britain because of the continent’s populist trend, but I think the opposite could also be true. A demand for change in the EU could converge with British arguments for reform.

It is a long shot, but Britain may benefit from the EU’s mounting storm.

Peter Mandelson is a former cabinet minister and EU Trade Commissioner.

scraped.title: Why do feminists defend fetishists?
scraped.author: Poppy Sowerby
scraped.h1: Why do feminists defend fetishists? BDSM endangers fragile women
scraped.body_text:
“Some kinks, after all, should be shamed.” (David McNew/Getty)

“Some kinks, after all, should be shamed.” (David McNew/Getty)

Sonia Exelby’s story was tragic from the start. The child of a mentally ill mother and addict father, she was shunted around the foster-care system with her five siblings. Her first encounter with therapy was at 13; later she would drop out of university with her own struggles. She was, for a time, a music teacher — but then she stopped that, too. She became a recluse; she attempted suicide. Then she found other people like her online.

Suicide forums vary widely: some exist on mainstream social-media sites while others crouch in darker corners. Some offer support — reassurance and guidance from peers with similar experiences. Others offer encouragement. We can assume Exelby ended up on the latter.

We don’t know where this troubled woman first encountered men who offered to kill her, but we do know that at some point she found Motherless, a now-defunct fetish-pornography platform where she met AlphaSadist. This was Dwain Hall , a 54-year-old roadside mechanic from Ocala, Florida and devotee of the Egyptian god of death Anubis; he loved BDSM; he had 276 pictures of rape, torture and mutilation on his phone. In October last year, aged 32, Exelby flew out to meet Hall in a remote Airbnb cabin in Florida; there, he brutalized her, killed her and left her body in a shallow grave. Last week, Hall was sentenced to two consecutive life sentences for Exelby’s kidnapping and murder.

By Poppy Sowerby

During the trial, his attorney made this argument to the jury: “This isn’t a question about what porn he likes. You can disagree with him about what he likes, but the case can’t be decided on you not liking his lifestyle.” Given the extent of physical and digital evidence against his client — videos, a knife, reams of messages — that lawyer can hardly have expected this defense to work. It is interesting, though, that he tried it. Something remarkable must have happened in our sexual culture to have culminated in a legal professional asking a panel of normal people to decouple a man’s proven extreme pornographic fetish from his likelihood to act out that fetish in real life.

Yet this is a plea that has, for years, been made by both the BDSM scene and the pornography lobby. Real-world sadism, from sexual choking to the murder pact an extremely unwell Exelby entered into to enact her suicidal impulses, is supposed to have nothing to do with porn. Even when the porn in question simulates precisely the kind of dangerous and deranged acts which hurt people in real life, we are meant to accept it as mere fantasy — cordoned off from the really vulnerable bodies of really vulnerable people. It is not true that, for example, strangulation pornography has mobilized hundreds of miniature Rippers to throttle random women in Britain’s back alleys. It is true, however, that this pornography has made strangulation during sex normal, acceptable and widespread. With this and other previously fringe acts, fantasy has broken its banks and leached into the sex lives of normal people.

Dwain Hall identified as a literal sadist. According to the tenets of BDSM, this is not an emergency but a legitimate sexual preference. According to Hall’s lawyer, it is even a “lifestyle”. Under Florida law you cannot consent to be killed, which is why Hall’s defense never stood a chance. But it’s important to understand that, in the subculture from which he emerged, this apologia holds water. In the topsy-turvy ethical framework of extreme fetish, anything goes — even the most high-risk, deplorable and degrading acts are immune to shaming, especially when they become part of the doer’s sexual “identity”. Any decision a willing adult makes, the BDSM schema goes, is valid — pardoned under the euphemistic premise of lifestyle. But how can hurting women be a lifestyle? It seems obvious that, for such a bizarre idea to have invaded modern sexuality, the kink lobby must have thoroughly hijacked the language of sex positivity and toleration — so thoroughly, in fact, that we are now embarrassed about expressing natural horror. You mustn’t shame Barry for wanting to carve pentagrams into the bodies of his Hinge dates — that’s his thing!

The general public has been conditioned by the sex-positivity movement into respecting any predilection as long as it operates “behind closed doors”. It is weird, the argument goes, to care about the bedroom habits of other people. Yet this same public is also largely ignorant to the subterranean fetish machine of the internet; it is only in extreme cases like Exelby’s that the horrific consequences of being “positive” about extreme kink are laid bare. One of those horrific consequences, which killjoy feminists have warned of for decades, is that kink is the ideal breeding ground for deranged men to take advantage of fragile women. It is not a coincidence that Exelby first encountered men who wanted to kill her on a suicide forum. Such men are not approaching potential victims on threads about being a girlboss or a strong independent woman; they are looking on sites populated by some of the most fragile women in the world. One such site has been linked to the deaths of more than 130 British people. It was fined £950,000 and geoblocked to protect users in the UK. Of course, VPNs are the inevitable workaround, but it seems reasonable that Ofcom’s action will stop at least some people encountering the site in the first place. On their own, these forums are horrifying enough — but the Exelby case shows that they are part of an ecosystem, and work in tandem with fetish platforms. Motherless, the one Exelby used — founded in New York by a man called Joshua G Lange in 2008 — went offline in July this year after a Dutch police server seizure related to an investigation about child sexual abuse material and drug-facilitated sexual assault shown on the site. The site had 62 million visits in February alone; it described itself as a “moral-free file host where anything legal is hosted forever”. As it turned out, lots of this stuff was in fact illegal.

The crime of drugging a “hotwife” and having men rape her without her knowledge has had lots of recent coverage, first from the case of Gisèle Pelicot in France, then last week from the conviction of four men for the rape and assault of Joanne Young, whose husband Philip Young, a former Conservative councilor, advertised her body online for 13 years as part of a cuckolding kink. Other stories are coming down the pipeline. Young found men to rape his wife on the primarily gay hookup app Grindr — but euphemistically termed “sleep content” was ubiquitous on Exelby’s site of choice, Motherless, with one linked Telegram chat with the name “Zzz” hosting nearly 1,000 participants. Users would share insights into how to drug and rape their partners, part of a “global rape academy”; footage of the crimes ( 20,000, according to CNN ) was then uploaded and organized into more than 100 searchable categories. In an honest and non-porn-brained sexual culture, we’d be able to admit that porn related to this fetish — even simulated, even legal — has directly and measurably led to the rape of women. How many of the men who frequent these forums would have discovered they were aroused by the idea of raping a sleeping woman had they not stumbled upon related “eye-check” porn (named, despicably, for the practice of ensuring the woman is unconscious by lifting up her eyelid)? I’d wager very few.

Clearly, drugging and raping are a conspicuous barrier to consent. But is this the only reason why it’s bad? The fetish lobby wants us to think that almost any choice made by an adult is beyond judgment. The problem is that the men and women who gravitate towards extreme kinks are very often deeply unwell (with, for example, a correlation between men liking BDSM and having previous suicide attempts ). In Exelby’s case, this was certainly true. Her long-term boyfriend Stevie Hunt was aware that she’d discussed her own murder with men online, describing it as “a type of self-harm”. He said being willing to “be spoken to in the manner she did” by self-described sadists was evidence of “low self-esteem”; in the consent-to-kill video recovered by police, a slurring Exelby told the camera that she wanted to die because she had “crushed everyone who ever loves me”. Clearly, this was a woman who needed help. But it just so happens that unwell women will be gladly abused by unwell men — and instead of stopping this, today our unwell sexual culture will abet it, even celebrate it.

By Poppy Sowerby

How did we let this happen? It started when we swallowed the pretzel logic of harmless fantasy being compartmentalized from real-world degeneracy, the greatest trick the porn lobby played on third-wave feminists. In believing it has no bearing on real life, we have forfeited our right to evaluate extreme pornography with any kind of common sense. It is obvious to anyone with the ability to think beyond their own boner that the mainstreaming of hardcore BDSM has put women at risk. At the same time, the bullshit language of the fetish movement, lapped up by latter-day liberal feminists, has robbed us of the ability to shame people who seek out degrading, dangerous, abhorrent things.

This “lifestyle-washing”, as I’m calling it, appeals to progressives keen to designate more and more categories of marginalization: don’t kink-shame me — I’m not a degenerate, I just like knifeplay! And, like all liberal dogmas which intend to be kind to one group, it ends in crushing another. I’m not sure why we can’t be frank with each other about the fact that some sexual “identities” are morally destitute and utterly worthy of opprobrium. Dwain Hall and Philip Young did not land a priori on their degenerate desires; they are the most extreme products of a morbid turn in modern sexuality which has lost its way on the internet. Though today it’s packaged in the swish language of liberation, we should no longer be fooled about whether sadism is a “valid identity”. There is perhaps no better evidence that our mores have become deranged than the fact that this, the most infuriatingly obvious of statements, is unsayable.

Cultural conservatives have heaped deserving scorn on other facets of bullshit identitarianism — disability LARPers, gender cranks, critical-race radicals — but seem curiously reluctant to touch the topic of BDSM. Why? Because it comes frighteningly close to revealing the problem of porn, the favorite bauble even traditionalists cannot bear to part with. Hall and Young did not materialize spontaneously; their cases should finally push us to look again at the wayward turn of our sexual culture. Some kinks, after all, should be shamed.

Poppy Sowerby is an UnHerd columnist.

scraped.title: Ted Kaczynski's deadly rationalism
scraped.author: Paul Sagar
scraped.h1: Ted Kaczynski's deadly rationalism Hubristic science is inhuman
scraped.body_text:
“If one’s worldview is only a few premises away from that of the Unabomber, something has gone seriously wrong.” (Bureau of Prisons/Getty)

“If one’s worldview is only a few premises away from that of the Unabomber, something has gone seriously wrong.” (Bureau of Prisons/Getty)

On 4 December 2024, Luigi Mangione shot and killed Brian Robert Thompson, the CEO of UnitedHealthcare. The self-radicalized murderer was just 26 years old, and claimed to be striking a blow against the US health insurance industry. Two years on from his crime, the sources of Mangione’s extremism remain disparate. But one stands out: Ted Kaczynski, the so-called Unabomber, who killed three people and injured 23 more in a campaign conducted over 17 years.

In 1995, the Unabomber persuaded The Washington Post to publish “Industrial Society and Its Future”, his 35,000-word manifesto. The paper agreed because the FBI hoped it would offer clues to his identity. It worked: Kaczynski’s sister-in-law correctly guessed who the real author was, and his brother reported him accordingly. Ted was arrested in 1996, and spent the rest of his life in prison, dying there in 2023.

What the FBI didn’t see coming, however, was the prolonged afterlife of Kaczynski’s ideas. Given its dry and analytic style, they expected his manifesto’s call for the destruction of current civilization, due to its irredeemable entanglement with modern technology, to be ignored by the wider world. But it wasn’t: “Industrial Society and Its Future” is surely one of the most widely read political texts since Marx and Engels published The Communist Manifesto back in 1848.

As well as flying off the shelves upon publication, and being freely available online in several languages, it remains a bestseller on Amazon in multiple print editions, replete with thousands of four- and five-star reviews. Kaczynski has remained popular elsewhere too. Just this week, after Claude solved the Riemann hypothesis, one of “Uncle Ted’s” letters went viral online — for its prediction that AI would lead to the demise of human-centered mathematics.

One Kaczynski enthusiast was Luigi Mangione, who posted a review of his ideas on Goodreads in January 2024. In private journal entries, meanwhile, he complained that Kaczynski went wrong not in his desire to kill people per se, but in doing so indiscriminately. This could only alienate the “normies”. What was needed, rather, were targeted assassinations — hence his ill-fated encounter with Thompson.

To what extent Kaczynski influenced Mangione directly will probably never be known. But it is not particularly surprising that one found much to admire in the other. The Unabomber was a childhood math prodigy, who went to Harvard age 16, became a professor at Berkeley — then quit his job to live alone in the Montana wilderness. Mangione, for his part, was valedictorian at the prestigious Gilman School in Baltimore before earning bachelor’s and master’s degrees in computer science from the University of Pennsylvania. In other words, both were STEM overachievers, and the private journals of the assassin indicate that he, like the bomber, came to see humans as deeply maladapted for their modern technological environments. A radical, violent, response struck both as appropriate.

Now, it hardly follows that STEM overachievers are fated to become political murderers. But there is at least one interesting detail in Mangione’s biography that stands out: his serious interest in the “rationalist” online subculture that has risen to prominence in recent years.

By Kathleen Stock

“Rationalism” first sprang up in the Bay Area in the late 2000s. Exhibiting a complex interrelationship with Silicon Valley, its founding premise is that human rationality, and thus the human condition, can be systematically improved by overcoming common and widespread biases in our thinking. Percolating for a while on the website LessWrong, it was in many ways the offspring of autodidact Eliezer Yudkowsky, whose most successful means of spreading the message turned out to be a 660,000-word fanfiction called Harry Potter and the Methods of Rationality . (Yes, really.)

More recently, Yudowsky has become famous for co-authoring the 2025 book If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies . As you can probably guess from the title, this is a statement of what has come to be known as “existential risk” and more specifically, the “doomer” prognosis that AI will wipe out humanity if it continues to develop on its current trajectory. Which is entirely fitting because, in the last decade or so, the rationalist movement has pivoted hard to being centrally preoccupied with AI safety, ranking this as the number one concern for any, well, rational person.

Rationalism has also been closely associated with “effective altruism”, which holds that the best thing you can do with your life is improve the well-being of others. This started out by telling bright university graduates not to work for charities, but to work for hedge funds and then give away as much of their income as possible to the most effective charities (in other words: choosing malaria nets over donkey sanctuaries). EA founder Will MacAskill has recently pivoted to emphasizing “long termism”, or the idea that when a sentient creature is born is ethically irrelevant — so our obligation is to try to improve the lives of potentially trillions of as-yet-unborn sentient beings, millions of years into the future (who may or may not be post-human AIs).

What rationalism and effective altruism share is an ultimately scientistic view of the human condition. What matters is precisely rationality, understood as a dry form of logical calculation. What matters ethically , in turn, is itself a form of dry calculation: maximizing the well-being of other creatures, as if the point of morality were essentially to make the big numbers on a universal spreadsheet go up for infinity.

And this can lead to some wacky places. What start off as sensible thoughts about overcoming cognitive bias and trying to promote more effective charitable work — end up with people earnestly proclaiming that the plot of The Terminator is about to be made real, or contending furiously on Substack that the welfare of shrimp ought to be of primary ethical concern (there are a lot of them, you see), and that insects matter more than human beings (there are even more of them , you see).

What does all this have to do with killers like Mangione and Kaczynski? In one way, nothing: it would be unfair to tar effective altruism and rationalism with the brush of association. But not entirely nothing. In Anti-Tech: The Ideas and Influence of the Unabomber , a recent book by Sean Fleming, Kaczynski is treated as an archival source — one whose intellectual inspirations and subsequent influence can be explored as more traditionally respectable political philosophers. This makes perfect sense: unlike subsequent killers who have posted “manifestos” to the internet, Kaczynski’s output, which he continued to produce from prison, is not the raving diatribe of a paranoid schizophrenic. It is a sober and, to some extent, coherent theoretical analysis.

As Fleming makes clear, while Kaczynski was not particularly original, he was also far from stupid. Grafting a selective understanding of Darwinian evolution onto the framework of French sociologist Jacques Ellul, the Unabomber devised a form of “bioprimitivism”: advocacy of the abandonment of all technology as a fundamental constraint for the freedom and flourishing of human beings. In any case, Kaczynski’s point was never to be “original”. His aim, rather, was to explain why humans in their present condition are doomed, and the appropriate response was… well, what exactly ?

In practical terms, Kaczynski decided the response was to post bombs to people he blamed for upholding modern technological systems. Initially he did this simply out of a desire to wreak “revenge” against the system, to punish those he felt deserved it. Later, he escalated this into a theory of revolution, seeing himself as the vanguard party for eventually bringing down the whole system. But a challenge for his worldview was that Kaczynski utterly disdained philosophy, and the political Left in particular, claiming to be motivated only by the findings of pure science. Except here he ran into a problem: why does it matter if humans are maladapted and suffering in their technological environment, if the only thing we can say with legitimacy has to be cashed out in rationalistic scientific terms?

By Paul Sagar

Ultimately, Kaczynski fell back onto a kind of mystical reification of nature as being somehow valuable in and of itself. Intellectually this was an incoherent betrayal of his own scientific proclamations. But it also reveals a difficulty for overly scientific views more generally. If all that matters is rational calculation, after all, how can “value” ever even enter the picture? Numbers by themselves are just numbers; so why do we give some of them meaning, but not others?

As Fleming neatly shows, the Unabomber and the rationalist outlooks are separated only by a few premises. Not in their attitude towards killing people — again, I’m not accusing the tech bros of that — but of where you go when you come to recognize humanity in its present condition as utterly entwined with, and dependent on, technologies that are vastly beyond the control or even the comprehension of individuals.

One response is to fully double down on tech. This is the response of scientistic philosophers like MacAskill and Nick Bostrom: to solving the crisis of our humanity by leaving our humanity behind, advocating for a transhumanist perspective where (hypothesized) future sentient beings matter more than we do now. Another is to go in precisely the opposite direction, and propose instead that we destroy all this technology once and for all. Indeed, Kaczynski himself offers a crude utilitarian calculation in his manifesto: it’s true that a lot of people will die when civilization collapses, but even more people will die if we let civilization continue only for it to collapse later. So we ought to collapse it now! EA long-termism, avant la lettre.

Most of us, of course, would rather steer for something in between. That means appreciating humans as humans, for all their flaws and foibles, even as we can accept technology as an unavoidable feature of what that humanity means. One way this difficult path has traditionally been navigated is through an engagement not with science alone, but with science alongside the humanities. To put it another way, you need literature and art to do good philosophy.

Which is bad news in 2026. I am currently trying to teach the value of the humanities to undergraduates who can farm out any attempt to think about the human condition for themselves to a technology of unprecedented power. A few brave and committed students still make the effort — but most increasingly don’t. The vast scope for cheating and taking shortcuts that AI has unleashed has hit the universities like a tsunami. I’m sure the Silicon Valley bros never meant this, but their hubristic scientism is washing us away regardless. Someone has built it, and the humanities are dying.

To which those of a scientistic mindset are apt to shrug in response. If the humanities can’t make the big number go up, who cares? I know from past experience that such a perspective is hard to dislodge. Unfortunately, it is the dominant outlook of our age. Nonetheless, I suggest that if one’s worldview is only a few premises away from that of the Unabomber, something has gone seriously wrong.

Paul Sagar is a Reader in Political Theory at King’s College London. His most recent book is Basic Equality (2024) . His Substack is called Diary of a Punter .

scraped.description: ZeroHedge - On a long enough timeline, the survival rate for everyone drops to zero
scraped.author: Tyler Durden
scraped.h1: Biden Judge Freezes Carr's War On ABC: 'This Is Not A Close Case'
scraped.body_text:
A federal judge in Washington on Wednesday blocked the FCC from pressing ahead with its early review of the broadcast licenses of ABC's eight owned stations , finding Disney is likely to prove the review was retaliation for coverage President Trump didn't like.

"This is not a close case," U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan wrote in a 45-page opinion that also threw out the FCC's motion to dismiss Disney's lawsuit. Her order bars the commission from "any continuing or further action" against the stations in the early renewal proceedings, "including issuing a Hearing Designation Order" - the step that would have sent the licenses to an evidentiary hearing.

AliKhan saved her sharpest words for FCC Chairman Brendan Carr. "Chairman Carr has taken President Trump's rhetoric as his marching orders," she wrote, noting that the same week Trump tapped him to run the agency, after months of Trump calling for "ABC [to] lose its license" over its campaign coverage, Carr praised "license revocation" as a "remedy" to "deter this kind of conduct."

The FCC's Media Bureau ordered the stations on April 28 to file their renewals years ahead of schedule; the licenses weren't due until 2028 at the earliest. That came the day after Trump attacked a Jimmy Kimmel skit about the First Lady. "It is no coincidence that President Trump criticized Mr. Kimmel's skit on social media and the very next day Defendants initiated the early license renewal proceedings," AliKhan wrote, citing "President Trump and Chairman Carr's call-and-response."

She quoted Carr's own words back to him. After the order went out, he said: "If you didn't take us seriously, now you should." After Kimmel's September 2025 remarks about Trump and his supporters, he said: "We can do this the easy way or the hard way. These companies can find ways to take action on Kimmel, or there is going to be additional work for the FCC ahead."

Carr has said the early review grew out of the agency's probe of Disney's diversity, equity and inclusion practices. AliKhan found the agency reached for the "harshest" tool available, one it "had not used in over half a century," which she said bolstered her "finding of pretext." The FCC's own supplemental brief admitted there were other ways to order an evidentiary hearing.

The judge also rejected the FCC's argument that a company with Disney's money couldn't be chilled. "Any broadcaster of ordinary firmness - wealthy or not - would not hesitate to think twice if faced with such an existential threat to its business," she wrote.

In July, when the White House asked networks to carry Trump's primetime address on "election interference," ABC streamed it online instead of airing it, and Carr said the FCC was "looking into" that decision as part of the renewal proceedings. Since the Media Bureau opened its February probe of The View , "no candidate for public office has appeared" on the show , according to a Disney declaration the judge cited, and ABC now weighs every political booking for whether the FCC "might later" cite it against the licenses.

AliKhan did decline to bar the FCC from "any actions, formal or informal, to coerce or threaten" ABC beyond the renewal proceedings, saying Disney hadn't spelled out what those might be. She set a $1 bond and gave the FCC until Dec. 2 to report on how it is complying.

The FCC said the ruling "is wrong on the facts and wrong on the law," a spokesperson told NBC News . "We will continue to use our lawful authority to hold broadcasters accountable to their public interest obligations," the spokesperson added. ABC called it "an important victory for the First Amendment."

Anna Gomez, the FCC's lone Democrat, said the decision "shows that this FCC is a paper tiger whose threats crumble when challenged by those willing to defend their rights."

NEWS: A federal court has stopped the FCC from continuing it's censorship campaign against ABC. This brings badly needed accountability to a Commission and an administration that have politicized the machinery of government in a sustained campaign of censorship and control. 🧵 pic.twitter.com/Rf1SdMdxhJ

— Anna M. Gomez (@AGomezFCC) November 26, 2026

Disney sued in August, arguing the FCC used the early reviews to apply " maximal coercive pressure " on ABC while dodging the courts. Carr has defended the review and told NBC News the suit was a "meritless case." The FCC is separately still reviewing whether The View broke the equal-time rule for political candidates , which the injunction doesn't touch.

scraped.author: Tyler Durden
scraped.h1: Over $280 Million Worth Of Marijuana Seized In California Raid
scraped.body_text:
Authored by Naveen Athrappully via The Epoch Times ,

A Bureau of Land Management (BLM)-led probe in California has led to the confiscation of more than 117 tons of processed marijuana with an estimated street value of around $282.8 million.

Investigators seized the drugs on Nov. 17 after serving a search warrant at multiple industrial warehouses in Chico, California. They discovered equipment used to de-stem, sort, and process marijuana flowers in the warehouses, with the processed marijuana found stored in boxes, large crates, and other containers. A total of 62 individuals were arrested for cultivation of marijuana in the crackdown , the Department of the Interior (DOI) said in a Nov. 24 statement.

Investigators alleged the warehouses were part of a larger network engaged in growing, processing, and distributing marijuana across California's northern region, including on lands managed by the U.S. Forest Service and the BLM .

The seizure underscores the extent of this network's alleged marijuana cultivation and distribution operations in northern California, the department said.

The operation advances the Trump administration's aim to eliminate illegal drug activities and restore safety in public lands, DOI said.

"America's public lands are set aside for the benefit and enjoyment of the American people, and it's our duty to keep them safe," Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum said in the statement.

"Interior will not tolerate criminals exploiting federal property. We're grateful for the dedication of our brave Bureau of Land Management agents and our local, state and federal partners for shutting down this illegal enterprise," Burgum said.

An earlier law enforcement crackdown in northern California disrupted a major narcotics operation in the state, leading to the confiscation of significant quantities of cocaine and fentanyl, the DOI said in a July 13 statement. The crackdown was part of efforts to counter drug trafficking in public lands managed by the BLM.

The fentanyl seized during the operation represented over 1.2 million potentially fatal doses.

Rep. James Gallagher (R-Calif.) called on FBI director Kash Patel last month to investigate transnational criminal groups running thousands of marijuana sites in California's Siskiyou and Shasta counties, highlighting that illegal cultivation has been documented on federal land , according to an Oct. 19 statement from the lawmaker's office.

Almost one million illegally cultivated cannabis plants were eradicated in California this year and 221 arrests have been made across 22 counties in the state under the Eradication and Prevention of Illicit Cannabis (EPIC) program, state Attorney General Rob Bonta's office said in a Nov. 16 statement.

"EPIC is the only task force in California that brings local, state and federal partners together to combat illegal cannabis cultivation on public lands," Thomas French, Bureau of Land Management Special Agent in Charge for Region 1-California, said in the statement, which described EPIC's work as disrupting the activities of organized criminal groups and rescuing individuals who were forced into labor.

"An illegal grow can divert a stream and leave toxic chemicals behind long after the plants are gone," French said. "We do this critical work every year so our kids and grandkids can explore these incredible lands and enjoy them the way we do today."
