scraped.title: Plan to decolonize Manitoba’s CFS system is a big task: minister
scraped.description: Manitoba’s child welfare system ‘the most complicated in the country,’ but a review is underway, says Min. Nahanni Fontaine.
scraped.author: Emma Honeybun
scraped.h1: Plan to decolonize Manitoba’s child welfare system is a big task that will take time, says minister
scraped.body_text:
APTN News

Stories about First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples

APTN News

Manitoba Minister of Families Nahanni Fontaine pictured in April 2026. Photo: Jared Delorme/APTN.

The director of Manitoba’s child advocacy office says that improving the current child welfare system needs a new approach that places control back to First Nations families.

However, doing so while First Nations are also struggling with a lack of resources and community spaces for the kids to thrive presents its own set of challenges.

“Decolonization is a huge undertaking,” said Sherry Gott, a member of Sapotaweyak Cree Nation who has been working in child welfare education for more than 30 years. “That means we must dismantle systems that have continued to colonize our people.”

Gott is the executive director of Manitoba’s Advocate for Children and Youth (MACY) , a non-partisan social work office funded by the province. On Nov. 18, it published its latest annual report, which, among other findings, indicated that 53 per cent of serious injuries involving youth (aged 0 to 20) that resulted in a report were caused by sexual assault.

She said her “dream” would be an outcome where a typical CFS wouldn’t be necessary, because First Nations would have the resources necessary to support children who may be in crisis, but that those resources are currently hard to come by.

“We have to believe that we have the knowledge to be able to look at the system in a way where it supports our families,” Gott said. “So we also have to believe that we have traditional knowledge that is valuable. We must believe that we have the answers to support our families to thrive.”

According to the latest report from MACY , the agency doesn’t have the resources to keep up with a growing number of children in crisis.

She said the resources MACY currently needs the most is adequate staffing, and that the shortage can be “really taxing on our mental health, when you look at what comes through the door.”

“Issues of sexual exploitation and abuse is a really, really difficult subject to deal with. And when you have a name behind that incident, then you start to know who the family is and who the children are, who’s involved, it gets even more personal,” Gott continued. “Because you have names attached to it, and communities, Nations, where these children come from. So it is really hard to work daily at that level … It’s hard on our staff. But we try our best to keep their mental health and well-being in check.”

According to the report, the office received 506 referrals from April 2025 to March 2026, but only 300 were able to be reviewed, according to the legal definition of a serious injury.

Because of the demand, only 135 of the 300 referrals legally eligible for review have ended with complete serious injury reports, as of writing. Only 99 were assessed for potential investigation, and 36 of those assessments were reviewed further.

According to the 2025-2026 annual report from the office of provincial Minister of Families Nahanni Fontaine, 80 per cent of children in care are First Nations.

Similarly, Gott said that approximately 80 per cent of children represented in MACY’s serious injury reports are Indigenous.

MACY also completed 60 child death reports in 2025-26, although there were 71 in scope for a review.

Sixty-eight per cent of the children in the completed reports were Indigenous, and 98 per cent of the reports were linked to CFS.

The most recent reported death in care is five-year-old Baileigh Berens in Winnipeg. Baileigh had autism and was non-verbal, but had no known health conditions and her cause of death has not been determined. She was found in a dryer.

The Assembly of Manitoba Chiefs (AMC) , which represents all 63 First Nations in Manitoba, held a sacred fire for the child at her mother’s house Wednesday evening.

Following the release of MACY’s annual report, AMC Grand Chief Kyra Wilson stated that “these findings are deeply concerning, but they are not new warnings.”

“First Nations families and survivors have been raising these concerns for decades. When children are placed in systems intended to protect them but continue to experience violence, exploitation, and abuse, we must hold those systems accountable,” she continued.

The AMC had called on Canada to examine “child welfare, child protection, and children in care” as part of the National Inquiry into Murdered and Missing Indigenous Women and Girls in 2018, a recommendation that made it into the final report.

However, AMC stated, “Despite these longstanding concerns, First Nations children remain disproportionately represented in Manitoba’s child welfare system,” and that the high number of First Nations children in that system, according to the province, is “underscoring the urgent need for prevention, family reunification, and culturally appropriate supports.”

AMC, along with its own First Nations Family Advocate Office (FNFAO) , stated the province would need to work “directly with First Nations governments to develop a comprehensive, culturally grounded prevention and protection strategy that addresses sexual exploitation and human trafficking, strengthens placement oversight, and ensures accessible, trauma-informed supports for children, youth, and families.”

FNFAO is a province-wide advocacy office that helps families “fighting to have their children returned to their homes or First Nations,” according to its website.

Since opening in 2015, it has worked with more than 1,500 families and has continuously urged for a total reform of the system.

According to Fontaine, changes are on the way. However, she also noted that they have taken a “very long time.”

“This is all new for everybody. But what I can tell you 100 per cent … and in five years, 10 years, and certainly in 15 years from now, child welfare will look incredibly different than it does right now. And what you will see is a system where First Nations and Métis families, leaderships, matriarchs and Elders and communities are caring collectively for children.”

Even in the last year, she said there was over a 200 per cent increase in kinship and customary care agreements, which are “voluntary, out-of-court child welfare arrangements” between the parents, the child and the respective agency.

Manitoba introduced the agreements to provincial law in 2024, to help safely keep children in their home communities without officially entering the system, Fontaine said.

“That’s phenomenal,” she said. “But what folks also have to remember is that we’re trying to decolonize a system that’s been around for 500 years, just in different forms and iterations.

“In many different iterations, Indigenous children have been harmed and have been targeted. And decolonizing these systems are going to take many, many years, but we’re doing that work right now,” Fontaine said.

CFS system review underway

In July 2026, Fontaine announced that Manitoba would conduct an independent review of its child welfare system by the end of the year, with a tentative release planned for Summer 2027. She confirmed with APTN that the process was ongoing.

“We’ve been doing all of those reviews, working with the authorities to make sure that they’re working with their agencies to ensure that children have the supports that they need,” Fontaine said. “But that work didn’t occur for many, many years. And so we’re doing that work, we’re looking at the totality of the system.”

She added that while it examines the system, the province is also working to give First Nations governments the “ability to assert jurisdiction over child welfare” when it involves their communities, and by extension, the Nation’s own laws.

“Our people are going to have a different way of doing child welfare,” Fontaine said. “It’s a way of keeping children in their communities, among their kin, among their lands, among their people. That’s something across the country that traditionally, child welfare didn’t do.”

In 2019, Ottawa passed Bill C-92, also known as an Act Respecting First Nations, Inuit and Métis Children, Youth, and Families, that, according to the government, “recognizes a simple truth: one size does not fit all when it comes to Indigenous child and family services.”

Co-developed with First Nation partners, the bill “enables Indigenous groups and communities to transition toward exercising partial or full jurisdiction over child and family services at a pace that they choose.”

While navigating the process of shifting jurisdiction in Manitoba, Fontaine acknowledged that the middle province has “the most complicated child welfare system in the country.”

Currently, child welfare in Manitoba is governed by four authorities — General Child and Family Services Authority , First Nations of Northern Manitoba Child and Family Services Authority , Southern First Nations Network of Care , and Métis Child and Family Services Authority — that oversee agencies that fall under their jurisdiction.

Although Indigenous serving authorities provide oversight and training to these agencies, it is done in accordance with provincial law and not under the jurisdiction of any specific First Nations government.

Fontaine said she’s been in care twice in her life, and although it was “needed,” she was far away from her community.

“At the end of the day, kids want to be with their family,” she said. “They want to be with their parents. They want to be with their kin. And we’re on this path to ensure that more children are staying with their family and their communities.”

However, although Gott said that Nations often have a drive to help, there is still a lack of resources.

“It’s limited, the funding that’s available,” she said. “So they make do with what they have. And when we think about things like a place for children or youth to hang out, that space needs to be safe. And it needs to have people that understand kids and where they’re coming from.

“I think it would be really important to have those in place so we’re not always responding to crisis, after crisis, after crisis,” she said.

Ultimately, Gott said, “I think what needs to be at the forefront of everybody’s mind is that children are suffering in Manitoba and I think we need to do better.”

“I hope that someday our families can go back to what they used to do, and look after our own.”

Emma is a Red River Métis with family roots in St. Malo, Manitoba. She graduated from RRC Polytech’s Creative Communications program in 2023 and went on to serve as a community journalist and photographer for the Free Press Community Review until she joined APTN in 2026. Equipped with a strong sense of justice, she enjoys covering stories in the central prairies for a larger audience. Her work has also appeared in Manitoba Inc. Magazine, the Free Press, and RRC Polytech’s student paper, The Projector.

scraped.title: Child welfare dispute in Peguis First Nation sparks lockdown
scraped.description: A dispute over the leadership and operations of Peguis First Nation’s Child and Family Services escalated Thursday.
scraped.author: Justin Hardy
scraped.h1: Child welfare dispute in Peguis First Nation in Manitoba sparks lockdown
scraped.body_text:
APTN News

Stories about First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples

APTN News

A dispute over the leadership and operations of Peguis First Nation’s Child and Family Services escalated Thursday with community members, the chief and a councillor gathering outside the agency’s main office.

The protest started Nov. 19 amid calls for changes to the agency’s leadership on the reserve located 200 km north of Winnipeg on the Interlake Region of Manitoba.

“Despite my attempts in the past to speak up for membership, there has been complete disregard for me as the chief of our nation, complete disregard for the concerns identified by members, and complete disregard for the safety and wellbeing of our children and our families,” Chief Stan Bird said in a video posted to social media in the days leading up to the protest.

RCMP officers arrived and spoke with the group. Bird has previously said he wants the band to take control of the CFS agency and reassert its inherent jurisdiction over child welfare.

He has also raised concerns about child safety and the agency’s operations.

Bird has not responded to further requests for comment.

Peguis CFS responded by announcing that its main office was in lockdown following Thursday’s incident.

“The agency is an essential service provider to Peguis members and wants to ensure to members that programs and services will continue as normal,” the announcement on their website read.

The dispute has also exposed disagreements within the community over how the agency should be governed and who should have authority over its operations.

Four of the community’s six councillors issued a notice to the community dated Nov. 21, condemning the protest, they said, was led by Bird and that that a quorum of council is needed to make any changes to the agency.

As of Nov. 25, the situation remains unresolved, with questions surrounding the agency’s leadership, its financial accountability and the future of child and family services in Peguis.

A band meeting was held in Peguis on Nov. 24. Media were not allowed in. Bird has called a news conference in Winnipeg on Thursday.

We will have more on that in the coming days.

Editor’s Note: The original story said the chief and others gathered at the agency chained the doors shut. This was not the case.

Justin Hardy is Anishinaabe from Biinjitiwaabik Zaaging Anishinaabek. Justin joined APTN National News in 2025 and covers the Territory of Nunavut.

Thanksgiving is a time to come together and enjoy time with your family and friends.

scraped.description: Former NBA champion David West makes screenwriting debut with The Neighbor, a psychological thriller featuring Stonebwoy and Myles Truitt.
scraped.author: Peter Kerich
scraped.h1: Former NBA champion David West makes screenwriting debut with ‘The Neighbor,’ featuring Myles Truitt and Stonebwoy
scraped.body_text:
The psychological thriller, inspired by true events, is filming in Cape Town, South Africa, and brings together a diverse cast.

Former NBA champion David M. West is transitioning from professional basketball to filmmaking, making his screenwriting debut with “The Neighbor”, an upcoming psychological thriller currently filming in South Africa.

West is also serving as an executive producer on the project, which is directed by Kyle Scott and features actors Myles Truitt, Joseph Steven Yang and Hana Kim, alongside Ghanaian Afropop and dancehall star Stonebwoy. Principal photography began on Nov. 4, 2026, in Cape Town, with the production bringing together creative and production teams from the United States, Australia and South Africa.

David West, who played 15 seasons in the NBA and won two championships with the Golden State Warriors, wrote the screenplay for “The Neighbor.” According to Deadline , the film marks a new creative chapter for the former All-Star as he explores storytelling beyond professional sports.

Set in the San Francisco Bay Area, the thriller follows a veteran professional basketball player and his wife as they attempt to build a peaceful new life. Their plans unravel when an unsettling presence in their neighborhood draws them into a dangerous situation involving obsession, manipulation and buried secrets. David West said basketball gave him a platform and opportunities that he now hopes to extend through filmmaking.

“As I step into filmmaking, I’m excited to expand that impact through storytelling and spark meaningful conversations,” he said, adding that he looks forward to bringing the project to audiences.

Kyle Scott, who directs and executive produces the film, described the project as his first psychological thriller and his third major production in less than a year. The production team includes lead producer Ama K. Abebrese, known for “Beasts of No Nation “; producer Ty Walker, whose credits include “Die Hart”; Sarsha Venord; and Emmy-winning production designer Warren Gray.

“The Neighbor” is being produced through a collaboration involving In Peace Productions in Raleigh, North Carolina; KeyScott Entertainment in Brisbane, Australia; Blue Ice Africa in Cape Town, South Africa; and Braveheart Entertainment in Atlanta, Georgia.

Scott said this is part of an effort to develop films that challenge convention and reach audiences beyond geographical and cultural boundaries. “Great cinema has no borders,” he said.

scraped.title: Atlanta's historic Mall West End being demolished for planned $450 million redevelopment
scraped.description: Atlanta’s Mall West End is being demolished for a planned $450 million, featuring affordable housing, retail and student housing.
scraped.author: Odafe Oghen
scraped.h1: Atlanta’s historic Mall West End being demolished for planned $450 million redevelopment
scraped.body_text:
The shopping center, which served as a hub for Black-owned businesses for more than five decades, will make way for housing, retail and community spaces.

Demolition is underway at Atlanta’s Mall West End, a shopping center that served Black residents and business owners for more than five decades. The mall once hosted rapper Lil Baby’s annual back-to-school festival . Its replacement will include affordable housing in a city where Black renters face a disproportionate share of eviction filings.

Crews began tearing down the mall this week, WSB-TV reported on Wednesday, Nov. 25. The property near Ralph David Abernathy Boulevard and Lee Street in southwest Atlanta is being redeveloped as One West End.

Casey Dantzler stopped by on Wednesday to collect two bricks from the building. He recalled childhood visits to stores such as Sunshine, Crest and Sil’s. “I’ve been going to this mall since I was probably 7 years old,” he told the station. Dave Money, who worked at the mall for 21 years, also recalled his relationships with tenants and shoppers.

The mall closed in January 2025. On Aug. 7, 2022, Lil Baby held his back-to-school festival there, providing children with free shoes, backpacks, school supplies and meals in partnership with Goodr and other businesses.

In October 2024, the city announced the acquisition of the 12-acre property through a partnership between Atlanta Urban Development and Atlanta Beltline. BRP Companies and The Prusik Group are leading the redevelopment, which the city originally estimated would cost $450 million.

The city’s initial plans called for approximately 900 rental apartments, with 20% reserved for households earning up to 50% of the area median income and another 10% for households earning up to 80%. The plans also included a grocery store, student housing, a hotel and medical offices.

The developers offered temporary spaces to existing tenants and committed at least $500,000 toward a proposed fund to help qualifying businesses with rent and renovations.

The first phase of the Mall West End redevelopment was originally expected to be completed in 2026. The developer’s website now lists 2028 as the target. WSB-TV reported that apartment rental rates had yet to be released.

scraped.author: Peter Kerich
scraped.h1: Colman Domingo responds to critic who called his ‘Michael’ performance ‘mid’: ‘Who hurt you?’
scraped.body_text:
Oscar-nominated actor Colman Domingo pushed back after an X user criticized his portrayal of Joe Jackson in the Michael Jackson biopic.

Colman Domingo has responded to an online critic who dismissed his performance as Joe Jackson in the musical biopic Michael, which has attracted awards-season attention. The actor fired back with a brief response after an X user questioned why awards prognosticators were including him in their Oscar and Golden Globe predictions.

“Hot take: Awards prognosticators adding Colman Domingo for Michael, you really don’t need to add a mid performance/bad movie. You really don’t,” the user wrote on Wednesday, Nov. 25. According to the report by Variety, Domingo responded directly: “Who hurt you?”

In “Michael”, Domingo portrays Joe Jackson, the father of pop icon Michael Jackson and patriarch of the Jackson family. The film stars Michael Jackson’s nephew, Jaafar Jackson, in the lead role, alongside Nia Long as Katherine Jackson and Miles Teller as attorney John Branca. Domingo’s performance received praise from some critics following the film’s release in April 2026.

TheGrio reported in August that Colman Domingo was set to receive the Vantage Award at 2026 Academy Museum Gala.

Before the film premiered, Domingo told The Wall Street Journal that he approached the role by seeking to understand Joe Jackson’s humanity and his influence on the careers of his children. “He created some of the most iconic artists that have ever walked this earth,” Domingo said. “What goes into the making of that man?” Domingo discussed allegations of abusive behavior by acknowledging that Joe Jackson chastised his children.

The biopic has generated discussion beyond its performances, particularly because of the allegations of sexual abuse involving Michael Jackson. In a November 2024 interview with Variety , Coleman Domingo said the allegations surrounding the pop star were not part of his approach to portraying Joe Jackson.

Despite the controversy, Michael has reportedly become the highest-grossing biopic ever made.

items.title: With Robert Pattinson Set as the New 007, Meet the Black Woman Who Invented the ‘Bond Girl’ Look

scraped.title: The Black Woman Behind the Iconic "James Bond" Bikini
scraped.h1: With Robert Pattinson Set as the New 007, Meet the Black Woman Who Invented the ‘Bond Girl’ Look
scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

Did you know the iconic white bikini worn by Ursula Andress in the first Bond film was designed by a Black woman? Meet Tessa Prendergast, the woman who is responsible for the signature sexy aesthetic of the Bond girl.

By

Mahalia Otshudy

Published

L, Tessa Prendergast (Photo by WATFORD/Mirrorpix/Mirrorpix via Getty Images); R, Ursula Andress (Photo by Sunset Boulevard/Corbis via Getty Images)

Now that Robert Pattinson has secured the role of James Bond, the hunt is on for the actress who will step into the iconic, seductive yet covert role of the next Bond girl. What many fans of the “James Bond” series might not know is that a Black woman, Tessa Prendergast, helped create the signature sexy aesthetic that still has folks obsessed with the fashion of Bond girls from the past, such as Halle Berry, Jane Seymour, and Ursula Andress in “Dr. No” (1962)—the film that started it all.

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

Prendergast, a Jamaican costume designer, actress and businesswoman, is credited with designing the iconic white bikini in the first Bond film and is often credited with inventing the Bond girl look. Gen Zs, such as Tiktok creator Arya (@arianaceciliaaa), are just learning about the designer. So, here is what you need to know about the glamorous woman.

Born in Kingston, Jamaica, in 1928, to plantation owner Louis Prendergast and an Afro-Jamaican mother who remains unidentified, Tessa came from a wealthy family and was naturally creative, becoming a well-known socialite who would later run a boutique in Jamaica. Her boutique and social skills would go on to become the very things that connected her to “Dr. No.”

Though born in the Caribbean, Prendergast was raised in London but often returned to Jamaica for brief periods. She soon moved to America to enroll at the College of New Rochelle in New York and later at the Sorbonne in Paris, then spent time living in Italy and became engaged to a member of one of the country’s oldest aristocratic families, the Massimos, according to The Telegraph.

Related: Black Actresses Who Should Be the Next Bond Girl

During her time in Europe, Prendergast briefly worked as an actress before returning to her native Jamaica to open a boutique, but the shop’s name remains unknown. However, reports say that while living in Rome, Prendergast became friends with Ursula Andress, who later sought her designer friend’s help while filming “Dr. No” in Jamaica.

In an interview in “The James Bond Archives” book, Andress said that when she landed on set, “A friend of mine from Rome, Tessa Prendergast, had a boutique in Jamaica, and she was also making dresses. So we made the bikini together.” It was a bikini that Andress would credit for turning her into a “success,” according to People. To really sell the spy look, Prendergast added a replica British Army belt and a leather-handled U.S. military knife in a scabbard on Andress’ left hip.

Ursula Andress’ iconic entrance in the film and Tessa Prendergast’s costume design set the bar for future Bond girls’ fashion in the six-decade-old franchise. In 2002, Halle Berry paid homage to Andress’ Honey Ryder in “Die Another Day” with the same entrance and a modernized version of the bikini, complete with a knife on the hip.

The swimsuits were displayed side by side in a 2016 exhibition, “Designing 007: Fifty Years of Bond Style,” in Paris, cementing the lasting impact of Prendergast’s sole film costume credit. Now, as fans wait for the highly anticipated Robert Pattinson version of James Bond, they are equally eager to see who will be crowned the next Bond girl and continue the fashion legacy Tessa Prendergast created.

scraped.title: What to Know About Porsha Williams' Fiancée, Sway McKinney
scraped.h1: Everything We Know About Porsha Williams’ New Fiancée Patrice ‘Sway’ McKinney
scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

‘RHOA’ star Porsha Williams is officially engaged to her girlfriend, Sway. Here’s everything we know about the two and their impending nuptials!

By

Shanelle Genai

Published

LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA – JUNE 28: Patrice “Sway” McKinney and Porsha Williams attend 2026 BET Awards at Peacock Theater on June 28, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Prince Williams/FilmMagic)

“The Real Housewives of Atlanta” star Porsha Williams is headed back down the aisle after getting engaged to her girlfriend, Patrice “Sway” McKinney. If you haven’t been tuned into the Bravo series or keeping up with their relationship evolution, here’s what you need to know about the happy couple.

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

While not much is known about Sway, after doing a little digging, we learned that she’s a salon suite business mentor and has been working in the hair industry for years as a licensed barber. She also works as a real estate developer and owns & Cheese Midtown, an Atlanta-area restaurant.

During an appearance on “The Marvin Francois Show” in January 2026, Sway said of their business journey: “I am a coach and mentor, specifically in the hair and beauty industry. So I primarily teach people how to start and scale their own salon suite business anywhere in the world without any experience, without any licensing.”

Williams and Sway publicized their big news on Tuesday night in a video posted to Instagram. In it, the two were decked out in black-tie attire and looking lovingly at each other before they held hands, kissed, and Williams flashed her mega ring in front of the camera. At the end, the video faded to black with the words, “Engaged 11/21/2026” written over it.

“I said YES – Engaged 11/21/26,” Williams captioned in her post. “I love you forever [Sway].”

According to Bravo, the ring features an emerald-cut diamond set on a platinum-colored band encrusted with smaller diamonds.

RELATED: Porsha Williams Confirms She’s Dating a Woman

While many “RHOA” viewers may be well aware of Williams’ tumultuous divorce from her ex-husband, Simon Guobadia, which was finalized in June 2025, it looks like Williams was able to find love in Sway at some point during that same year.

That would explain them going “Instagram official” in November of that same year, officially parting ways with the other gentleman suitor she’d also been dating at the same time as her and Sway. The & Cheese restauranteur would soon make appearances across season 17, which aired at the top of 2026.

As we previously told you, Williams spoke out on her reasoning for going public with her and Sway’s relationship on the show, saying in an interview with PEOPLE : “I’ve been in reality TV for 10-plus years, okay. But yes, this was definitely different for obvious reasons. I didn’t want to hide any parts of me. I felt if I did hide it and it had to be caught somewhere, it just wouldn’t feel authentic.

She continued: “I want to live in my truth, and so in doing that, I have found someone who I really enjoy getting to know, and it’s been great.”

items.title: Why a White Influencer’s Viral Mac and Cheese Recipe Has Black Folks On Social Media Divided
items.summary: Black folks online are debating whether one white chef's popular mac and cheese recipe is cultural appropriation.Read more...

scraped.title: Why a White Influencer’s Viral Mac and Cheese Recipe Has Black Folks On Social Media Divided – The Root
scraped.h1: Why a White Influencer’s Viral Mac and Cheese Recipe Has Black Folks On Social Media Divided
scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

Black folks online are debating whether one white chef’s popular mac and cheese recipe is cultural appropriation.

By

Phenix S Halley

Published

Screenshot from TikTok, Photo courtesy of the Thomas Jefferson Foundation

If it’s the holiday season, you know Black folks are on some corner of social media debating about mac and cheese. This year, TikTok chef and influencer Tini Younger, who is white, is back at the center of the conversation after her baked mac and cheese recipe reignited a familiar debate about cultural ownership and appropriation.

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

On one side, some Black women on TikTok, like @itsdanielle2u, encouraged the community to stop giving attention to white creators making mac and cheese and instead celebrate the traditional recipes passed down through Black families.

“At the end of the day, you’re still a white woman,” she said of Younger on the app. “And at the beginning of the day, these are still Black recipes.” She specifically called out the professional chef for allegedly “exploiting the Black community.”

Younger’s mac and cheese recipe first went viral in 2023, catapulting her into internet fame and opening the door to major brand deals, millions of followers, and eventually, her own cookbook–which, of course, features the now-famous recipe. However, unlike many traditional African American recipes, Younger’s version uses cavatappi noodles instead of elbow macaroni, a roux-based cheese sauce, and a squeeze of Dijon mustard.

RELATED : Don’t Want to Cook? Enjoy a Thanksgiving Feast at One of These Black-Owned Restaurants

Those differences have some people debating whether her recipe is simply a modern take on a beloved comfort food or another example of a dish with Black culinary roots being repackaged for mainstream audiences.

But others aren’t convinced the situation deserves that much outrage. Some on social media

“What fascinates me about the Tini mac and cheese discourse is how often the popularization of something becomes mistaken for its invention,” @antaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa wrote. “I love Tini for being her authentic self online. I hate that popular news outlets are doing this, though.”

The history of Black American mac and cheese is rooted in chattel slavery. While pasta and cheese dishes existed in Europe long before they became popular in America, Black cooks played an important role in shaping the dish’s place in American food culture. One man in particular deserves recognition.

James Hemings was an enslaved chef owned by President Thomas Jefferson. Hemings traveled to France with Jefferson, where he received extensive culinary training. He later brought French cooking techniques back to America, including macaroni pie–which later became baked macaroni and cheese. Over generations, Black Southern cooks made the dish their own. Different households make their own versions, with some using eggs and evaporated milk, while others swear by a roux-based recipe.

That’s part of why the conversation surrounding Younger strikes a nerve. The argument isn’t necessarily that white people shouldn’t cook mac and cheese. It’s about a larger pattern of Black cultural contributions being overlooked while white creators receive visibility, fame and fortune.

Some social media users argued that mac and cheese is enjoyed across cultures and that the professional chef and content creator shouldn’t be criticized simply for making a dish she enjoys.

“She’s a chef. I thought that’s what chefs are supposed to do,” @mr.nailssss said on TikTok. He admitted to using Younger’s recipe for the holiday season. “Some of us had to learn how to cook from the internet,” the creator continued, explaining that in his family, recipes weren’t passed down across generations.

Younger has never needed to label her recipe as Black cuisine for people to recognize its connection to a broader American food tradition. She’s previously pushed back against appropriation accusations, maintaining that she developed her recipe through years of experimentation.

Still, Black families have also been perfecting their recipes for generations, often without the recognition or platforms that today’s food influencers enjoy. So if this annual debate reminds us of anything, it’s that food traditions deserve more than seasonal arguments. They should be documented, passed down and given their rightful place in American history.

scraped.title: Ukraine’s Zelenskyy Fires Warning Shot at Trump, Seeks Revenge After Democratic Takeover of Congress
scraped.description: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy isn’t messing around anymore. He’s warning President Donald Trump that if there’s no peace plan with Russia by the
scraped.author: Shelby Erdman
scraped.h1: Ukraine’s Zelenskyy Fires Warning Shot at Trump, Seeks Revenge After Democratic Takeover of Congress
scraped.body_text:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy isn’t messing around anymore. He’s warning President Donald Trump that if there’s no peace plan with Russia by the end of the year, he plans to bypass Trump altogether.

In an interview with Bloomberg, the Ukrainian leader said if Trump can’t convince his “friend” Russian President Vladimir Putin to end the fighting, he plans to go directly to the new Democratic-controlled Congress for help.

Zelenskyy told Bloomberg if Putin is still waging war on Kyiv, he’ll ask Democrats for more military aid and tougher sanctions against Moscow, according to reports.

“There must be such a level of support for Ukraine and such sanctions that they send a clear signal to the Russians,” Zelenskyy stated.

“It’s time to sit down at the negotiating table and end the war,” he added.

Russia invaded Ukraine back in February of 2022, almost five years ago. When Trump ran for re-election, he promised to end the war on “Day One.” Of course that hasn’t happened.

“There’s a desire to move very quickly, both we and the Russians understand that,” Zelenskyy told Bloomberg, referring to the incoming Democratic leadership. Trump could find himself severely restricted in dictating U.S. policy toward Russia under a Democratic-controlled Congress.

“We understand what the price might be. We very much want peace too, but not at Ukraine’s expense alone,” he added, referring to a previous Trump peace plan that was a non-starter.

A year ago, Trump’s 28-point peace plan leaked, and it shockingly kowtowed to Putin, giving the Russian dictator everything he wanted while presenting it as a diplomatic breakthrough, according to the Center for American Progress .

The plan demanded Ukrainians surrender territory to Putin, accept limits on its military, and limited Western military aid.

Trump’s negotiating team, his buddy real estate mogul Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner, are leading efforts to broker peace between the two nations and the countdown to get it done is underway.

The pair arrived in Berlin on Nov. 19 to meet with European leaders and Ukrainian officials to try and end Putin’s war on Ukraine, according to Reuters .

The news outlet reported that a U.S. official said the meetings focused on developing “credible post-war security guarantees” for Kyiv, preparing for another round of peace talks, and an economic recovery plan for Ukraine.

This latest round of meetings follows talks in Abu Dhabi last week with Russia and Ukraine, the first such discussions on ending the war in nine months.

Witkoff and Kushner then met Putin in Moscow, Reuters reported.

In a social media post on Nov. 16, Kushner said the pair are making progress even though both sides appear nowhere near an agreement.

Putin is demanding Ukraine’s Donbas region in exchange for peace, Reuters reported, while Ukraine is unwilling to give up any territory.

And the pressure to resolve the conflict quickly is real. Putin should be very worried about the incoming Congress.

Democrats, along with GOP support, could increase financial and military assistance to Kyiv and launch investigations into Trump’s dealings with Moscow. Witkoff and Kushner could also find themselves at the center of investigations and congressional hearings

The Kyiv Independent put it this way.

“The argument for Moscow is that the terms available now may not remain on the table for long. If the new Congress pushes for a tougher approach toward Russia, the Kremlin could lose an opportunity to secure concessions from Washington.

Either way, there’s no love lost between Zelenskyy and the Trump administration.

Back in February 2025, shortly after Trump’s second term began, the president and his Vice President, JD Vance, publicly belittled Zelenskyy during a televised Oval Office meeting.

In a shocking display of vitriol and something never seen before by an American president, Trump berated Zelenskyy for not being grateful enough for American support and tried to force him to make a deal with Russia, The New York Times reported at the time.

Trump also threatened to abandon Ukraine altogether if Zelenskyy did not capitulate to American demands.

Well, the tide is turning, and the old adage “revenge is a dish best served cold” certainly applies to Zelenskyy now.

scraped.title: NBA Finals Star Jalen Brunson Eyes New Opportunities After Hollywood Debut Goes Better Than Expected
scraped.description: The Knicks star admits his first scripted acting role challenged him in ways basketball never did. But his latest comments leave the door open for another shot at Hollywood.
scraped.author: Maurice Cassidy
scraped.h1: NBA Finals Star Jalen Brunson Eyes New Opportunities After Hollywood Debut Goes Better Than Expected
scraped.body_text:
The Knicks star admits his first scripted acting role challenged him in ways basketball never did. But his latest comments leave the door open for another shot at Hollywood.

Jalen Brunson has a trophy case most players would trade their whole careers for.

The New York Knicks captain helped his team win the 2026 NBA Finals.

But he just admitted there was one job this year that had him completely out of his element.

It wasn’t the title chase, parade through the city, or the target that now sits on the defending champions’ backs every night.

For Brunson, it was a gig that lasted about a minute, and just like when he stepped into a Taylor Swift fan fight over the summer, people online still haven’t stopped picking it apart.

Some fans are begging for an encore. Others are hoping he never gets one. And Brunson himself just made it pretty clear which way he’s leaning.

The 30-year-old point guard, who led New York to its first NBA championship in 53 years back in June and walked away with Finals MVP, made his scripted acting debut.

Brunson appeared in on NBC’s “Law & Order: Special Victims Unit” earlier this month.

He played Detective Jay Madison in the season 28 episode “Forsaken,” which aired Nov. 5. The character’s last name is a not-so-subtle nod to Madison Square Garden, and the role was the payoff of a wish Brunson made moments after the Knicks closed out the San Antonio Spurs.

He was asked what came next and answered, “Try to get on ‘SVU.'”

The wish didn’t last long, thanks largely to Mariska Hargitay, a courtside regular at the Garden and one of Brunson’s closest celebrity friends.

Hargitay told Variety back in August that the role was “definitely happening,” adding, “He is just open and ready. I don’t think there is much Jalen can’t do.”

For anyone who missed it, the scene, which NBC has posted online, is short. Madison is off duty, working through a pizza at a restaurant counter, when Hargitay’s Captain Olivia Benson walks in.

Sharp-eyed viewers caught a bonus cameo, too. Brunson’s real-life father, Knicks assistant coach Rick Brunson, strolls through the door right before she does.

Benson congratulates Madison on his promotion, and Brunson responds, “Thanks, Captain. Focused on my goals, gave 110%, things worked out.” She’s really there about an old traffic stop involving a father named Rick, no relation, and his teenage son.

“Blew a 0.25 and started yelling at me,” Madison recalls, before mentioning an item he left in the car because of a “legal gray area.” That detail sends Benson rushing off to chase a warrant.

A clip of the scene posted by a Knicks fan account on X has pulled in more than 3 million views, and the replies turned into a full-blown review session. Some viewers were generous. “Better than some Tubi actors…” one user joked.

Another wrote, “Hey not a bad acting job for the time around.” A third went all in: “seriously just go ahead and give him the emmy right this second.”

Others weren’t nearly as kind. “Sorry this is as bad as it gets—no emotion, no expression, no pauses in speech, no improvised lines,” one critic wrote. Even loyal Knicks fans couldn’t fully defend him. “My baby sound like he’s giving a post-game interview but that’s alright,” one admitted, before adding, “Acting credit added to his resume. We take it.”

Whether or not he’s scrolled through the reviews, Brunson finally opened up about the experience in a new interview with Complex tied to a Lowe’s holiday partnership.

Asked which was harder, the NBA Finals or his turn on the long-running crime drama, he laughed and picked the Finals. He explained that “there weren’t any do-overs.” But he didn’t pretend the TV set was a breeze.

“SVU was tough. It was out of my element,” Brunson admitted, before adding, “In the end, I had a lot of fun.”

Then came the part a lot of fans didn’t see coming.

Asked whether he was calling it a career in front of the camera, Brunson didn’t flinch. “I’m not calling it. I’m open. Down the line,” he said, describing these offers as “once-in-a-lifetime opportunities,” adding, “I can’t really pass these up.”

The “SVU” spot capped a whirlwind offseason that also saw Brunson host the Season 52 premiere of “Saturday Night Live” in September.

It’s been a stretch of headlines away from the court, too, including when he wouldn’t confirm a trip to Donald Trump’s White House.

His refusal said a lot as the Knicks owner James Dolan announced the team had already said yes.

As for whether Hollywood calls again, Brunson isn’t in a rush. With a title defense to worry about, he kept it simple. “We’ll see how it goes,” he said. “It was fun.”

"Blew a 0.25 and started yelling at me" –– Detective Madison aka Jalen Brunson to Mariska Hargitay on Law & Order SVU With cameo from Rick Brunson pic.twitter.com/18bDIOQxtp

scraped.title: Trump Flaunts His Access to Putin and Xi to Impress Wealthy Investors, But His Show-and-Tell Raises Uncomfortable Questions
scraped.description: Donald Trump’s private cryptocurrency gala draws scrutiny over how he showcases his presidential relationships before investors.
scraped.author: Angelina Velasquez
scraped.h1: Trump Flaunts His Access to Putin and Xi to Impress Wealthy Investors, But His Show-and-Tell Raises Uncomfortable Questions
scraped.body_text:
Donald Trump’s private cryptocurrency gala draws scrutiny over how he showcases his presidential relationships before investors.

Donald Trump is recycling old news for financial gain.

His most devoted supporters are eager to spend money to be in Trump’s presence.

However, the 80-year-old president doesn’t show up at non-White House events simply to enjoy the company of others.

He often seems intent on maintaining his image as a worthy investment among the wealthy and powerful.

Trump’s Nov. 22 appearance at a cryptocurrency gala held at the Trump National Golf Club in Potomac Falls, Virginia, has people dissecting what some see as a new low in his approach to courting admiration.

A reported 185 investors with the largest holdings of the $Trump meme coin gathered at the event.

The Republican launched the digital currency days before his January 2025 inauguration.

Since then, Trump and his family have reportedly earned more than $2 billion from their various cryptocurrency ventures, according to estimates cited by NPR and Reuters.

The “Veto King of the World” gifted attendees Trump watches and fragrances, pushed his Super Intelligence agenda during the dinner, and then tried to impress them by flaunting photos of world leaders he considers friends.

Trump held up multiple photos of himself with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin during their Nov. 19 summit in Asia.

“This is a serious couple of days,” Trump said. “This is a picture of the three of us.”

The crowd of Oohs” and “woohoos” then rang out as he expect.

“I didn’t have to make a speech. I could have done this,” the U.S president added, half-joking that his keynote address was unnecessary.

“I’m getting a much bigger response. My remarks are fine, but this is getting a much bigger response. I got a lot of other pictures. I could just hold up the pictures all night long.”

The social media crowd was not as easily persuaded by his show-and-tell moment. Instead, Threads users viewed the presentation as a pitiful attempt to boost his ego.

“His staff print these things out for him in order to soothe him. Seeing these images are meaningful to him. He then presents it to others as evidence of his achievements,” read one assessment.

“They say a way to a man’s heart is through his stomach and a way to Trump’s heart is through his ego and he falls for it hook, line and sinker!” a Threads user stated.

The pile-on continued with comments like, “He thinks he finally has friends that really like him.”

Trump’s affinity for profits led a fourth person to theorize the photos were a money grab, writing, “He’s copyrighted them and will sell them. He’s a sick mf.”

Hecklers compared the presentation to a school-age tradition with a twist. It was described as “Show-and-tell on the dementia unit.”

Trump has faced a battery of rumors about his cognitive fitness throughout his second term.

In January, Trump pushed back against chatter about his cognitive health during an interview with New York magazine.

The subject turned to his family history when he discussed his father, Fred Trump , who died at age 93 after developing Alzheimer’s disease in his late 80s.

When Trump struggled to recall the name of the disease, then-White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt supplied the word.

‘Like an Alzheimer’s thing. Well, I don’t have it,’ the president replied.”

He has repeatedly bragged about acing tests that gauge his ability to identify animals and simple objects.

The White House insists that Trump is fit for office despite growing concerns about his health, which include slurred speech, repeated naps during meetings and his strange gait.

scraped.title: US bill to speed up clean energy projects could also fast-track fossil fuels
scraped.description: Environmental science and conservation news
scraped.h1: US bill to speed up clean energy projects could also fast-track fossil fuels
scraped.body_text:
If you liked this story, share it with other people.

On Nov. 19, the U.S. Senate passed a bill that aims to speed up permitting for energy infrastructure projects.

The 62-33 vote on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) included support from pro-environment Democratic senators like Sheldon Whitehouse from Rhode Island.

The legislation would ease development for renewable energy and transmission lines, but environmental organizations warn it will also fast-track fossil fuels by undermining environmental regulations.

“A technology-neutral fast track in the hands of an administration openly hostile to clean energy is not a bargain. It is a one-way ratchet for fossil fuels,” Brad Campbell, CEO of the Conservation Law Foundation, said in a statement .

Currently, new U.S. infrastructure projects must comply with bedrock environmental laws including the Clean Water Act, Endangered Species Act, and National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). If BAAJA becomes law, those environmental hurdles will become easier to clear.

Fewer projects would require NEPA review, the time frame for environmental assessments would be shorter, and the window to sue over approved projects would shrink. Consultation on potential impacts to endangered species would also be shortened.

Proponents of the bill say those changes would ease renewable energy development and lower U.S. carbon emissions.

“BAAJA is a big step forward in our fight against climate change,” Whitehouse, who co-sponsored the bill, wrote on social media . “The bill lowers emissions by 1.5 gigatons through 2040.”

However, the weakened environmental review would also apply to fossil fuel projects and data centers. In an open letter , more than 120 scientists urged the House of Representatives to reject the bill.

On land , BAAJA could lower barriers for oil, gas and mining projects on public and tribal lands. Several Native American organizations have condemned the bill.

At sea, BAAJA would “roll back ocean and wildlife protections, opening the door to more offshore oil and gas drilling, more pollution, and greater threats to marine life,” U.S.-based NGO Oceana said in a statement.

Section 1401 of the bill, also known as the “project certainty” provision, would bar agencies from making changes to permits once they’ve been granted.

“Once issued, these approvals would be nearly impossible to revisit in the future, even if they were expedited, legally flawed, or if new science uncovers serious harm,” Oceana said in a statement .

Sabrina Suluai-Mahuka, founder of Finafinau, an environmental NGO based in American Samoa, told Mongabay by email that she welcomes economic development but not at the cost of jeopardizing American Samoa’s existing ocean-based economy. The U.S’s first-ever offshore critical mineral lease sale took place off America Samoa on Nov. 19, the same day BAAJA cleared the Senate.

“If progress requires weakening environmental protections, diminishing Indigenous voices, and asking communities with limited political power to shoulder disproportionate risks, then perhaps we need to reconsider our definition of progress,” she said.

The House of Representatives is expected to vote on the legislation next week.

items.title: A retired cranberry bog is helping Nantucket fight flooding
items.summary: As warming temperatures made cranberry farming more difficult, one group restored a former bog to its natural wetland state.

scraped.author: YCC Team
scraped.h1: A retired cranberry bog is helping Nantucket fight flooding
scraped.body_text:
Yale Climate Connections

Transcript:

For more than a century, the cranberries on many Thanksgiving tables came from Nantucket Island in Massachusetts.

Karen Beattie is with the Nantucket Conservation Foundation , which has grown cranberries for decades. She says they used to thrive in the island’s wetlands and cool climate.

Beattie: “Cranberries are a northern plant species, and they require cold winters and cooler summers.”

But global warming is making it harder to grow them on Nantucket. So her group decided to stop farming cranberries in an area called Windswept Bog and to instead restore the former farm as a wetland.

First, crews scraped off thick layers of sand that growers had spread to promote cranberry growth.

And they filled in drainage channels that crisscrossed the bog. So now water flows naturally across the area.

Beattie: “It’s creating sort of meandering flow paths that slow the movement of water.”

Beattie says wetland plants and soils filter polluted runoff before it flows toward Nantucket Harbor.

And by soaking up water like a sponge, the wetland reduces the risk of nearby flooding, as seas rise and storms grow more extreme.

So the retired cranberry bog is now helping build Nantucket’s resilience to climate change.

scraped.author: Jessica Corbett
scraped.h1: Armed Conflict Hinders Efforts to Contain Deadly Ebola Outbreak in the Congo
scraped.body_text:
The outbreak has killed more than 5,900 people, while fighting prevents health workers from reaching affected communities.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation .

Three months after the United Nations senior Ebola coordinator warned that the outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo was “growing exponentially,” government data showed Thursday that confirmed cases have topped 12,000 and left over 5,900 people dead.

The epidemic’s figures still rank behind the 2014-16 West African outbreak — which infected more than 28,600 people and killed over 11,000 — but it is “the deadliest of Congo’s 17 outbreaks and is on track to surpass the death toll” from a decade ago, according to The Associated Press , which published a series of graphs demonstrating how fast-growing this crisis is.

Since the outbreak — caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus — was declared in May, it has spread to eight of the DRC’s 26 provinces. Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data recently revealed that just 15% of new cases come from contacts known to health authorities, and a Reuters analysis of satellite ⁠imagery found the death toll may be underestimated in two hard-hit areas.

Dozens of residents in eastern Congo say they have been unable to locate the bodies of relatives who died in the ongoing Ebola outbreak, while others say loved ones have been buried without their knowledge https://t.co/o5tKFPtRTS pic.twitter.com/PdCpb9Wa6R

The World Health Organization (WHO) said last Friday that “no new cases have been reported from Kenya or Nigeria ; and no new country has reported confirmed cases,” but “the high-level transmission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo calls for continued need for readiness in the region, including cross-border surveillance, points of entry monitoring, timely case detection, and coordinated preparedness and response measures.”

The response in the DRC has been hindered by lack of community trust in authorities, poor infrastructure , and armed conflict, particularly between the army and the Convention for the Popular Revolution (CRP) — one of dozens of militant groups in the resource-rich eastern part of the country, and led by Thomas Lubanga, who was convicted⁠ of conscripting child soldiers by the International Criminal Court in 2012.

Summarizing remarks from Dr. Catherine Smallwood, the WHO’s incident manager in the DRC, the AP reported Wednesday that “the fighting between the army and rebel groups has prevented teams from reaching some communities, disrupted monitoring of people exposed to the virus, and left some treatment centers with fewer staff.”

According to the AP :

Smallwood said that about a dozen people, including two WHO personnel and Congolese health officials, were evacuated to Bunia on Tuesday after three full days trapped in a hospital in Akwe, northeast of the provincial capital, amid intense crossfire.

“They were caught really in the crossfire, very intense fighting, and we managed to evacuate them,” Smallwood said.

WHO temporarily moved its Mongbwalu team and partner staff to Bunia after fighting disrupted road access, Smallwood said. Mongbwalu, a mining town northwest of Bunia, is where the outbreak was first detected in May.

The United Nations Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (MONUSCO) said Wednesday that “the security situation has deteriorated significantly in several localities” due to clashes between DRC forces and the CRP, and Bangladeshi peacekeepers helped with that evacuation of health workers .

UN peacekeepers faced “significant logistical challenges,” including “difficult terrain, poor road conditions, and the fragile state of a wooden bridge,” before they reached the healthcare workers, who were evacuated by air to Bunia, MONUSCO noted.

“These healthcare workers, who are actively involved in the response to the Ebola outbreak, play a vital role in assisting communities already weakened by violence and displacement,” the mission said. “This intervention is part of MONUSCO’s support for Ebola response efforts, particularly through the protection of healthcare personnel and the facilitation of safe access to healthcare for populations affected by violence.”

. @WHO staff, @MinSanteRDC and other colleagues have been safely evacuated from the hospital in Akwe, Ituri Province, where they were sheltering amid fierce conflict for over three days. They have been brought to safety thanks to combined efforts across health, government and…

After the evacuation, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus thanked all those involved and stressed that “healthcare, health workers, Ebola responders, and humanitarian [aid] must be protected at all times!”

scraped.title: Genocide, Displacement and Malnutrition Threaten Pregnancies in Gaza
scraped.description: Doctors in Gaza report rising congenital abnormalities as pregnant women face exposure to bombs and toxic substances.
scraped.author: Tareq S. Hajjaj
scraped.h1: Genocide, Displacement and Malnutrition Threaten Pregnancies in Gaza
scraped.body_text:
Doctors in Gaza report rising congenital abnormalities as pregnant women face exposure to bombs and toxic substances.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation .

This article was originally published in Mondoweiss.

Faiqa al-Arini, 33, gave birth to her first child on October 19 at Al-Awda Maternity Hospital in central Gaza. She was forced to deliver early, at the beginning of her ninth month of pregnancy, after developing high blood pressure.

Al-Arini gave birth to a baby girl through a cesarean section. They named her Nour. After the delivery, the new mother remained in the intensive care unit while the newborn was transferred to the neonatal ward. Al-Arini did not see her daughter at all that first day.

Whenever she asked, “Where is my baby?” the nurses and her family members reassured her that the infant was in the neonatal ward.

The following day, Al-Arini began to feel that something was wrong. She recalled not hearing her daughter cry when she was born. She started questioning her family and was determined to get up and look for the baby herself if the nurses did not bring her. Eventually, her husband, Muhammad Abdel Jawad, 37, confronted her with the news.

“You know it is better to hear this from us than from someone else,” he told her. “Our baby has a congenital deformity. She was born without hands.”

Abdel Jawad had seen his daughter immediately after her birth. When he had asked the doctors about the main factors that could cause such abnormalities in newborn babies, the doctors pointed to the dust from missiles, toxic chemicals, and the unhealthy environment where displaced people are forced to live across the Gaza Strip.

According to Gaza’s Ministry of Health, the number of recorded congenital abnormalities among newborns has been increasing year after year. The ministry confirmed that 260 cases of congenital abnormalities had been recorded among newborns by the end of September 2026, compared with 184 cases in 2022. The number of recorded cases reached 322 in 2025, representing a 75% increase over a three year time period. However, the Ministry of Health says these figures alone do not establish the rate of congenital abnormalities among newborns or determine their causes.

Ashraf Qeshta, an obstetrics and gynecology specialist at Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis, says that the number of cases of miscarriage and congenital abnormalities among pregnant women has exceeded normal levels. He attributes this to several factors produced by the genocide, most notably the inhalation of toxic gases, exposure to missile remnants, living in an unhealthy environment, malnutrition, and other hardships imposed by war.

“We are seeing a significant number of congenital abnormalities. For example, babies are being born without skulls, others without limbs, and some with serious health problems, such as non-functioning or damaged kidneys, or heart defects,” Qeshta told Mondoweiss .

Even in cases where doctors believe that the congenital abnormality is caused by exposure to bombs and toxic substances, proving this requires advanced medical testing, sophisticated equipment, and qualified specialists. According to Qeshta, these are precisely the resources the Ministry of Health lacks, making it difficult to investigate and establish the different causes with scientific certainty.

Al-Arini said her pregnancy was extremely difficult. She was repeatedly displaced from one place to another and faced severe economic hardship, including famine, as her pregnancy began during the final months of the famine in 2025.

“Like all women in the Gaza Strip, we live under the same conditions,” al-Arini said. “We are displaced, we go hungry, we live in fear, and we narrowly escape death almost every day. Bombs and missiles explode beside us, and shrapnel flies over us. This is the reality for all women in Gaza.”

“But the effects of all these things are now beginning to show on us. I am happy that I gave birth to a girl, and I love her very much. I had indeed wished she would be born with limbs, but their absence does not make her any less my daughter, nor does it change anything about my feelings toward her. However, it makes me think deeply about the condition of our homeland, and about how even giving birth here has become fraught with danger. A baby can be born with congenital abnormalities because of the conditions we are living in,” she said.

A report published by Human Rights Watch on January 28, 2025, documented the grave health and humanitarian risks that pregnant women in the Gaza Strip are facing as a result of the siege, destruction of healthcare facilities, shortages of food, water, and medicine, and Israel’s genocidal war.

The report noted that pregnant women in Gaza face a severe shortage of medical care before, during, and after pregnancy, in addition to malnutrition, dehydration, and anemia. They also struggle to reach hospitals and obtain the medical examinations, vitamins, and supplements necessary for a healthy pregnancy.

The report added that the deterioration of maternity and childbirth services had increased the risks of complications, including bleeding, preeclampsia, and infections, amid shortages of incubators and medical supplies. These conditions threaten the lives of mothers, fetuses, and newborn babies alike.

In addition, a report issued by the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) on August 7, 2026, presented the findings of a survey conducted between June 2 and June 16. The survey covered a sample of 1,335 children and found that 12.2% suffered from stunting relative to their age as a result of chronic malnutrition and inadequate access to sufficient food.

Farah Abu Mustafa, 25, lives in the al-Mawasi area of Khan Younis with her nine-month-old daughter, Zainab. Abu Mustafa’s pregnancy was fraught with unexpected hardships, repeated displacement, daily bombardment, witnessing people die, and exposure to gases and missile remnants.

Abu Mustafa says her daughter, Zainab, was born under difficult circumstances marked by deprivation of food and a lack of medical services during pregnancy. Since her birth, she has spent almost as much time in the hospital as she has in the tent of their displacement camp.

Zainab is suffering from malnutrition, brain atrophy, delayed neurological and muscular development, and recurrent seizures. When she’s in the hospital, her weight and health improve because of the care she receives. But as soon as the family returns to the tent in al-Mawasi, Khan Younis, her condition deteriorates again.

Abu Mustafa says her daughter requires specialized medical care and strict adherence to medications and treatment. But in the tents, she can barely provide her with something to sleep on, let alone a clean and suitable place to recover.

“This is the life of displacement,” Abu Mustafa said. “Even the simplest things require a miracle for us to obtain them. Everything around us is crushing and grinding down displaced people.”

Abu Mustafa also points out that even preventive treatments intended to reduce the risk of congenital abnormalities are not available in pharmacies or easily accessible.

“Our Israeli occupier is waging war on the very air we breathe,” she said. “It is creating an environment conducive to diseases, congenital abnormalities, and miscarriages. Every woman I know has experienced a miscarriage, and I know many women who have given birth to babies with congenital abnormalities.”

“The occupation wants to eliminate generations, not just leave them with deformities,” she said.

scraped.title: The FCC Approves SpaceX’s Plan for 1 Million Space Satellites
scraped.description: Environmental advocates warn that expanding satellites will impact “everyday lives as well as the future of our planet.”…
scraped.author: Julia Conley
scraped.h1: The FCC Approves SpaceX’s Plan for 1 Million Space Satellites
scraped.body_text:
Environmental advocates warn that expanding satellites will impact “everyday lives as well as the future of our planet.”

Environmental advocates warn that expanding satellites will impact “everyday lives as well as the future of our planet.”

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

The Federal Communications Commission’s approval on Wednesday of SpaceX’s plan to deploy one million orbital data center satellites into space by 2040 was not “just irresponsible,” said one environmental advocate.

“It’s reckless,” said Tim Whitehouse, executive director of Public Employees for Environmental Responsibility. “The potential for these projects to degrade the atmosphere with pollution and debris and harm wildlife needs to be carefully considered before licensing these projects.”

Whitehouse was among the critics who noted that the approval had been granted without an environmental review, which is required by the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA).

FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said the deployment of one million “orbital space modules,” which SpaceX has said would form a new data center constellation called “Starmind,” would open “a bold new frontier” and allow the U.S. to lead “the world into the era of super intelligence.”

The satellites would process massive amounts of data to be used on Earth, according to SpaceX, the space exploration company led by Republican megadonor Elon Musk .

The environmental legal group Earthjustice said they also risk “changing our atmosphere, disrupting our daily activities that rely on satellites currently operating, disturbing wildlife, and fundamentally altering our night sky,” and denounced the commission for releasing the decision as families across the U.S. were preparing to celebrate Thanksgiving.

“Drastically expanding satellites in space has a direct impact on people’s everyday lives as well as the future of our planet,” said Jan Hasselman, senior attorney at Earthjustice. “Agencies that authorize companies looking to space as the next frontier still must operate within the law, and the law requires the FCC to consider all the risks and impacts of these proposals. It is dismaying that the FCC has ignored the law so blatantly and tried to mask the fact with a holiday filing.”

The number of satellites in space has already grown rapidly in the last several years, with 15,000 satellites in orbit in 2026 — up from 1,400 just over a decade ago.

Satellites cause emissions as they are placed in space through rocket launches, and other environmental impacts include debris from potential collisions — especially as the number of satellites grows — degradation of the ozone layer, and light pollution.

Astronomers spoke out against SpaceX’s plan earlier this year, saying it would prevent scientists from studying the night sky with modern telescopes, as well as disrupting ecosystems and humans’ biological clocks due to extreme light pollution.

On Wednesday, the American Astronomical Society (AAS) said it was “disheartened and dismayed” by the FCC’s licensing of Musk’s plan.

“The proposed constellation would significantly undermine decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities and the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky,” said the group. “The intended and unintended radio emissions from a constellation of such unprecedented size would imperil radio astronomy research, and the waste heat generated by the data centers would produce a thermal signature that would increase the infrared background of the sky and threaten the efficacy of sensitive instruments used in regular astronomy research. In addition, atmospheric pollution from the launches and reentries of so many satellites, as well as increased collision risks in orbit, remain significant concerns; both of these factors threaten research astronomy.”

“The AAS is gravely concerned about the future of federally funded astronomical research under such a fundamentally altered night sky, and the resulting waste of taxpayer dollars invested in astronomical facilities throughout the country and the world,” the AAS added.

Earthjustice emphasized that the approval came as Congress is considering the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), the permitting reform bill that would prevent future administrations from revoking licenses for projects including data centers and would block courts from enforcing environmental review laws for such projects if they had been violated previously.

“This approval to deploy a million data centers in space without any thought to the impacts on Earth is just a glimpse of what we’ll see during the next two years of [President Donald] Trump,” said Sam Sankar, senior vice president of Earthjustice. “This is great example of why Congress should not pass a flawed bill like BAAJA that would lock in terrible projects like this one. Donald Trump is going to do a lot more dirty and lawless deals over the next years, and BAAJA prevents future presidents from reconsidering them.”

scraped.title: Cranberries with a side of solar
scraped.description: Massachusetts projects pairing cranberry bogs with PV panels show how agriculture and clean energy can coexist.
scraped.author: Sarah Shemkus
scraped.h1: Cranberries With a Side of Solar
scraped.body_text:
Solar panels at a cranberry bog. Distributed Energy Infrastructure/Canary Media

This story was originally published by Canary Media and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

It’s cranberry season in southeastern Massachusetts. At bogs throughout the region, growers are collecting the ruby-red berries destined for holiday cakes, juice bottles, and cans of jellied sauce. At two farms, however, the harvesting process looks a little different: Pickers are navigating equipment around metal poles in the shade of solar panels.

The two bogs are the first in the country—perhaps the world—to grow cranberries beneath an operating solar installation. This fall marks the second season cranberries have been harvested from beneath the panels.

“We are literally proving it can be done,” said Prateek Tare, co-founder and executive vice president of Distributed Energy Infrastructure. His company constructed the two projects—a 4.4-megawatt array paired with a 13.5-megawatt-hour battery in the town of Kingston, and a 1-MW solar array in neighboring Plymouth.

Solar development is a major part of Massachusetts’ plan to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2050. The state has offered solar incentives since 2001, evolving and expanding them over the decades to drive even more development.

However, the question of where to site solar projects has become a major point of contention in the densely populated and heavily wooded state. Building on rooftops and parking lots in developed areas can increase costs and limit generation capacity. But proposals for arrays on previously undeveloped land often spark protests from locals worried about the character of their community and environmental groups opposed to disrupting ecosystems. Using pre-cleared farmland has potential, but raises concerns about taking agricultural acres out of production. Many of these same dynamics are at play in communities across the US.

“It is picking up steam, and the lessons learned have been significant.”

One of the solutions Massachusetts has been encouraging is agrivoltaics, or dual-use solar, which involves building solar panels above active agricultural operations. This strategy, which is gaining traction nationwide, allows farmland to be used for energy generation even as livestock graze or crops flourish beneath the elevated arrays.

In 2018, Massachusetts became the first state to offer a financial boost to dual-use solar projects like these. The state’s solar incentive program pays participants a set rate for every kilowatt-hour of electricity they generate; an array with a capacity between 1 MW and 5 MW currently gets a base rate of 23.17 cents. Agrivoltaic projects get an extra 9 cents per kilowatt-hour.

That can be enough money to attract developers interested in leasing land for solar arrays or, less commonly, buying property outright with an agreement to keep it in agricultural use. Farmers who agree to lease are also generally paid for their services maintaining the landscape around the panels and poles.

In Kingston and Plymouth, clean energy developer Greenbacker Renewables bought the land, which had been home to cranberry-growing operations for decades, from farmers who were ready to get out of the business. Greenbacker then worked with Distributed Energy Infrastructure to build the arrays, and hired Iain Ward, a solar consultant and longtime cranberry farmer in the area, to manage the growing operations. Both projects use a community solar model, selling power to customers interested in the lower prices and environmental benefits offered by renewable energy.

Solar can be particularly advantageous for cranberry farmers in Massachusetts, which grows more of the fruit than any state other than Wisconsin. While sheep farms and cornfields can often be sold to housing or commercial developers, cranberry bogs are protected wetlands: Even if they go out of production, they cannot be built on. Not all bogs are well placed to connect to the grid, but for those that are, solar panels can be a financial lifeline.

“This is a farm viability opportunity,” Ward said.

Figuring out how to build a solar array over a cranberry bog was a unique puzzle, Tare said. The first challenge was the foundations. For most solar arrays, the foundation goes 8 to 10 feet into the ground, he said. But in a cranberry bog, you have to go well past that to find ground solid and stable enough to hold the pilings. It took some trial and error to find the right machine to sink piles that deep. Wiring couldn’t be buried in the boggy ground, so it had to be hung overhead.

“You’re trying to figure it out from a farmer’s perspective,” said Tare, who worked closely with Ward on the design of the two projects.

The resulting installations have photovoltaic panels mounted 10 feet off the ground on an axis that allows them to tilt throughout the day to follow the sun. Pilings are spread farther from each other than standard so that harvesting equipment can be moved freely through the bog.

These successes in Kingston and Plymouth have led to more agrivoltaic opportunities for Tare’s company, including arrays in apple orchards, a cattle pasture, and a Christmas tree farm. Preliminary work is also underway at another bog.

Meanwhile, a stalled cranberry solar project in the nearby town of Carver could be resuscitated. Five years ago, a different pair of bogs there were set to become the nation’s first cranberry agrivoltaic operations. The arrays were built, and crops are growing beneath them, but the company behind the developments went bankrupt before they could get up and running. Today, the new bog owner has ​“every intention to finish them,” Ward said.

“They’re not a failure,” Ward said. ​“There is an opportunity for them to be finished.”

Tare expects future cranberry projects to get easier each time, as the company carries forward the lessons it learns. Though momentum has been slow so far, Ward expects development to accelerate soon. “It is picking up steam, and the lessons learned have been significant,” he said. ​“When you change a paradigm it takes a little time.”
